removed.quote:
Let $K$ be a probability kernel from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B(\mathbb R))$. Define
$$a(s,t):=K(s,(t,\infty)),\qquad b(s,t):=K(s,\{t\}).$$
Both maps are $\Sigma\otimes\mathcal B(\mathbb R)$-measurable. If $S_0$ and $T_0$ are measurable random elements of $S$ and $\mathbb R$ on one probability space, and $U$ is any measurable real random variable on that space, then $a(S_0,T_0)$, $a(S_0,T_0)+b(S_0,T_0)$, and $a(S_0,T_0)+U b(S_0,T_0)$ are measurable. The middle expression equals $K(S_0,[T_0,\infty))$.

source_guards.exact_current_claim: A statistic $T:(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)\to(\mathcal Y,\mathcal B)$ is **complete** for $(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta}$ if, for every measurable real-valued $g$ such that $E_\theta|g(T)|<\infty$ for every $\theta$, the conditions $E_\theta[g(T)]=0$ for every $\theta$ imply $P_\theta(g(T)=0)=1$ for every $\theta$. Integrability is part of the premise; completeness is a property of the statistic relative to the specified family.

Let $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ be standard Borel, let $\mu$ be a $\sigma$-finite positive measure, let $h:\mathcal X\to[0,\infty)$ be measurable, and let $T:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R^k$ be a measurable statistic. For $\eta\in\mathbb R^k$ put

$$Z(\eta)=\int h(x)e^{\eta\cdot T(x)}\,\mu(dx),\qquad H=\{\eta:0<Z(\eta)<\infty\},\qquad A(\eta)=\log Z(\eta).$$

For a parameter set $\Omega\subseteq H$, the associated **exponential family** has laws $P_\eta$ with density

$$p_\eta(x)=h(x)\exp\{\eta\cdot T(x)-A(\eta)\}\quad(\eta\in\Omega).$$

The normalization $A(\eta)=\log Z(\eta)$ makes each density integrate to one. In this item **full-rank** means that $\Omega$ contains a nonempty open subset of $\mathbb R^k$ and there do not exist $b\ne0$ and $c\in\mathbb R$ with $b\cdot T=c$ $\mu$-almost everywhere on $\{h>0\}$. A parameter set containing an open subset is also called regular in some sources; terminology varies, so this definition controls here. The condition is stronger than needed for the completeness theorem below but rules out redundant displayed coordinates.

For a family $(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta}$ on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$, a sub-$\sigma$-field $\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal A$ is **sufficient** if for every bounded measurable $u:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R$ there is one $\mathcal G$-measurable bounded function $v_u$ such that

$$\int_A u\,dP_\theta=\int_A v_u\,dP_\theta\quad(A\in\mathcal G,\ \theta\in\Theta).$$

For each $\theta$, this says that $v_u$ is a version of $E_\theta[u\mid\mathcal G]$, with the same pointwise version used for every parameter. Define the family-null ideal $\mathcal N=\{N\in\mathcal A:P_\theta(N)=0\text{ for every }\theta\}$. We say $\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal H\pmod{\mathcal N}$ if for every $A\in\mathcal G$ there is $B\in\mathcal H$ with $A\triangle B\in\mathcal N$. A sufficient $\sigma$-field $\mathcal G_*$ is **minimal sufficient** if $\mathcal G_*\subseteq\mathcal H\pmod{\mathcal N}$ for every sufficient $\mathcal H$.

Assume AC. Let $\mathcal E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a statistical experiment with $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R$, dominated by a
fixed sigma-finite positive measure $\mu$. Let $T:(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)\to
(\mathbb R,\mathcal B(\mathbb R))$ be a statistic. Choose the simultaneous
finite-valued nonnegative density representatives $p_\theta=dP_\theta/d\mu$
from [[def-likelihood-density]].

For $\theta_1<\theta_2$, define the extended likelihood ratio on
$U_{\theta_1,\theta_2}=\{x:p_{\theta_1}(x)+p_{\theta_2}(x)>0\}$ by
$$R_{\theta_2,\theta_1}(x)=\begin{cases}p_{\theta_2}(x)/p_{\theta_1}(x),&p_{\theta_1}(x)>0,\\+\infty,&p_{\theta_1}(x)=0<p_{\theta_2}(x).\end{cases}$$
The family has a **monotone likelihood ratio (MLR) in $T$** when, for each
ordered pair $\theta_1<\theta_2$, there is a nondecreasing Borel function
$r_{\theta_2,\theta_1}:\mathbb R\to[0,+\infty]$ such that
$R_{\theta_2,\theta_1}(x)=r_{\theta_2,\theta_1}(T(x))$ for $\mu$-almost every
$x\in U_{\theta_1,\theta_2}$. The set where both densities vanish is
irrelevant. No common exceptional null set for all parameter pairs is
asserted. This definition concerns the likelihood ratio of the full data;
$T$ need not be sufficient.

In a parametric model $\mathsf P:\Theta\to\mathcal P(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$,
two parameter values $\theta,\eta\in\Theta$ are **observationally
equivalent**, written $\theta\sim\eta$, if and only if
$$
P_\theta=P_\eta,
$$
that is, $P_\theta(A)=P_\eta(A)$ for every $A\in\mathcal A$
([[def-parametric-statistical-model]]). Equivalent parameter values therefore
give exactly the same sampling law. No distinctness of $\theta$ and $\eta$ is
required.

Suppose an experiment on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ also has a measurable
parameter space $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ ([[def-measurable-space]]). A
**Markov kernel** (or **probability kernel**) representation is a function
$$
K:\Theta\times\mathcal A\to[0,1]
$$
such that, for every $\theta\in\Theta$, the set function
$A\mapsto K(\theta,A)$ is a probability measure on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$,
and, for every $A\in\mathcal A$ and every Borel set $C\subseteq[0,1]$,
$$
\{\theta\in\Theta:K(\theta,A)\in C\}\in\mathcal T.
$$
Here the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,1]$ is generated by its relatively open
subsets $U\cap[0,1]$, where $U$ is open in $\mathbb R$. Thus the second
condition says that each event-probability map $\theta\mapsto K(\theta,A)$ is
measurable. The kernel represents the given experiment exactly when
$K(\theta,A)=P_\theta(A)$ for every $\theta$ and $A$
([[def-statistical-experiment]], [[def-probability-measure]]).

This is an optional parameter-measurable version of a model. An arbitrary
experiment does not include a measurable structure on $\Theta$ or imply this
kernel condition.

Let $\mathcal E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a statistical experiment dominated by a fixed sigma-finite positive measure
$\mu$, and let $p_\theta$ be selected finite-valued measurable
Radon–Nikodym density representatives as in
[[def-likelihood-density]]. The simultaneous selection of this arbitrary-index
family uses the Axiom of Choice. No measurability of $\theta\mapsto P_\theta$
or common exceptional null set for an arbitrary uncountable $\Theta$ is
implied.

Let $\Theta$ be open in $\mathbb R^d$, and fix a parameter $\theta$ at
which the selected family $\eta\mapsto p_\eta(x)$ is differentiable for
$\mu$-almost every $x$, with measurable coordinate derivatives. On
$\{x:p_\theta(x)>0\}$, define the log-likelihood
$\ell_\theta(x)=\log p_\theta(x)$ and the **score**
$$S_\theta(x):=\nabla_\theta\ell_\theta(x) =\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta_j}\log p_\theta(x)\right)_{j=1}^d.$$
Set $S_\theta(x)=0$ where $p_\theta(x)=0$, which is $P_\theta$-null.
For $d=1$, this is $S_\theta=\partial_\theta\log p_\theta$.

The scalar **Fisher information** is
$$I(\theta):=\mathbb E_\theta[S_\theta(X)^2]\in[0,+\infty].$$
When $d>1$ and $S_\theta$ is square-integrable, the **Fisher information
matrix** is $I(\theta)=\mathbb E_\theta[S_\theta(X)S_\theta(X)^\mathsf T]$;
its $i,j$ entry is $\mathbb E_\theta[S_{\theta,i}S_{\theta,j}]$.
The information matrix is a second-moment matrix by definition; it equals the
score covariance matrix when the score has mean zero.

The derivatives, score and information are defined relative to the specified
differentiable representative family. The Radon–Nikodym definition alone
does not supply parameter differentiability or a canonical score version.
Let $T$ and $U$ be statistics into standard Borel spaces for a family $(P_\theta)$. If $T$ is complete and sufficient and $U$ is ancillary, then $T$ and $U$ are independent under every $P_\theta$.

current_steps.exact_text: Fix a Borel set $C$ in the target of $U$. The function $q_C(y)=K(y,U^{-1}(C))$ is Borel by [F4]. For every $\theta$, the conditional-law identity [F1] shows $q_C(T)$ is a version of $P_\theta(U\in C\mid T)$. [F1, F4, given, construct]

By ancillarity [F3], $p_C=P_\theta(U\in C)$ is constant in $\theta$. Hence the bounded function $g_C(y)=q_C(y)-p_C$ satisfies $E_\theta g_C(T)=0$ for every $\theta$. Completeness [F2] implies $q_C(T)=p_C$ $P_\theta$-almost surely for each $\theta$. [F2, F3, step 1.1, given, algebra]

For any Borel $D$ in the target of $T$, $P_\theta(T\in D,U\in C)=E_\theta[1_{\{T\in D\}}q_C(T)]=p_C P_\theta(T\in D)=P_\theta(U\in C)P_\theta(T\in D)$. This holds for every pair of Borel sets $D,C$, which is the definition of independence. [F1, F3, step 2.1, given, algebra] ∎

source_guards.exact_current_claim: Assume AC. Let $(P_\eta)_{\eta\in\Omega}$ be the exponential family of [[def-exponential-family]] on a standard Borel sample space, with $\Omega\ne\varnothing$, and let $T$ be its canonical statistic. Then $T$ is sufficient.

current_steps.exact_text: Fix any $\eta_0\in\Omega$; nonemptiness is part of the family being considered. The density in [F1] is positive exactly on $\{h>0\}$ for every parameter. For $\eta\in\Omega$, dividing the densities there gives $dP_\eta/dP_{\eta_0}=\exp\{(\eta-\eta_0)\cdot T-(A(\eta)-A(\eta_0))\}$ $P_{\eta_0}$-almost surely. The right side is a Borel function of $T$. [F1, given, algebra]

The reference $P_{\eta_0}$ is a member of the model and dominates every other member because the densities have the common support $\{h>0\}$. Apply [F3] to the derivative in step 1.1; its criterion yields a common conditional law of $X$ given $T$. By [F2], $T$ is sufficient. [A1, F2, F3, step 1.1, given] ∎

source_guards.exact_current_claim:
**Input:** naturals $n,d\ge1$, a fixed design $X\in\mathbb R^{n\times d}$, a data
vector $y\in\mathbb R^n$, and a penalty $\tau^2\ge0$.

List all supports $S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,d\}$ in lexicographic order of their
length-$d$ indicator vectors, using $0<1$. For each $S$, let $V_S$ be the span
of the corresponding columns of $X$, compute $\widehat\mu_S=P_{V_S}y$, and
score

$$q_S:=n^{-1}\|y-\widehat\mu_S\|_2^2+\tau^2|S|.$$

Initialize the incumbent at the first support and scan the rest in order,
replacing it exactly when a strictly smaller score is found; on a tie retain the
earlier support. Return the selected support $\widehat S$ and fitted vector
$\widehat\mu_{\mathrm{BIC}}=\widehat\mu_{\widehat S}$. The candidate family is
finite by [[cor-cardinality-of-the-power-set]], and the fitted-vector selection
is Borel measurable by [[lem-finite-support-projection-selection-is-borel]].
This is an exhaustive combinatorial procedure, not an efficiency guarantee.

**Input:** naturals $n,d\ge1$, a fixed design $X\in\mathbb R^{n\times d}$, a data
vector $y\in\mathbb R^n$, and a natural $s$ with $0\le s\le d$.

**Candidate supports:** list all subsets $S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,d\}$ with
$|S|\le s$ in lexicographic order of their length-$d$ indicator vectors,
using $0<1$. This is a finite nonempty list because it contains $\varnothing$
and is contained in the finite power set of $\{1,\ldots,d\}$.

**Procedure:** for each candidate $S$, let $V_S$ be the span of the columns of
$X$ indexed by $S$ and compute $\widehat\mu_S=P_{V_S}y$. Compute its residual
score $q_S=\|y-\widehat\mu_S\|_2^2$. Initialize the incumbent at the first
candidate. Scan the remaining candidates in the stated order, replacing the
incumbent exactly when a strictly smaller score is found; retain the earlier
candidate on a tie. Return the selected support and its fitted vector
$\widehat\mu_s$.

Each $V_S$ is finite-dimensional, so the projections are defined by
[[def-fixed-design-projection-estimator]]. The fitted-vector selection is Borel
measurable by [[lem-finite-support-projection-selection-is-borel]]. The procedure
performs a finite exhaustive support search; no computational-efficiency claim is
made.
For every finite group action and every null law, the inclusive group-average upper-tail rank is superuniform, even when the null law is not invariant under the group.

current_steps.exact_text: For $x=1$, the transformed statistic values are $T(e\cdot1)=1$ and $T(s\cdot1)=0$, so exactly one of the two group elements has value at least $T(1)$ and $p_0(1)=1/2$. For $x=0$, both transformed values $1,0$ are at least $T(0)=0$, so $p_0(0)=1$. [F1, F2, F3, A1, given, algebra]
Therefore $\{p_0\le1/2\}=\{X=1\}$ and $P(p_0\le1/2)=9/10>1/2$, contradicting superuniformity. [F1, step 1.1, given, algebra]

The same example also defeats tie randomization: $p_U(1)=U/2$ and $p_U(0)=(1+U)/2$. Hence $P(p_U\le1/2)=9/10$, since at $X=1$ the event always occurs and at $X=0$ it requires $U=0$, an event of probability zero under the independent uniform law in the Given. [F3, A1, step 1.1, given, algebra] ∎

source_guards.exact_current_claim:
Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega=[0,1]$, let $\mathcal A$ be the countable-cocountable sigma-algebra, and define

$$P(A):=\begin{cases}0,&A\text{ is countable},\\1,&\Omega\setminus A\text{ is countable}.\end{cases}$$

For $U:=[0,1/2]$, take the uncountable class of functions $\mathcal F:=\{f_t:t\in U\}$ with $f_t(\omega):=\mathbf1_{\{t\}}(\omega)$. Every $f_t$ is measurable and $Pf_t=0$, but for one observation $Z(\omega)=\omega$,

$$\sup_{t\in U}|f_t(Z(\omega))-Pf_t|=\mathbf1_U(\omega),$$

which is not measurable because $U$ is neither countable nor cocountable.

current_steps.exact_text: By [F1], $\Omega$ is uncountable. The empty set is at most countable, and complementation exchanges the countable and cocountable alternatives, so $\mathcal A$ contains the empty set and is complement-closed. For a sequence $(A_n)$ in $\mathcal A$, if every $A_n$ is countable then [A1] makes their union countable; otherwise some $A_j$ is cocountable, and $\Omega\setminus\bigcup_n A_n\subseteq\Omega\setminus A_j$ is countable by [F2]. Thus the union lies in $\mathcal A$ in either case, proving all sigma-algebra axioms in [F5]. The assignment $P$ is well-defined: a set and its complement cannot both be countable, since their union would make $\Omega$ countable. [A1, F1, F2, F5, given]

Let $(A_n)$ be pairwise disjoint members of $\mathcal A$. If every $A_n$ is countable, [A1] makes their union countable; then $P(\bigcup_nA_n)=0=\sum_nP(A_n)$. Otherwise choose $j$ with $A_j$ cocountable. For $n\ne j$, disjointness gives $A_n\subseteq\Omega\setminus A_j$, a countable set, so [F2] makes $A_n$ countable. The union is cocountable and its measure is $1=P(A_j)+\sum_{n\ne j}P(A_n)$. Also $P(\Omega)=1$ and $P$ is nonnegative, so [F3] shows that $P$ is a probability measure. [A1, F2, F3, step 1.1, given, choose]
For each $t\in U$, the singleton $\{t\}$ is in $\mathcal A$ by [F2], so $f_t=\mathbf1_{\{t\}}$ is measurable. Its integral is $Pf_t=P(\{t\})=0$. [F2, F3, given, step 2.1]

For any $\omega\in\Omega$, if $\omega\in U$ then the index $t=\omega$ gives $f_t(\omega)=1$, while if $\omega\notin U$ every $t\in U$ differs from $\omega$ and all the function values are zero. Hence the displayed supremum equals $\mathbf1_U(\omega)$. Both $U$ and $\Omega\setminus U$ contain a nondegenerate interval and are uncountable by [F1]; therefore $U\notin\mathcal A$, so the supremum is nonmeasurable. [F1, step 3.1, given] ∎

source_guards.exact_current_claim:
For each positive integer $m$, let $N:=16^m$ be the natural number obtained by multiplying $16$ by itself $m$ times. Equip $\mathcal X_m:=\{1,\ldots,N\}$ with the uniform probability $Q_m(\{i\})=1/N$. For $k=0,\ldots,N$, define the threshold function $f_k:=\mathbf1_{\{1,\ldots,k\}}$, with $f_0\equiv0$. Put $\mathcal F_m:=\{f_0,\ldots,f_N\}$.

These are nested threshold indicators. Their VC-subgraph index is $V=2$, while for $r=m$ and $\epsilon=1/64$,

$$N(\epsilon,\mathcal F_m,L^m(Q_m))=N+1=16^m+1.$$

Thus a purported entropy bound whose right side has no dependence on $r$ is false even when the VC index is fixed.

current_steps.exact_text: The real-power definition gives $16^1=\exp(\log16)=16$. Its exponent law gives $16^{j+1}=16^j16$ for every natural $j$, so induction identifies the real power $16^m$ with the natural product defining $N$. By [F3], $$N^{-1/m}=(16^m)^{-1/m}=16^{-1}=1/16.$$ [F3, given, algebra, induction]

The subgraphs $C_{f_k}=\{(i,t):t<f_k(i)\}$ are nested in increasing $k$. A point $(1,1/2)$ belongs to $C_{f_N}$ and not to $C_{f_0}$, so a singleton is shattered. No two-point set is shattered by a nested family, since shattering would require both opposite singleton traces, which nested sets cannot realize. Therefore the VC-subgraph dimension is exactly one and its index is $V=2$. [F1, given]
For $k\ne\ell$, the functions differ on exactly $|k-\ell|$ atoms. By [F2] and [F4], $$\|f_k-f_\ell\|_{Q_m,m}=\left(\frac{|k-\ell|}{N}\right)^{1/m}\ge N^{-1/m}=1/16.$$ [F2, F4, step 1.1, algebra]

Since $1/16>2\epsilon=1/32$, a closed $L^m(Q_m)$ ball of radius $\epsilon$ centered at a class member cannot contain two distinct class members: the triangle inequality would make their distance at most $2\epsilon$. Thus every cover needs at least $N+1$ centers; taking each member as its own center gives a cover with $N+1$. This proves the exact covering number. [F2, step 2.1, algebra]

Fix any proposed right side that depends only on $\epsilon$, the VC index, and constants independent of $r$. At $\epsilon=1/64$ and $V=2$ it is a fixed finite number. By [F5], choose $m$ so large that $16^m+1$ exceeds that number. Step 3.1 then contradicts the proposed bound. The corrected bound retains $r$ in its base through $(2/\epsilon)^r$. [F5, step 3.1] ∎

source_guards.exact_current_claim:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $n=d\ge2$, let $1\le s\le n/2$, and take
the fixed design $X=\sqrt n\,I_n$. For
$$\Theta_s:=\{\theta\in\mathbb R^n: |\{j\in\{1,\ldots,n\}:\theta_j\ne0\}|\le s\},$$
observe $Y=X\theta+\varepsilon$ with one common noise law
$\varepsilon\sim N_n(0,\sigma^2I_n)$, where $\sigma>0$. For Borel fitted-vector
estimators $T:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n$, define
$$R^*_{n,s}:=\inf_{T\ \mathrm{Borel}}\ \sup_{\theta\in\Theta_s} \mathbb E_\theta\left[\frac1n\|T(Y)-X\theta\|_2^2\right].$$
Then for $C=32(4+2\log6)$,
$$\frac{\sigma^2s\log(en/s)}{200000n} \le R^*_{n,s} \le\sup_{\theta\in\Theta_s}\mathbb E_\theta\left[ \frac1n\|\widehat\mu_s(Y)-X\theta\|_2^2\right] \le C\frac{\sigma^2s\log(en/s)}n,$$
where $\widehat\mu_s$ is the constrained support-search fitted vector. Thus
this Gaussian orthogonal-sequence model has a matching minimax rate up to
universal constants. The sparse upper-bound theorem itself is choice-free; this corollary
assumes AC for its Gaussian law and Fano lower-bound suppliers.

current_steps.exact_text: By [F3], the noise satisfies the centered vector proxy condition required by [F1]. The support-search fitted vector is Borel by [F2], so it is an admissible estimator for [F6]. Applying [F1] at each $\theta\in\Theta_s$ and taking the supremum and then the infimum gives the upper bound. [A1, F1, F2, F3, F6, algebra]

Fix any Borel fitted-vector estimator $T$. Put $Z=Y/\sqrt n$ and $S(z)=T(\sqrt n z)/\sqrt n$, which is Borel by [F8]. Under the independent realization in [F4], the coordinates of $Z$ are coordinatewise measurable affine transforms of independent standard normals. By [F7], they remain independent and have laws $N(\theta_j,\sigma^2/n)$, exactly the sequence experiment in [F5]. Applying [F5] to the Borel estimator $S$ gives $$\sup_{\theta\in\Theta_s}\mathbb E_\theta\|S(Z)-\theta\|_2^2 \ge\frac{\sigma^2s\log(en/s)}{200000n}.$$ [A1, F4, F5, F7, F8, algebra]

Since $X=\sqrt n I_n$, pointwise $$\frac1n\|T(Y)-X\theta\|_2^2 =\left\|\frac{T(Y)}{\sqrt n}-\theta\right\|_2^2 =\|S(Z)-\theta\|_2^2.$$ By [F6] these pointwise losses define the respective risks. Thus every Borel $T$ has supremum fitted-value risk at least the lower bound in step 1.2. Taking the infimum over $T$ proves the minimax lower bound. [F6, step 1.2, algebra]
The upper bound in step 1.1 and the lower bound in step 2.1 give the displayed comparison, with universal constants $1/200000$ and $C$. [step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

source_guards.exact_current_claim: Let $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A,\{P_\theta\}_{\theta\in\Theta})$ be a statistical experiment with nonempty disjoint null and alternative parameter sets $\Theta_0,\Theta_1\subseteq\Theta$. Let $\mathcal S$ be a topological space with its Borel sigma-algebra $\mathcal B(\mathcal S)$, and let $S:\mathcal X\to\mathcal S$ be measurable. Write $\sigma(S):=\{S^{-1}(C):C\in\mathcal B(\mathcal S)\}$, the sigma-algebra generated by $S$ as in [[def-sigma-algebra-generated-by-a-function]]. A possibly randomized test is a measurable function $\varphi:\mathcal X\to[0,1]$ as in [[def-test-size-and-power]]. For each $\theta\in\Theta_0$, a **conditional rejection probability given $S$** is a supplied version $q_\theta$ of $E_\theta[\varphi(X)\mid\sigma(S)]$, where conditional expectation is understood as in [[def-conditional-expectation-given-a-sigma-algebra]]. The test has **conditional level at most $\alpha$ given $S$ on $\Theta_0$** if such versions can be supplied with $q_\theta\le\alpha$ $P_\theta$-almost surely for every $\theta\in\Theta_0$. The almost-sure qualification is separate under each null law; no common null set or pointwise statement at conditioning values of probability zero is asserted.

A pseudometric $d$ on a set $T$ is a nonnegative symmetric function $d:T\times T\to[0,\infty)$ with $d(t,t)=0$ and $d(s,t)\le d(s,u)+d(u,t)$; distinct points may have distance zero. For a nonempty subset $\mathcal F\subseteq T$ and $\epsilon>0$, the covering number $N(\epsilon,\mathcal F,d)$ is the least finite $k$ for which there are centers $f_1,\ldots,f_k\in\mathcal F$ such that every $f\in\mathcal F$ satisfies $d(f,f_j)\le\epsilon$ for some $j$. It is $+\infty$ if no finite cover exists. Set $N(\epsilon,\varnothing,d)=1$.

The packing number $D(\epsilon,\mathcal F,d)$ is the largest size of a finite subset $\{f_1,\ldots,f_k\}\subseteq\mathcal F$ whose distinct members have pairwise distance strictly greater than $\epsilon$. If the sizes of such finite subsets are unbounded, put $D=+\infty$; put $D(\epsilon,\varnothing,d)=0$. These conventions give the radius comparison proved in [[lem-packing-covering-number-comparison]]. The metric entropy is $H(\epsilon,\mathcal F,d):=\log N(\epsilon,\mathcal F,d)$ for nonempty classes, with $\log(+\infty)=+\infty$.

For a probability measure $Q$ on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ and a measurable real function $g$, set $\|g\|_{Q,r}:=(\int |g|^r\,dQ)^{1/r}$ for $1\le r<\infty$, using the positive-base real-power convention of [[def-real-power]]. The function $|g|$ is measurable by [[thm-arithmetic-and-lattice-operations-preserve-measurability]], and [[lem-real-power-preserves-measurability]] makes $|g|^r$ measurable, so this integral is well-defined. On a class of functions with finite such norms, $d_{Q,r}(f,g):=\|f-g\|_{Q,r}$ is a pseudometric: nonnegativity, symmetry, and zero diagonal follow from the absolute value, and the triangle inequality is [[thm-minkowski-inequality-for-integrals]]. Functions that agree $Q$-almost everywhere have distance zero. We write $N(\epsilon,\mathcal F,L^r(Q))$ for this covering number.

For measurable real endpoints $\ell\le u$ $Q$-almost everywhere, the bracket $[\ell,u]$ is the set of measurable functions $f$ satisfying $\ell\le f\le u$ $Q$-almost everywhere. Its $L^r(Q)$ width is $\|u-\ell\|_{Q,r}$. The bracketing number $N_{[]} (\epsilon,\mathcal F,L^r(Q))$ is the least number of such brackets of width at most $\epsilon$ that cover $\mathcal F$, or $+\infty$ if no finite cover exists; for the empty class set it equal to $1$. Centers of metric covers are in $\mathcal F$; bracket endpoints need not be.

For a class $\mathcal H$ of measurable real functions under a probability measure $Q$, an **envelope** $H$ means a nonnegative measurable function with $|h|\le H$ $Q$-almost surely for every $h\in\mathcal H$. Cauchy–Schwarz [[cor-cauchy-schwarz-inequality-for-l-two]] gives $QH\le\|H\|_{Q,2}<\infty$ when $H\in L^2(Q)$.

Let $(S,\mathcal A,P)$ be a probability space, let $X_1,X_2,\ldots$ be iid with law $P$, and let $\mathcal F$ be a nonempty class of measurable real-valued functions with a nonnegative measurable envelope $F$ satisfying $PF^2<\infty$. A class is **pointwise measurable** if it has a countable subclass $\mathcal F_0$ such that for each $f\in\mathcal F$ there is a sequence in $\mathcal F_0$ converging pointwise to $f$. Write $\mathbb G_n(f)=\sqrt n(P_nf-Pf)$ using [[def-empirical-process-and-rademacher-process]], and put

$$\rho_P(f,g)=\{P[(f-g)-P(f-g)]^2\}^{1/2}.$$

This is a pseudometric: distinct functions can have zero distance when their centered difference vanishes $P$-almost surely. The empirical process is **asymptotically equicontinuous in probability** with respect to $\rho_P$ if for every $\eta>0$,

$$\lim_{\delta\downarrow0}\limsup_{n\to\infty}P^*\left(\sup_{f,g\in\mathcal F:\,\rho_P(f,g)<\delta}|\mathbb G_n(f)-\mathbb G_n(g)|>\eta\right)=0.$$

Here $P^*(A)=\inf\{P(B): A\subseteq B,\ B\in\mathcal A\}$ is outer probability; bounded nonmeasurable functionals are handled by the corresponding outer expectation $E^*Y=\inf\{EY':Y'\text{ measurable and }Y'\ge Y\}$. For a pointwise-measurable class these conventions agree with ordinary probability whenever the displayed supremum is measurable.

Write $\ell^\infty(\mathcal F)$ for the bounded real-valued functions on the index set $\mathcal F$, with norm $\|z\|_{\mathcal F}=\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}|z(f)|$. The class is **$P$-Donsker** if $\mathbb G_n$, as a process in this space, converges weakly in the outer-expectation sense to a tight Borel law of a centered Gaussian process $\mathbb G_P$ with covariance

$$\operatorname{Cov}(\mathbb G_P(f),\mathbb G_P(g))=P[(f-Pf)(g-Pg)].$$

Here outer weak convergence means $E^*H(\mathbb G_n)\to EH(\mathbb G_P)$ for every bounded uniformly continuous real function $H$ on $\ell^\infty(\mathcal F)$; the outer expectation is the infimum of expectations of measurable majorants. The law is tight in the sense of [[def-tight-family-of-probability-measures]]. Finite-dimensional convergence means weak convergence of the vector of process values at every finite list of indices, as in [[def-convergence-in-distribution-of-random-elements]].

Let $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A,P)$ be a probability space, let $n\ge1$ be an integer, and let $Z_1,\ldots,Z_n$ be IID random elements with law $P$. For a class $\mathcal F$ of measurable, integrable real-valued functions on $\mathcal X$, write

$$Pf:=\int f\,dP,\qquad P_nf:=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n f(Z_i),\qquad \mathbb G_n(f):=\sqrt n\,(P_nf-Pf).$$

The map $f\mapsto P_nf-Pf$ is the centered empirical process, and $\mathbb G_n$ is its $\sqrt n$-scaled version. More generally, for independent processes $X_1(t),\ldots,X_n(t)$ whose marginal expectations are finite for each index $t\in T$, the centered process sum is

$$S_n(t):=\sum_{i=1}^n\bigl(X_i(t)-\mathbb E X_i(t)\bigr),\qquad t\in T.$$

On an auxiliary probability-space extension, let $\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_n$ be independent signs, each taking $+1$ and $-1$ with probability $1/2$, independent of the observations. The empirical Rademacher process is

$$R_n(f):=\sum_{i=1}^n\sigma_i f(Z_i),\qquad f\in\mathcal F.$$

The centered Rademacher process $\sum_i\sigma_i(f(Z_i)-Pf)$ is a distinct process; no equality between it and $R_n$ is part of this definition.

For a countable class of measurable functions, each displayed supremum of measurable sample paths is measurable. For an uncountable class, ordinary probability or expectation is used only when a specified countable subclass has the same supremum almost surely for the process in question; this is the separable-version convention used here. Otherwise state results using outer probability

$$P^*(A):=\inf\{P(B):A\subseteq B,\ B\in\mathcal A\}$$

and, for a nonnegative possibly nonmeasurable random quantity $Y$, outer expectation

$$\mathbb E^*Y:=\inf\{\mathbb E U: U\text{ is measurable, nonnegative, and }U\ge Y\}.$$

In particular, measurability of every $f$ separately does not by itself make an uncountable supremum measurable.

A **finite-group randomization setup** consists of a finite probability space $(\Omega,w)$ as in [[def-finite-probability-space-and-event]], a finite group $G$ acting on $\Omega$ as in [[def-group-action]], a statistic $T:\Omega\to\mathbb R$, and a family $\mathcal P_0$ of null probability laws on $\Omega$ that is invariant under the action. Invariance means that for every $P\in\mathcal P_0$, $g\in G$, and $A\subseteq\Omega$, $P(\{x:g\cdot x\in A\})=P(A)$. The **orbit** of $x$ is $O(x):=\{g\cdot x:g\in G\}$, a finite subset of $\Omega$. The setup itself does not assert that the action is free or that distinct group elements give distinct orbit points.

Use the empirical-measure convention of [[def-empirical-process-and-rademacher-process]]: for iid observations $X_1,X_2,\ldots$ with common law $P$, $P_nf=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f(X_i)$ and $Pf=\int f\,dP$. Let $\mathcal F$ be a nonempty class of measurable real-valued functions with a nonnegative measurable integrable envelope $F$, meaning $|f|\le F$ $P$-almost surely for every $f\in\mathcal F$ and $PF<\infty$. It is **pointwise measurable** if there is a countable subclass $\mathcal F_0$ such that every $f\in\mathcal F$ is the pointwise limit of a sequence from $\mathcal F_0$. For a pointwise-measurable class, dominated convergence [[thm-dominated-convergence]] gives $Pf_k\to Pf$ along the approximating sequence, and finite empirical averages converge pointwise, so the supremum defining the uniform law is determined by $\mathcal F_0$. The class is **$P$-Glivenko–Cantelli** if

$$\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}|P_nf-Pf|\longrightarrow0$$

in probability. It is **strongly $P$-Glivenko–Cantelli** if the same convergence holds almost surely. For an uncountable class with a countable pointwise-dense subclass, the supremum is interpreted using outer probability unless the chosen version makes it measurable. For a pointwise-measurable class the supremum is determined by the countable subclass and is measurable. That subclass has a common conull envelope bound, so the supremum is finite almost surely; after choosing a real-valued version, almost-sure convergence implies convergence in probability by [[thm-almost-sure-convergence-implies-convergence-in-probability]].

Let $M\ge2$ be an integer, let $P_1,\ldots,P_M$ be probability measures on
one measurable sample space, and let $J$ be uniform on $[M]=\{1,\ldots,M\}$.
Conditional on $J=j$, let the observation $X$ have law $P_j$. Define the
mixture law
$$\bar P:=\frac1M\sum_{j=1}^M P_j$$
and the **mutual information** of this finite experiment by
$$I(J;X):=\frac1M\sum_{j=1}^M D(P_j\|\bar P).$$
Here $D$ is the directional KL divergence of
[[def-kullback-leibler-divergence]], and logarithms are natural. Each
$P_j\ll\bar P$, since $\bar P(A)=0$ forces $P_j(A)=0$ for every $j$. Moreover,
$dP_j/d\bar P\le M$ almost everywhere, because $\bar P\ge P_j/M$ as measures;
the negative part of $t\log t$ is bounded. Thus every term in the finite sum
is well-defined and finite.

The uniform prior is part of this definition. A nonuniform prior requires its
own weights in the mixture and in the KL average.

Let $m\ge1$, let $S=(z_1,\ldots,z_m)$ be a fixed sample in a measurable space $\mathcal X$, and let $\mathcal F$ be a nonempty finite or countable class of measurable real functions such that the displayed supremum is finite and measurable on the finite sign space. Let $\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_m$ be independent uniform signs. The **one-sided empirical Rademacher complexity** is

$$\widehat{\mathfrak R}_S(\mathcal F):=\frac1m\,\mathbb E_\sigma\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}\sum_{i=1}^m\sigma_i f(z_i).$$

There is no absolute value in this definition and $0$ need not belong to $\mathcal F$. It differs from the absolute-value complexity $m^{-1}\mathbb E_\sigma\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}|\sum_i\sigma_i f(z_i)|$.

For a finite-group randomization setup with statistic $T$, the **inclusive orbit upper-tail rank** at $x\in\Omega$ is
$$p_0(x):=\frac{\#\{g\in G:T(g\cdot x)\ge T(x)\}}{|G|}.$$
If $U$ is independent of the observed data and uniform on $[0,1]$, the **tie-randomized orbit rank** is
$$p_U(x,U):=\frac{\#\{g\in G:T(g\cdot x)>T(x)\}+U\,\#\{g\in G:T(g\cdot x)=T(x)\}}{|G|}.$$
Both counts are over group elements, with multiplicity. Thus a nonfree action counts a distinct orbit point as many times as it has preimages under $g\mapsto g\cdot x$.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$ be a
statistical experiment with $\Theta\ne\varnothing$, and let
$(S,\mathcal S)$ be a measurable space. A
family of measurable maps $q_\theta:\mathcal X\to S$, one for each
$\theta\in\Theta$, is a **pivot** if the pushforward law
$$\nu_\theta(B):=P_\theta(q_\theta^{-1}(B)),\qquad B\in\mathcal S$$
is the same probability measure $\nu$ for every $\theta\in\Theta$.
Each section is a random element on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A,P_\theta)$, so
its pushforward is a probability measure by
[[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]].
No measurability in $\theta$ is asserted or needed.

For $S=\mathbb R$, a pivot is a real-valued statistic whose sampling
distribution is parameter-free. A pivot need not be invertible in the
parameter, and its inversion need not be an interval.

Fix one null probability law $P_0$. Let $S$ be a random element of a measurable space and let $T$ be a real random variable on the same probability space. Suppose a conditional law kernel $K(s,\cdot)$ of $T$ given $S$ is supplied, in the sense of [[def-conditional-law-given-a-random-element]]. On an auxiliary extension, let $U$ be independent of $(S,T)$ and have the uniform Borel probability law on $[0,1]$, characterized by $P(U\le u)=u$ for $0\le u\le1$. The **randomized conditional upper-tail p-value** is
$$p_U:=K(S,(T,\infty))+U K(S,\{T\}),$$
and its **nonrandomized upper-tail value** is
$$p_0:=K(S,[T,\infty)).$$
The strict tail and atom terms are evaluated at the realized pair $(S,T)$; the independent $U$ randomizes only within the tie mass. Their measurability, including measurability of both displayed p-values, follows from [[lem-conditional-kernel-tail-and-atom-evaluations-are-measurable]]. The inclusive tail is the sum of the strict tail and the atom at $T$. This definition asserts no existence of the conditional kernel; it is supplied as part of the input.

Let $\mathcal C\subseteq\mathcal P(X)$ be a family of subsets of an arbitrary set $X$. For a finite $T\subseteq X$, its trace is

$$\mathcal C|_T:=\{C\cap T:C\in\mathcal C\}.$$

The family $\mathcal C$ **shatters** $T$ when $\mathcal C|_T=\mathcal P(T)$. This extends the finite-ground-set trace convention of [[def-shattering-and-vc-dimension]]: any finite $T$ can be relabeled by $[|T|]$, and relabeling preserves all traces and their cardinalities.

For a nonempty class, its **VC dimension** $d(\mathcal C)$ is the greatest size of a finite shattered set if those sizes are bounded, is $0$ if no singleton is shattered, and is $+\infty$ if finite shattered sets have unbounded size. When the dimension is finite, its **VC index** is

$$V(\mathcal C):=d(\mathcal C)+1,$$

equivalently the least positive integer $V$ such that no $V$-point subset is shattered. The empty class is assigned $V=0$ by convention and is treated separately in the entropy theorem.

Let $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ be a measurable space and let $\mathcal F$ be a class of measurable real-valued functions on it. The **subgraph** of $f\in\mathcal F$ is

$$C_f:=\{(x,t)\in\mathcal X\times\mathbb R:t<f(x)\}.$$

It is measurable in $\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal B(\mathbb R)$: the coordinate lifts are measurable by [[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]], their difference is measurable by [[thm-arithmetic-and-lattice-operations-preserve-measurability]], and its strict negative set is measurable by [[thm-threshold-characterisations-of-real-and-extended-real-measurability]]. The class $\mathcal F$ is a **VC-subgraph class** when the set family $\mathcal C_{\mathcal F}:=\{C_f:f\in\mathcal F\}$ has finite VC index as defined in [[def-vc-class-of-sets-and-index]]. For nonempty $\mathcal F$, write $d(\mathcal F)$ for the greatest size of a finite shattered set (zero if none is shattered) and

$$V(\mathcal F):=d(\mathcal F)+1,$$

equivalently the least positive integer $V$ for which no $V$-point set is shattered. If no finite such integer exists, set $V=+\infty$. The empty class is treated separately and assigned index $V=0$ by convention. Thus for every nonempty finite-index class, the VC dimension is exactly $V-1$.

A **measurable envelope** of $\mathcal F$ is a nonnegative measurable function $F$ on $\mathcal X$ such that $|f(x)|\le F(x)$ for every $f\in\mathcal F$ and $x\in\mathcal X$. In an $L^r(Q)$ assertion, changing $F$ on a $Q$-null set does not change its norm or the distances in that assertion.
Let $\mathcal X=\{0,1\}$ with $P(\{0\})=P(\{1\})=1/2$. Let $Z\sim P$, and take the two-function class $\mathcal F=\{f_0,f_1\}$ with $f_0(x)=0$ and $f_1(x)=x$.

current_steps.exact_text: Direct evaluation gives $Pf_0=0$, $Pf_1=1/2$, $P_1f_0=0$, and $P_1f_1=Z$. Hence $\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}|P_1f-Pf|=|Z-1/2|=1/2$ for both possible observations. [F1, given, algebra]

If $Z=0$, then $\sup_f\sigma f(Z)=0$ for either sign. If $Z=1$, then $\sup_f\sigma f(Z)=\max(0,\sigma)$, whose uniform-sign expectation is $1/2$. Thus $\widehat{\mathfrak R}_{(Z)}(\mathcal F)=Z/2$ and its expectation over the sample is $1/4$. [F2, step 1.1, algebra]

Applying [F3] with $n=1$ and $|\mathcal F|=2$ gives $$P\left(\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}|P_1f-Pf|\ge\epsilon\right)\le4e^{-2\epsilon^2}$$ for every $\epsilon>0$. At $\epsilon=1/2$ the event has probability one by step 1.1, and the displayed estimate is the stated finite-class guarantee for this class. [F3, step 1.1] ∎

source_guards.exact_current_claim: Let $G=S_3$ permute the coordinates of $\Omega=\{e_1,e_2,e_3\}\subset\{0,1\}^3$, give the three points equal probability, take $T(x)=x_1$, and use an independent $U\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)$. Each point has a stabilizer of size two. The group-average inclusive ranks are $p_0(e_1)=1/3$ and $p_0(e_2)=p_0(e_3)=1$. The randomized values are $p_U(e_1)=U/3$ and $p_U(e_2)=p_U(e_3)=1/3+2U/3$, illustrating how tied ranks fill adjacent intervals even when each orbit point has multiple group preimages.

current_steps.exact_text: The group $S_3$ permutes the three one-hot vectors transitively. Each vector has weight $1/3$, so every permutation preserves the law and the null is invariant. The permutations fixing a given coordinate position are the identity and the transposition of the other two positions; hence each orbit point is produced by exactly two of the six group elements. [F1, F4, given, algebra]

At $e_1$, $T(e_1)=1$; two transformed values equal $1$ and four equal $0$. Thus $p_0(e_1)=2/6=1/3$ and $p_U(e_1)=2U/6=U/3$. At $e_2$ or $e_3$, the observed statistic is $0$; two transformed values are strictly greater and four tie, so $p_0=6/6=1$ and $p_U=(2+4U)/6=1/3+2U/3$. [F2, step 1.1, given, algebra]

Under the uniform null, $e_1$ occurs with probability $1/3$, and $e_2,e_3$ together with probability $2/3$. Conditional on the first case, $p_U$ is uniform on $[0,1/3]$; conditional on the second, it is uniform on $[1/3,1]$. These intervals have lengths $1/3$ and $2/3$, equal to their mixture weights, so the mixture is uniform on $[0,1]$. The inclusive rank is $1/3$ with probability $1/3$ and $1$ with probability $2/3$, which is superuniform. [F3, step 2.1, given, algebra] ∎

source_guards.exact_current_claim:
Take two independent Bernoulli samples of sizes $n_1,n_2\ge1$ and test the one-sided alternative that the first success probability exceeds the second. Under the null, all $N=n_1+n_2$ trials have a common success probability $p\in[0,1]$. Let $K$ be the number of successes in the first sample and $S$ the total number in both samples. For every integer margin $s\in\{0,\ldots,N\}$, define the supplied conditional-law kernel $Q$ by
$$Q(s,\{k\})=\frac{\binom{n_1}{k}\binom{n_2}{s-k}}{\binom{N}{s}},\qquad \max(0,s-n_2)\le k\le\min(n_1,s),$$
and set $Q(s,\{k\})=0$ outside the displayed range. For each $s$, these weights sum to one because they count all $\binom Ns$ ways to choose the $s$ success positions according to how many lie in the first sample. At margins of positive probability this is the conditional law and it does not depend on $p$; at endpoint nulls $p=0,1$, the formula also supplies a version at the other, probability-zero margins. Large values of $K$ support the one-sided alternative that the first sample has a larger success probability. For $n_1=n_2=2$ and $s=2$, the conditional masses at $k=0,1,2$ are $1/6,4/6,1/6$; the inclusive upper-tail p-values are $1,5/6,1/6$.

current_steps.exact_text: Write $\Omega=\{0,1\}^{N}$ and give each coordinate the two-point Bernoulli$(p)$ law. By [F1], a sequence with $s$ ones has weight $p^s(1-p)^{N-s}$; the product weights sum to $(p+(1-p))^N=1$, and [F2] gives the independent-trial model. For $0<p<1$, every sequence with $S=s$ has the same positive weight. [F1, F2, given, algebra]

There are $\binom{N}{s}$ sequences with $s$ successes. Exactly $\binom{n_1}{k}\binom{n_2}{s-k}$ of them have $K=k$: choose $k$ of the first $n_1$ positions and $s-k$ of the other $n_2$. These counts partition all size-$s$ subsets, so the displayed kernel weights sum to one for every $s$, and when $P_p(S=s)>0$, dividing by the total count using [F3] gives the conditional mass; the feasible range is precisely where both binomial coefficients are nonzero. At $p=0$ only $S=0$ occurs and $K=0$; at $p=1$ only $S=N$ occurs and $K=n_1$, so the supplied kernel has the required conditional law on the realized margin. At the other, probability-zero margins the same formula is simply the chosen kernel extension. [F1, F3, step 1.1, given, construct, algebra]

For $n_1=n_2=2$ and $s=2$, the feasible values are $k=0,1,2$, with counts $1,4,1$ among the six two-success sequences. Their probabilities are therefore $1/6,4/6,1/6$. Summing the masses at or above each observed value gives inclusive p-values $1,5/6,1/6$. The strict-tail-plus-tie formulas are respectively $5/6+U/6$, $1/6+2U/3$, and $U/6$; their intervals $[5/6,1]$, $[1/6,5/6]$, and $[0,1/6]$ have lengths matching the three conditional masses. [F3, F4, step 2.1, given, algebra]

For each margin $s$ with $P_p(S=s)>0$, [F5] makes the nonrandomized p-value conditionally superuniform and the randomized value conditionally uniform under the null. Rejecting when the nonrandomized value is at most $\alpha$ is therefore a conditional level-$\alpha$ test, so [F6] gives unconditional size at most $\alpha$. The test function of the randomized rule is $\varphi_\alpha(x)=P_U(p_U(x,U)\le\alpha)$; it is measurable because the sample space is finite. By finite conditioning and independence of $U$, $E_p[\varphi_\alpha(X)\mid S=s]=P_p(p_U\le\alpha\mid S=s)=\alpha$, so the randomized rule has conditional and unconditional size exactly $\alpha$. At $p=0$ and $p=1$ the only observed margin has a degenerate conditional law; its inclusive value is $1$ and its randomized value is $U$, so the same validity conclusions hold. [F3, F5, F6, step 2.1, step 3.1, given] ∎

source_guards.exact_current_claim:
Let $Y$ be a measurable real random variable on a probability space with $0\le Y\le1$ almost surely. Then, for every $\lambda\in\mathbb R$,

$$\mathbb E\exp\{\lambda(Y-\mathbb EY)\}\le \exp(\lambda^2/8).$$

This proof uses only finite product and scalar integral arguments; it does not assume the Axiom of Choice.

current_steps.exact_text: Let $X$ be any measurable real random variable. For $a<0$, $\{e^{\lambda X}>a\}$ is the whole probability space by [F6]. For $a\ge0$ and $\lambda=0$, this set is the whole space if $a<1$ and empty if $a\ge1$. For $a\ge0$ and $\lambda\ne0$, it is the whole space when $a=0$; when $a>0$, strict increase of the exponential and the inverse relation with $\log$ give $$\{e^{\lambda X}>a\}=\begin{cases}\{X>(\log a)/\lambda\},&\lambda>0,\\\{X<(\log a)/\lambda\},&\lambda<0.\end{cases}$$ Every set on the right is measurable by [F7]. Thus $e^{\lambda X}$ is measurable by the threshold characterization, with no appeal to a continuous-map Borel measurability result qualified by Countable Choice. [F6, F7, given, algebra]

Put $p:=\mathbb EY$. By [F1], $p\in[0,1]$. The shifted variable $Y-p$ is measurable because $\{Y-p>a\}=\{Y>a+p\}$ for every real $a$. Applying step 1.1 to $X=Y$ and $X=Y-p$ establishes measurability of both exponentials. Applying [F2] with endpoints $0,\lambda$ gives $e^{\lambda y}\le1-y+ye^\lambda$ for every $y\in[0,1]$; taking expectations yields $\mathbb E e^{\lambda Y}\le1-p+pe^\lambda$. [F1, F2, F7, step 1.1, given]

Define $g(\lambda):=1-p+pe^\lambda>0$ and $\psi(\lambda):=\log g(\lambda)-p\lambda$. Positivity follows from [F6] and $p\in[0,1]$. With $q(\lambda):=pe^\lambda/g(\lambda)\in[0,1]$, [F3]–[F4] give $\psi(0)=\psi'(0)=0$ and $\psi''(\lambda)=q(\lambda)(1-q(\lambda))\in[0,1/4]$. The formula also covers $p=0$ or $p=1$, since then $g$ remains positive. [given, F3, F4, F6, step 2.1, algebra]

The function $\psi''$ in step 3.1 is continuous. For $\lambda\ge0$, integrating twice by [F5] gives $\psi(\lambda)=\int_0^\lambda(\lambda-s)\psi''(s)\,ds\le\lambda^2/8$. For $\lambda<0$, the same endpoint formula written from $\lambda$ to $0$ gives $\psi(\lambda)=\int_\lambda^0(s-\lambda)\psi''(s)\,ds\le\lambda^2/8$. [F5, step 3.1, algebra]

By step 2.1 and the exponential addition formula [F8], $\mathbb E e^{\lambda(Y-p)}=e^{-\lambda p}\mathbb E e^{\lambda Y}\le e^{-\lambda p}g(\lambda)=e^{\psi(\lambda)}$; step 4.1 bounds this by $e^{\lambda^2/8}$. This proves the claim for every real $\lambda$, including $\lambda=0$. [F8, step 2.1, step 4.1, algebra] ∎

source_guards.exact_current_claim:
Let $K$ be a probability kernel from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B(\mathbb R))$. Define
$$a(s,t):=K(s,(t,\infty)),\qquad b(s,t):=K(s,\{t\}).$$
Both maps are $\Sigma\otimes\mathcal B(\mathbb R)$-measurable. If $S_0$ and $T_0$ are measurable random elements of $S$ and $\mathbb R$ on one probability space, and $U$ is any measurable real random variable on that space, then $a(S_0,T_0)$, $a(S_0,T_0)+b(S_0,T_0)$, and $a(S_0,T_0)+U b(S_0,T_0)$ are measurable. The middle expression equals $K(S_0,[T_0,\infty))$.

current_steps.exact_text: Let $\pi_S:S\times\mathbb R\to S$ be the first-coordinate projection and define $\widetilde K((s,t),C):=K(s,C)$. The projection is measurable because $\pi_S^{-1}(A)=A\times\mathbb R$ for every $A\in\Sigma$; hence [F1] and [F2] show that $\widetilde K$ is a probability kernel from $(S\times\mathbb R,\Sigma\otimes\mathcal B(\mathbb R))$ to $\mathbb R$. [F1, F2, construct]

The relation $\{(t,y):y>t\}$ is $\bigcup_{q\in\mathbb Q}(-\infty,q)\times(q,\infty)$: density in [F3] supplies a rational strictly between $t$ and $y$, and every point in a displayed rectangle has $t<y$. The relation $\{(t,y):y<t\}$ has the analogous representation $\bigcup_{q\in\mathbb Q}(q,\infty)\times(-\infty,q)$. These are countable unions of Borel rectangles by [F3] and [F4], and the equality relation is their joint complement. Therefore all three relations belong to $\mathcal B(\mathbb R)\otimes\mathcal B(\mathbb R)$. The coordinate map $(s,t,y)\mapsto(t,y)$ is measurable because inverse images of generating rectangles are $S\times B\times C$; taking inverse images now proves the two relation indicators in the domain of $\widetilde K$ are product-measurable. [F2, F3, F4]

Apply [F5] to $\widetilde K$ and the two indicator functions of the relation sets in step 1.2. Their section integrals are $\int 1_{\{y>t\}}K(s,dy)=K(s,(t,\infty))=a(s,t)$ and $\int 1_{\{y=t\}}K(s,dy)=K(s,\{t\})=b(s,t)$, so both maps are product-measurable. [F1, F5, step 1.1, step 1.2]

The rationals are countable and dense by [F3]. For $n=2,3$, rational open boxes form a countable base of $\mathbb R^n$: each point of an open set lies in such a box contained in that set. Thus each open set is a countable union of rectangles in the finite product sigma-algebra, giving $\mathcal B(\mathbb R^n)\subseteq\mathcal B(\mathbb R)^{\otimes n}$. Conversely, each coordinate projection $\pi_i:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ is continuous, so [F7] makes $\pi_i^{-1}(A)$ Borel for every $A\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R)$; finite intersections show every measurable rectangle is Borel, giving the reverse inclusion. Hence the Borel product and Euclidean Borel sigma-algebras agree in both dimensions. The map $\omega\mapsto(S_0(\omega),T_0(\omega))$ is measurable because the inverse image of each generating rectangle $A\times B$ is $S_0^{-1}(A)\cap T_0^{-1}(B)$; therefore $a(S_0,T_0)$ and $b(S_0,T_0)$ are measurable by [F6] and [F7]. The sets $(t,\infty)$ and $\{t\}$ are disjoint and their union is $[t,\infty)$, so finite additivity gives $a(S_0,T_0)+b(S_0,T_0)=K(S_0,[T_0,\infty))$. current_steps.exact_text: Starting from the given list, repeatedly take the maximum of the remaining entries and remove every index carrying that value. By [F2] each nonempty remaining list has a maximum, and each iteration removes at least one of the original $m$ indices, so the process ends after at most $m$ iterations. On that event, $R_0=(c_j+r_j)/m$ and, by [A1] and [F3], $R_U=(c_j+r_jU)/m$, uniform on the interval $I_j=[c_j/m,(c_j+r_j)/m]$ of length $r_j/m$. [F1, F2, F3, A1, given, construct]

The intervals $I_j$ are consecutive: the right endpoint of $I_j$ is the left endpoint of $I_{j+1}$, the first begins at $0$, and the last ends at $1$. These blocks form an initial segment; if the last is $j$, the sum telescopes to $(c_j+r_j)/m\le u$, and if there is no such block the sum is zero. Hence $P(R_0\le u)\le u$. $$\int_0^D\sqrt{\log N(\epsilon,T,d)}\,d\epsilon<\infty,$$

where $N(\epsilon,T,d)$ is the least number of closed $d$-balls of radius $\epsilon$ covering $T$ ([[def-covering-packing-bracketing-number-and-metric-entropy]]), then for every $t_0\in T$,

$$\mathbb E\sup_{t\in T}|X_t-X_{t_0}|\le C\int_0^D\sqrt{\log N(\epsilon,T,d)}\,d\epsilon$$

The proxy-zero case of step 1.1 applied to each increment, together with separability and [F6] for the countable intersection of probability-one events, makes the supremum zero. Assume $D>0$. Since the specified countable dense set is listed, choose the first finite tuple under its induced enumeration that is an $\epsilon_k$-net and has cardinality at most this cover size; such a tuple exists by the construction. Denote it by $T_k$. For each $t$, choose the least-index point $\pi_k(t)\in T_k$ within $\epsilon_k$. These canonical choices across scales require no choice axiom. Put $T_0^{(0)}=\{t_0\}$ and $\pi_0(t)=t_0$. [F1, F6, step 1.1, given, construct]

For a finite subset $A\subset T_0$, telescope $X_t-X_{t_0}$ through $\pi_1(t),\ldots,\pi_m(t)$ for every $t\in A$. At level $1$ there are at most $|T_1|$ increments, each with proxy at most $D^2$; for $k\ge2$ there are at most $|T_k||T_{k-1}|$ increments, each with proxy at most $(\epsilon_k+\epsilon_{k-1})^2=(3\epsilon_k)^2$. Letting $m\to\infty$ for this fixed finite $A$ removes the residual. Let $M\ge2$ be finite, let $P_1,\ldots,P_M$ be sample laws on one
measurable space, and let $t_1,\ldots,t_M$ lie in a metric space

$\rho(t_j,t_l)\ge\Delta>0$ whenever $j\ne l$. Let $J$ be uniform on
$[M]=\{1,\ldots,M\}$, with conditional observation law $P_j$ given $J=j$.
For any probability reference law $Q$, define
$$K_Q:=\frac1M\sum_{j=1}^M D(P_j\|Q)\in[0,+\infty].$$

with squared metric loss $\rho(a,t_j)^2$, its uniform average risk and its
maximum risk are each at least
$$\frac{\Delta^2}{4} \left(1-\frac{K_Q+\log2}{\log M}\right).$$
The minimax risk over all randomized estimators obeys this bound as well.
When $K_Q=+\infty$, the displayed lower bound is interpreted as $-\infty$
and is vacuous. Logarithms are natural.

[A1, F1, F2, F3, F4, given, algebra]

Let $L$ be any randomized decision in $[M]$ based on $X$, with $q_l(x)=P(L=l\mid X=x)$ given by its probability kernel. Put $w_l=\int q_l\,d\bar P$. When $w_l>0$, the conditional probability vector of $J$ given $L=l$ has entries $\eta_{lj}=w_l^{-1}\int q_l(x)\pi_j(x)\,\bar P(dx)$. Apply Jensen to $u\mapsto u\log u$ for each coordinate under the probability measure $q_l\,d\bar P/w_l$, sum over $j$, and use $\sum_j\pi_j=\sum_j\eta_{lj}=1$. The result is $H(\eta_l)\ge w_l^{-1}\int q_l(x)H(\pi(x))\,\bar P(dx)$. Multiplication by $w_l$ and summation over positive $w_l$ yields $H(J\mid L):=\sum_lw_lH(\eta_l)\ge\int H(\pi(x))\,d\bar P$; zero-probability outputs contribute zero. Hence $\log M-H(J\mid L)\le I(J;X)$ by step 1.1. [F1, F3, F4, F5, step 1.1, algebra]

If some $P_j\not\ll Q$, then $K_Q=+\infty$ and the bound is vacuous. Otherwise write $r_j=dP_j/dQ$. If the positive part of $r_j\log r_j$ has infinite integral, then $D(P_j\|Q)=+\infty$; if it is finite, the negative part is finite by [F2] and Jensen [F3] for the convex function $u\log u$ gives $D(P_j\|Q)=\int r_j\log r_j\,dQ\ge0$. [F7] makes this product law invariant under swapping the two coordinates in any selected pair. The product rectangles form a generating pi-system and the finite product spaces are sigma-finite, so [F3] and the rectangle identity in step 1.2 imply $r\,dQ=P$ on the entire product sigma-algebra. Therefore $r=dP/dQ$ as a Radon–Nikodym class. [A1, F3, F4, step 1.2]

Each $r_i$ is finite $Q_i$-almost everywhere because $\int r_i\,dQ_i=1$, and $P_i(\{r_i=0\})=\int_{\{r_i=0\}}r_i\,dQ_i=0$; thus $0<r_i<\infty$ $P_i$-almost everywhere. Therefore [F6] gives $\log r=\sum_{i=1}^n\log r_i(x_i)$ $P$-almost everywhere. Each $\log r_i$ has integrable negative part by [F1], and the negative part of their finite sum is bounded by the sum of those negative parts. Split each summand into positive and negative parts: Tonelli factors each nonnegative part through the product law, and Fubini applies to the negative parts, which are integrable. Hence, allowing $+\infty$ for positive parts, $\int\log r\,dP=\sum_{i=1}^n\int\log r_i\,dP_i=\sum_{i=1}^nD(P_i\|Q_i).$ By [F1] and step 2.1 the left side is $D(P\|Q)$, proving the claim. [A1, F1, F5, F6, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

source_guards.exact_current_claim:
Let $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A,Q)$ be a probability space, let $1\le r<\infty$, and let $\mathcal F$ be a nonempty VC-subgraph class of measurable real functions with finite VC index $V$. Suppose a measurable envelope $F$ satisfies $|f(x)|\le F(x)$ for every $f\in\mathcal F$ and $x\in\mathcal X$, and

$$0<\|F\|_{Q,r}:=\left(\int F^r\,dQ\right)^{1/r}<\infty.$$

For every $0<\epsilon<1$, put $K_0:=3e^2/(e-1)$ and $K:=4K_0$. Then

$$N\!\left(\epsilon\|F\|_{Q,r},\mathcal F,L^r(Q)\right)\le\left[K(2/\epsilon)^r\log\!\left(3e(2/\epsilon)^r\right)\right]^{V-1}\le\left(\frac{A}{\epsilon}\right)^{ArV},\qquad A:=12eK+2.$$

The exponent in the first bound is the finite-r logarithmic form. No Axiom of Choice or Countable Choice is used in this proof.

current_steps.exact_text: Put $M:=\int F^r\,dQ=\|F\|_{Q,r}^r$. By [F8] $F^r$ is measurable; the hypotheses give $0<M<\infty$. By [F7], the density $F^r/M$ is measurable. Define $R$ by $dR=(F^r/M)\,dQ$; its total mass is one by [F4]. [F4, F7, F8, given, algebra]

Set $\delta:=\epsilon^r/2^{r+1}$. Then $0<\delta<1$, so [F9] supplies an integer $J\ge1$ with $1/J\le\delta$. Use the grid $U_J$ and probability $\nu_J$ of [F6], and form the product probability $\widetilde Q:=R\otimes\nu_J$ on $\mathcal X\times U_J$ using [F5]. [F5, F6, F9, given, algebra, step 1.1]

Let $X_+:=\{x:F(x)>0\}$ and define $A_f:=\{(x,u):x\in X_+,\ uF(x)<f(x)\}$ for $f\in\mathcal F$. The coordinate projections are measurable because their preimages of measurable sets are rectangles; hence [F7] makes $X_+$ and each $A_f$ product-measurable. On $X_+\times U_J$, the map $\psi(x,u):=(x,F(x)u)$ is injective and $A_f=\psi^{-1}(C_f)$. If a finite set of pairs is shattered by $\{A_f:f\in\mathcal F\}$, its image under $\psi$ is a same-size set shattered by $\{C_f:f\in\mathcal F\}$. Thus the nonempty set class $\mathcal C_J:=\{A_f:f\in\mathcal F\}$ has finite VC index $V_J\le V$. [F1, F7, given, step 2.1]

Fix $f,g\in\mathcal F$. For $x\in X_+$, put $a(x):=\min(f(x),g(x))/F(x)$ and $b(x):=\max(f(x),g(x))/F(x)$. The envelope gives $-1\le a(x)\le b(x)\le1$, and the section $(A_f\triangle A_g)_x$ is exactly $\{u\in U_J:a(x)\le u<b(x)\}$. By [F6], its $\nu_J$-mass differs from $|f(x)-g(x)|/(2F(x))$ by at most $1/J$. The set $X\setminus X_+$ has $R$-measure zero, since the density $F^r/M$ vanishes there. [F6, F8, step 1.1, step 3.1, given]

Apply [F3] to $\mathcal C_J$ under $\widetilde Q$ at radius $\delta$. Since $e>1$, $K_0=3e^2/(e-1)>1$, and $\delta<1$ makes $\log(3e/\delta)>1$; thus the bracketed base is greater than one, so $V_J\le V$ yields $N(\delta,\mathcal C_J,L^1(\widetilde Q))\le\left[K_0\delta^{-1}\log(3e/\delta)\right]^{V-1}<\infty$. Choose a cover with this many centers $A_{g_1},\ldots,A_{g_k}$, each represented by some $g_j\in\mathcal F$. The cover uses finitely many centers, so this uses only finite choice. [F3, F12, given, choose, step 2.1, step 3.1]

Integrating the section estimate under $R$ and using [F5] gives $\left|\widetilde Q(A_f\triangle A_g)-\frac12\int_{X_+}\frac{|f-g|}{F}\,dR\right|\le\frac1J$. For $x\in X_+$, put $a:=|f(x)-g(x)|\le2F(x)$. If $a=0$ the inequality $a^r\le2^{r-1}F(x)^{r-1}a$ is immediate; if $a>0$ and $r>1$, [F8] raises $a\le2F(x)$ to the positive power $r-1$ and multiplication by $a$ gives it; for $r=1$ it is equality. Hence [F2] gives $\|f-g\|_{Q,r}^r\le2^{r-1}M\int_{X_+}\frac{|f-g|}{F}\,dR\le2^rM\left(\widetilde Q(A_f\triangle A_g)+\frac1J\right)$. The last inequality uses the discrepancy bound and the definition of $R$. [F2, F5, F8, F10, step 1.1, step 4.1, algebra]

For every $f\in\mathcal F$, some center satisfies $\widetilde Q(A_f\triangle A_{g_j})\le\delta$. Steps 5.1 and 2.1 then give $\|f-g_j\|_{Q,r}^r\le2^rM(\delta+1/J)\le2^{r+1}M\delta=\epsilon^rM$. Thus the function class is covered by the same $k$ centers at radius $\epsilon\|F\|_{Q,r}$, and its covering number is no larger than the set covering number in step 4.2. [step 2.1, step 5.1, step 4.2, algebra]

Put $L:=\log(3e(2/\epsilon)^r)$. From $\delta^{-1}=2(2/\epsilon)^r$ and $\log(3e/\delta)=L+\log2\le2L$ (since $3e(2/\epsilon)^r>2$, so $L>\log2$), the base in step 4.2 is at most $4K_0(2/\epsilon)^rL=K(2/\epsilon)^rL$. Since this base exceeds one, step 6.1 proves the first asserted entropy bound. [F11, F12, step 4.2, step 6.1, algebra]

Put $\eta:=(\epsilon/2)^r\in(0,1)$. For $u\ge1$, the function $h(u):=u-\log u$ has $h(1)=1$ and $h'(u)=1-1/u\ge0$; the mean value theorem [F11] gives $\log u\le u$. Hence $K\eta^{-1}\log(3e/\eta)\le3eK\eta^{-2}=3eK(2/\epsilon)^{2r}$. Let $A:=12eK+2$. From [F12], $e-1<e$, so $K_0=3e^2/(e-1)>3e>3$ and $K=4K_0>4$. Thus $x:=3eK>1$ and $A/2=6eK+1\ge x$, whence $(A/2)^{2r}\ge x^{2r}\ge x$ because $r\ge1$. This gives $3eK(2/\epsilon)^{2r}\le(A/\epsilon)^{2r}$. [F11, F12, step 7.1, algebra]

The first bound is the step 7.1 base raised to $V-1$. Since $A/\epsilon>1$, $A\ge2$, and $V\ge1$, we have $2r(V-1)\le ArV$. Thus the first bound is at most $(A/\epsilon)^{ArV}$, proving the second inequality. [step 7.1, step 8.1, algebra] ∎

source_guards.exact_current_claim:
The claim that, for every fixed $\beta>1$, $p\ge n^\beta$, $0\le q<1$, and
$c_{n,p}\le M n^{(1-q)/2}(\log p)^{-(3-q)/2}$, the minimax squared operator
risk over $\mathcal P_q(\tau,c_{n,p})$ is comparable to
$c_{n,p}^2(\log p/n)^{1-q}+\log p/n$ is false without an upper restriction on
$\log p/n$ or a cap on the risk expression.

current_steps.exact_text: Since $\log p_n\ge n^2$, $c_{n,p_n}\le M n^{-5/2}<1$ for all sufficiently large $n$; also $p_n\ge e^{n^2}\ge n^2$. The point mass at zero has zero covariance, zero off-diagonal entries, and directional tail probability zero, so it belongs to $\mathcal P_0(\tau,c_{n,p_n})$. Thus this class is nonempty. For any $P$ in it and any unit vector $v$, set $Y=v^{\mathsf T}(X-EX)$. By [F1]–[F2], $v^{\mathsf T}\Sigma(P)v=E_PY^2=\int_0^\infty P(Y^2>u)\,du \le\int_0^\infty e^{-u/(2\tau)}\,du=2\tau.$ By [F3], $\Sigma(P)$ is symmetric and $v^{\mathsf T}\Sigma(P)v=E_P[(v^{\mathsf T}(X-EX))^2]\ge0$. Taking the maximum over unit $v$ and using [F4] gives $\|\Sigma(P)\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le2\tau$. [F1, F2, F3, F4, given, algebra]

The constant estimator $\widehat\Sigma\equiv0$ is measurable on the n-sample space. By [F5] and step 1.1, $\mathfrak R_n\bigl(\mathcal P_0(\tau,c_{n,p_n})\bigr) \le\sup_{P\in\mathcal P_0}E_{P^{\otimes n}}\|\widehat\Sigma-\Sigma(P)\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2 \le4\tau^2.$ This bound is independent of $n$ and $p_n$. [F5, step 1.1, algebra]

Since $e^{n^2}\le p_n<e^{n^2}+1\le2e^{n^2}$, we have $n\le\log p_n/n\le n+(\log2)/n$, so $\log p_n/n\sim n$. Hence $c_{n,p_n}^2\frac{\log p_n}{n}+\frac{\log p_n}{n} \ge\frac{\log p_n}{n}\longrightarrow\infty.$ No positive comparison constant independent of $n$ can make this diverging expression a lower bound for the uniformly bounded minimax risk in step 2.1. This contradicts the claimed equivalence. [step 2.1, algebra] ∎

source_guards.exact_current_claim:
Let $p\in\mathbb N_0$, $n\ge p+1$, and $a<b$. A clamped knot vector is a nondecreasing finite sequence
$$\xi_1=\cdots=\xi_{p+1}=a<\xi_{p+2}\le\cdots\le\xi_n<\xi_{n+1}=\cdots=\xi_{n+p+1}=b,$$
with $\xi_j<\xi_{j+p+1}$ for every $1\le j\le n$. Empty interior ranges are omitted. The multiplicity $\mu(\eta)$ of an interior knot $\eta$ is its number of occurrences among $\xi_{p+2},\ldots,\xi_n$.

Write $\mathcal P_p$ for the real polynomials of degree at most $p$. The degree-$p$ spline space $S_{p,\xi}$ consists of functions that restrict to a member of $\mathcal P_p$ on each nonempty knot interval and whose derivatives through order $p-\mu(\eta)$ agree across each interior knot $\eta$. The convention $C^{-1}$ means that no matching condition is imposed. For this piecewise definition, take knot cells left-closed and right-open; at a knot with no matching condition, the value is the one from the cell on its right, and at $b$ use the left limit. Thus the function value at a discontinuous knot is specified.

The degree-zero B-spline is $B_{j,0,\xi}=\mathbf 1_{[\xi_j,\xi_{j+1})}$. For $p\ge1$, define recursively
$$B_{j,p,\xi}(x)=\frac{x-\xi_j}{\xi_{j+p}-\xi_j}B_{j,p-1,\xi}(x)+\frac{\xi_{j+p+1}-x}{\xi_{j+p+1}-\xi_{j+1}}B_{j+1,p-1,\xi}(x),$$
where a term with zero denominator is defined to be zero. At $b$, set $B_{j,p,\xi}(b)$ equal to its left limit. The basis and regularity properties of this recursively defined family are proved in [[thm-spline-polynomial-reproduction]].

Let $P$ be a probability measure on a measurable observation space $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$, and let $X_1,X_2,\ldots$ be IID with law $P$; IID means a common law and mutual independence of the whole family ([[def-probability-measure]], [[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]]). Let $(\Theta,d)$ be a metric candidate space with its Borel sigma-algebra ([[def-metric-space]], [[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]). For each $\theta\in\Theta$, let $m_\theta:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R$ be measurable and assume $P|m_\theta|<\infty$. Define
$$P_nm_\theta=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n m_\theta(X_i),\qquad Pm_\theta=\int m_\theta\,dP.$$

A measurable estimator sequence $\hat\theta_n$ into the Borel target $\Theta$ is an **M-estimator** if it maximizes or minimizes $\theta\mapsto P_nm_\theta$; measurability is as in [[def-estimator-sequence-in-iid-experiments]]. It is an exact maximizer when $P_nm_{\hat\theta_n}=\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}P_nm_\theta$, and an $o_P(1)$-approximate maximizer when the finite measurable gap $\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}P_nm_\theta-P_nm_{\hat\theta_n}$ is $o_P(1)$. For minimization use the gap $P_nm_{\hat\theta_n}-\inf_{\theta\in\Theta}P_nm_\theta$. The notation $o_P(1)$ is that of [[def-op-and-little-op-stochastic-bounds]].

The maximizing and minimizing forms are both included; replacing $m_\theta$ by $-m_\theta$ converts one to the other. This definition does not assert that a maximizer exists, nor that the population criterion $Pm_\theta$ has a unique maximizer. Whenever a random candidate is substituted into the empirical or population criterion, assume that evaluation is measurable and finite.

Let $\mathcal Q$ be a family of probability laws on a common measurable sample space $(\mathcal Z,\mathcal C)$, and let $\Sigma(Q)\in\mathbb R^{p\times p}$ be a specified matrix parameter for each $Q\in\mathcal Q$, with fixed $p\ge1$. Give $\mathbb R^{p\times p}$ its usual Euclidean topology and Borel sigma-algebra. An estimator is a measurable map $\widehat\Sigma:(\mathcal Z,\mathcal C)\to(\mathbb R^{p\times p},\mathcal B(\mathbb R^{p\times p}))$. Define its squared operator risk at $Q$ and the minimax risk over $\mathcal Q$ by
$$R_Q(\widehat\Sigma)=\mathbb E_Q\|\widehat\Sigma-\Sigma(Q)\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2,\qquad\mathfrak R(\mathcal Q)=\inf_{\widehat\Sigma}\sup_{Q\in\mathcal Q}R_Q(\widehat\Sigma).$$

For a family $\mathcal P$ of one-observation laws on a common measurable space $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ and an integer $n\ge1$, the $n$-observation experiment observes $n$ independent observations, each with law $P$. Its sample space is $(\mathcal X^n,\mathcal A^{\otimes n})$ and its sample law is the finite product probability measure $P^{\otimes n}$; this is the joint law of the IID family in [[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]] and [[def-independent-random-elements]]. For estimators $\widehat\Sigma:(\mathcal X^n,\mathcal A^{\otimes n})\to(\mathbb R^{p\times p},\mathcal B(\mathbb R^{p\times p}))$, define
$$R_{n,P}(\widehat\Sigma)=\mathbb E_{P^{\otimes n}}\|\widehat\Sigma-\Sigma(P)\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2,\qquad\mathfrak R_n(\mathcal P)=\inf_{\widehat\Sigma}\sup_{P\in\mathcal P}R_{n,P}(\widehat\Sigma).$$

An infinite expectation is allowed, so every measurable estimator has an extended nonnegative risk. Suprema of risks are taken in the ordered range $[0,\infty]$, with $\sup\varnothing:=0$, its least element. Thus when $\mathcal Q$ or $\mathcal P$ is empty the corresponding supremum is zero for every estimator, and its minimax risk is zero. The estimator class is nonempty because the constant zero matrix map is measurable. The operator norm is from [[def-operator-norm-on-a-finite-dimensional-inner-product-space]].

Assume AC as in [[def-regression-target-version]]. Fix a sample size $n\ge1$,
a prediction point $x\in\mathbb R$, a bandwidth $h>0$, a finite-valued
nonnegative Borel function $K:\mathbb R\to[0,\infty)$, and a fixed fallback
$a_0\in\mathbb R$. For data $(X_i,Y_i)_{i=1}^n$, put
$$D_{n,h}(x)=\sum_{i=1}^n K((x-X_i)/h).$$
The **Nadaraya–Watson estimator** of the pointwise target $m(x)$ is
$$\widehat m_{\mathrm{NW},h}(x)= \begin{cases} \dfrac{\sum_{i=1}^n K((x-X_i)/h)Y_i}{D_{n,h}(x)},&D_{n,h}(x)>0,\\[6pt] a_0,&D_{n,h}(x)=0. \end{cases}$$
For fixed $x,h,n$, this is a statistic of the observed sample with real target
$m(x)$, in the sense of [[def-statistic-and-estimator]]. The fallback is part
of the definition. Kernel regularity and bandwidth assumptions used for bias
or variance results are stated in those results.

Assume AC. Let $[a,b]$ be a bounded interval, let $(x_i,y_i)_{i=1}^n\in([a,b]\times\mathbb R)^n$, assume at least two distinct input values, and let $\lambda>0$. For $g\in W^{2,2}(a,b)$ use its unique continuous representative on $[a,b]$ supplied by the one-dimensional Sobolev representative theorem. The natural cubic smoothing spline is the unique minimizer, whose existence and uniqueness are proved in [[thm-natural-cubic-smoothing-spline-exists-uniquely]], of
$$J(g)=\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-g(x_i))^2+\lambda\int_a^b|D^2g(t)|^2\,dt.$$

The requirement of two distinct inputs is essential. The penalty is the squared $L^2$ norm of the second weak derivative; the data term uses the distinct-input interpolation convention in [[def-natural-cubic-spline]].

Assume AC as used to select the regression version. Fix a statistical experiment indexed by $\theta$, a point $x$, a real
regression target $m_\theta(x)$, and a real-valued estimator
$T_x$ of that target, meaning a measurable statistic with target space
$\mathbb R$ as in [[def-statistic-and-estimator]]. At this point, use the
squared-error loss
$$L_x(\theta,a)=(a-m_\theta(x))^2,\qquad a\in\mathbb R.$$
Its **pointwise squared-error risk** is the possibly infinite quantity
$$R_x(\theta,T_x)=\int (T_x(z)-m_\theta(x))^2\,P_\theta(dz)\in[0,\infty].$$
This is the deterministic-rule specialization of the risk in
[[def-loss-function-and-risk]]: the action space is $\mathbb R$ with its
Borel sigma-algebra, the action is $T_x(z)$, and the loss section is
measurable because it is continuous in $a$. The integral is nonnegative, so
it is defined without a finite-moment assumption.

Let $\mathcal X$ be a set, let $\mathcal A$ be a sigma-algebra on it, let $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be nonempty, and let $\mu$ be a fixed sigma-finite measure on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$. Suppose $(p_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta}$ is a specified family of nonnegative measurable densities with $\int p_\theta\,d\mu=1$. Let $P$ be the actual data probability measure; it need not equal any model law $p_\theta\mu$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). Assume $p_\theta(X)>0$ $P$-almost surely and $\ell_\theta(X):=\log p_\theta(X)$ is integrable under $P$ for every parameter considered. Expectation means integration against $P$ ([[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]).

The population log-likelihood criterion is $M_P(\theta):=\mathbb E_P[\ell_\theta(X)]$. A **pseudo-true parameter** is any maximizer $\theta^*\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{\theta\in\Theta}M_P(\theta)$. It is unique when this argmax set is the singleton $\{\theta^*\}$. The model is **misspecified relative to $P$** when $P\ne p_\theta\mu$ for every $\theta\in\Theta$. This definition does not assert existence, uniqueness, interiority, or separation of the maximizer; those are theorem hypotheses when needed.

Let $\mathsf P:\Theta\to\mathcal P(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ be a parametric
model, let $\Theta$ be open in $\mathbb R^d$, and let a supplied sigma-finite
measure $\mu$ dominate every $P_\theta$
([[def-parametric-statistical-model]], [[def-dominated-statistical-experiment]]).
Supply as part of the setup a family of nonnegative finite-valued measurable
functions $p_\theta:\mathcal X\to[0,\infty)$ satisfying
$P_\theta(A)=\int_Ap_\theta\,d\mu$ for every $A\in\mathcal A$
([[def-measure-with-density]]). Thus each $p_\theta$ integrates to one.
The density family is supplied, rather than selected from domination alone;
no choice principle, joint measurability in $(\theta,x)$, or common
exceptional null set is asserted. A supplied extended-valued probability
density can be made finite-valued by setting it to zero on its measurable
infinite-value set, which has measure zero because its integral is one.
The QMD condition is unchanged by replacing any supplied density by an
almost-everywhere equal version: for each fixed $h$, the norm in the
condition below changes only on the union of two null sets.
At an interior point $\theta_0$, the model is
**quadratic-mean differentiable (QMD)** with score $s_{\theta_0}$ if
$s_{\theta_0}:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R^d$ is measurable,
$\mathbb E_{\theta_0}\|s_{\theta_0}(X)\|^2<\infty$, and
$$
\int\left(\sqrt{p_{\theta_0+h}}-\sqrt{p_{\theta_0}}- \tfrac12 h^Ts_{\theta_0}\sqrt{p_{\theta_0}}\right)^2d\mu=o(\|h\|^2)
$$
as $h\to0$ with $\theta_0+h\in\Theta$. Values of the score on
$\{p_{\theta_0}=0\}$ do not affect this condition. The Fisher information
associated with this QMD score is
$I_{\theta_0}=\mathbb E_{\theta_0}[s_{\theta_0}s_{\theta_0}^T]$; it may be
singular. QMD is an $L^2(\mu)$ condition and does not assert pointwise
differentiability of $p_\theta$ or local mutual absolute continuity of
$P_\theta$ and $P_{\theta_0}$.

Let $n,p\ge1$ be integers and let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be independent identically distributed random vectors in $\mathbb R^p$ with finite second moments, mean $\mu=\mathbb E X_1$, and covariance matrix
$$\Sigma=\mathbb E[(X_1-\mu)(X_1-\mu)^{\mathsf T}].$$
The oracle-centered sample covariance and the sample-centered covariance are respectively
$$\widehat\Sigma_\mu=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n(X_i-\mu)(X_i-\mu)^{\mathsf T},\qquad \widehat\Sigma^\ast=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n(X_i-\bar X)(X_i-\bar X)^{\mathsf T},\quad \bar X=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nX_i.$$
For a matrix estimate $A$, squared operator loss is $\|A-\Sigma\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2$, with the operator norm of [[def-operator-norm-on-a-finite-dimensional-inner-product-space]]. This definition distinguishes the known-mean raw second moment from the estimator that removes an unknown mean.

Assume AC for the supplied density representatives in
[[def-score-and-fisher-information]] and [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. Let
$X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be iid from a dominated parametric model on an open
$\Theta\subset\mathbb R^d$, and let $\ell_n(\theta)=\sum_{i=1}^n\log
p_\theta(X_i)$. For any nested null $\Theta_0\subseteq\Theta$ for which the
maxima exist, the **likelihood-ratio statistic** is
$$L_n=2\left\{\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\ell_n(\theta)-\sup_{\theta\in\Theta_0}\ell_n(\theta)\right\}.$$

For the Wald and score statistics, specialize to a **regular equality null of
codimension $q$** at an interior point $\theta_0$: this is a null set which,
in a $C^1$ local parameter chart
$\theta=(\psi,\eta)\in\mathbb R^q\times\mathbb R^{d-q}$, is $\psi=0$ near
$\theta_0=(0,\eta_0)$. Its local tangent is the $\eta$-coordinate subspace.
Assume the QMD information $I(\theta_0)$ is positive definite. Let
$\hat\theta_n$ maximize $\ell_n$ over the full local model and
$\tilde\theta_n$ maximize it over the null, so the general likelihood-ratio
definition is $L_n=2\{\ell_n(\hat\theta_n)-\ell_n(\tilde\theta_n)\}$.

For the score statistic, assume $\log p_\theta(x)$ is differentiable in the
local chart at the parameter values where it is evaluated, and write
$s_\theta(x)=\nabla_\theta\log p_\theta(x)$. Require explicitly that this
pointwise derivative at $\theta_0$ agrees $P_{\theta_0}$-almost surely with
the QMD score; this compatibility is an assumption, not a consequence of QMD
alone. The pointwise score and its information-matrix convention are those in
[[def-score-and-fisher-information]].

Partition the score and information in $(\psi,\eta)$ coordinates:
$s=(s_\psi,s_\eta)$ and
$$I=\begin{pmatrix}I_{\psi\psi}&I_{\psi\eta}\\I_{\eta\psi}&I_{\eta\eta}\end{pmatrix},\qquad I_{\mathrm{eff}}=I_{\psi\psi}-I_{\psi\eta}I_{\eta\eta}^{-1}I_{\eta\psi}.$$
The matrix $I_{\mathrm{eff}}$ is the information for the tested coordinates
after accounting for the nuisance coordinates. If $d=q$, interpret empty-block
products as zero, so $I_{\mathrm{eff}}=I_{\psi\psi}=I$ and $C$ below is the
empty $q\times0$ matrix. If $d>q$, then $I_{\eta\eta}$ is positive definite;
for $z\ne0$, the quadratic form of $I$ at
$(z,-I_{\eta\eta}^{-1}I_{\eta\psi}z)$ equals
$z^TI_{\mathrm{eff}}z>0$. Thus $I_{\mathrm{eff}}$ is positive definite in
either case. Put
$$
U_n(\theta)=n^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^n s_\theta(X_i).
$$
For a consistent estimator $\widehat I_{\mathrm{eff},n}$ of
$I_{\mathrm{eff}}$ and a consistent estimator $\widehat C_n$ of
$C=I_{\psi\eta}I_{\eta\eta}^{-1}$, set
$U_{\mathrm{eff},n}=U_{\psi,n}(\tilde\theta_n)-
\widehat C_nU_{\eta,n}(\tilde\theta_n)$. The **score statistic** is
$S_n=U_{\mathrm{eff},n}^T\widehat I_{\mathrm{eff},n}^{-1}U_{\mathrm{eff},n}$.
For a consistent covariance estimator $\widehat V_{\psi,n}$ of the
$\psi$-block of $I^{-1}$, the **Wald statistic** is
$W_n=n\hat\psi_n^T\widehat V_{\psi,n}^{-1}\hat\psi_n$, where
$\hat\psi_n$ is the tested coordinate of $\hat\theta_n$. When a displayed
inverse does not exist, set that statistic to zero; under the regularity
conditions used in the later calibration theorem, the inverse exists with
probability tending to one. This definition gives the statistics and their
normalizations; it asserts no finite-sample or asymptotic distribution.

Let $P$ be a probability measure on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$, let $X_1,X_2,\ldots$ be IID with law $P$ ([[def-probability-measure]], [[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]]), and let $(\Theta,d)$ be a metric candidate space with its Borel sigma-algebra ([[def-metric-space]], [[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]). Fix a finite integer $q\ge1$ and a norm on $\mathbb R^q$. For each $\theta\in\Theta$, let $\psi_\theta:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R^q$ be measurable with $P\|\psi_\theta\|<\infty$. Define
$$\Psi_n(\theta)=P_n\psi_\theta=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\psi_\theta(X_i),\qquad \Psi(\theta)=P\psi_\theta.$$

A measurable estimator sequence $\hat\theta_n$ into the Borel target $\Theta$ is a **Z-estimator** if it is an exact or $o_P(1)$-approximate root: $\Psi_n(\hat\theta_n)=0$ for every $n$, or $\|\Psi_n(\hat\theta_n)\|=o_P(1)$. Measurability is as in [[def-estimator-sequence-in-iid-experiments]], and $o_P(1)$ has the convention of [[def-op-and-little-op-stochastic-bounds]]. Whenever a random candidate is substituted into an estimating equation, assume the evaluation is measurable.

Because $q\ge1$ is finite, [[thm-all-norms-on-rn-are-equivalent]] gives constants $c,C>0$ with $c\|v\|_2\le\|v\|\le C\|v\|_2$ for every $v\in\mathbb R^q$. Thus for every $\mathbb R^q$-valued sequence, convergence of the chosen-norm tails to zero is equivalent to the Euclidean $o_P(1)$ convention in [[def-op-and-little-op-stochastic-bounds]].

This definition does not infer a Z-estimating equation from an M-criterion. Differentiating an M-criterion is justified only under additional differentiability and interior-point hypotheses; a nonsmooth criterion need not have a score equation.

Let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be IID $N(\theta,1)$ and take $\theta_0=0$. This
one-dimensional model is QMD at zero with score $s(x)=x$ and information
$I=1$. For every fixed $h$, the local laws $P_{n,h}=N(h/\sqrt n,1)^{\otimes n}$
are exactly dominated by $P_{n,0}$ and
$$\log\frac{dP_{n,h}}{dP_{n,0}}(X_1,\ldots,X_n) =h\Delta_n-\tfrac12h^2,\qquad \Delta_n=\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_{i=1}^nX_i.$$
The sample mean estimator is regular, with
$$\sqrt n\left(\bar X_n-\frac h{\sqrt n}\right)\Rightarrow N(0,1)$$
under $P_{n,h}$ for each fixed $h$.

current_steps.exact_text: Let $g_\theta(x)=\sqrt{\phi(x-\theta)} =(2\pi)^{-1/4}e^{-(x-\theta)^2/4}$. By [F6] its derivative is $\partial_\theta g_\theta(x)=\tfrac12(x-\theta)g_\theta(x)$, so $\partial_\theta g_0(x)=\tfrac12xg_0(x)$. For $|\theta|\le1$, $|\partial_\theta g_\theta(x)| \le C(1+|x|)e^{-((|x|-1)_+)^2/4}=:G(x),$ whose square is integrable: it is bounded on $[-2,2]$, and for $|x|\ge2$ it is bounded by $C'(1+x^2)e^{-x^2/8}$. Substituting $x=2y$ reduces the tail integral to a constant times $\int(1+4y^2)e^{-y^2/2}dy$, finite by the second moment statement in [F2]. By [F7], $(g_t-g_0)/t=\int_0^1\partial_\theta g_{rt}\,dr$; this converges pointwise to $\tfrac12xg_0$. Its difference is bounded by $2G$, so [F5] applied to the squared difference gives convergence in $L^2(dx)$. Thus the QMD residual has norm $o(|t|)$, which is exactly the scalar QMD condition. [F1, F2, F5, F6, F7, F11, given, algebra]

The density ratio is $\prod_{i=1}^n\frac{\phi(X_i-h/\sqrt n)}{\phi(X_i)} =\exp\!\left(\frac h{\sqrt n}\sum_{i=1}^nX_i-\frac{h^2}{2}\right).$ Each density is positive, so this is a full mean-one likelihood ratio. By [F2]–[F4], the characteristic function of $\Delta_n$ is $\prod_{i=1}^n\exp\left(-\frac{t^2}{2n}\right)=e^{-t^2/2},$ so $\Delta_n\sim N(0,1)$ exactly. Comparing with [F9] proves exact LAN with $K=1$ and no remainder. [F1, F2, F3, F4, F9, F11, given, algebra]

The score is $s(x)=x$. By [F2], $E_0s=0$ and $E_0s^2=1$, so the information is $I=1$. By [F10], the general QMD-to-LAN result applies and predicts the same score and information; the direct computation below also shows the proxy is the exact alternative law. [F2, F10, step 1.1, algebra]

Under $P_{n,h}$, the variables $X_i-h/\sqrt n$ are IID $N(0,1)$.
