The same characteristic-function product using [F3]–[F4] gives $\sqrt n\left(\bar X_n-\frac h{\sqrt n}\right) =\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_i(X_i-h/\sqrt n)\sim N(0,1)$ exactly, which implies the displayed convergence. The limiting law does not depend on fixed $h$, which is regularity by [F9]. The calculation includes $h=0$ and every finite $h$. [A1, F2, F3, F4, F9, given, algebra] ∎

source_guards.exact_current_claim:
Assume AC. Let $L:\mathbb R^d\to[0,M]$ be Borel measurable, symmetric and quasi-convex, with $M>0$. For integers $N\ge2$ and $m\ge1$, put $\delta=M/N$, $C_k=\overline{\{x:L(x)\le k\delta\}}$ and
$$g_{N,m}(x)=\delta\sum_{k=1}^{N-1}\min(1,m\,d(x,C_k)).$$
For $C_k=\varnothing$ the corresponding summand is defined to be one, and for $C_k=\mathbb R^d$ it is zero. Then $0\le g_{N,m}\le L$, and $g_{N,m}$ is bounded and Lipschitz. For every nondegenerate Gaussian $H\sim N_d(b,S)$,
$$\inf_a E g_{N,m}(a-H)=E g_{N,m}(H-b),\qquad \lim_{N\to\infty}\lim_{m\to\infty}E g_{N,m}(H-b)=E L(H-b).$$
Each summand is symmetric and quasi-convex; no quasi-convexity of their sum is asserted.

current_steps.exact_text: Each sublevel $A_k=\{L\le k\delta\}$ is convex and symmetric by hypothesis. Its closure $C_k$ is closed; it is convex by [F10] when $A_k$ is nonempty, and is convex by vacuity when $A_k=\varnothing$. If $x\in C_k$, [F11] supplies $x_j\in A_k$ with $x_j\to x$; then $-x_j\in A_k$ and $-x\in C_k$, so $C_k$ is symmetric (the empty case is symmetric as well). For a nonempty closed convex $C$, choose $c_x,c_y\in C$ within $\epsilon$ of $d(x,C),d(y,C)$ using [F6]. Their convex combination lies in $C$, and [F7] gives $d((1-t)x+ty,C)\le(1-t)d(x,C)+td(y,C)+\epsilon$. Let $\epsilon\downarrow0$ to prove convexity of the distance function. When $C=-C$, replacing each $c$ by $-c$ in the infimum shows $d(-x,C)=d(x,C)$. Thus for a nonempty proper $C_k$, $q(x)=\min(1,m d(x,C_k))$ is symmetric; its sublevel at $0\le t<1$ is $\{d(x,C_k)\le t/m\}$, which is convex, and its sublevel for $t\ge1$ is the whole space. It is Borel and $m$-Lipschitz by [F1] and [F9]. For empty $C_k$ or $C_k=\mathbb R^d$, the stated constant conventions have the same properties. [A1, F1, F6, F7, F9, F10, F11, given, choose, construct, algebra]

If $L(x)\le k\delta$, then $x\in C_k$ and the $k$th term is zero. Every remaining term is at most one, so $0\le g_{N,m}(x)\le\delta\#\{1\le k<N:k\delta<L(x)\}\le L(x)$. The finite sum is bounded by $M$ and has Lipschitz constant at most $M m$. Apply F3 separately to each summand. Every summand's expected loss is minimized at $a=b$ (use its symmetry to replace $b-H$ by $H-b$), so the same action minimizes their sum by [F8]. This proves the first displayed identity without assuming the sum quasi-convex. [F3, F8, A1, step 1.1, algebra]

Since $C_k$ is closed, its $k$th term increases to $\mathbf1_{C_k^c}$ as $m\to\infty$. If $C_k=\mathbb R^d$, then [F10] gives $\operatorname{int}\{L\le k\delta\}=\mathbb R^d$, so the level set is all of $\mathbb R^d$ and both indicators vanish. If $C_k=\varnothing$, the level set is empty and both indicators equal one. Otherwise the difference between $\{L>k\delta\}$ and $C_k^c$ is contained in the boundary of the convex set $\{L\le k\delta\}$, which is null by [F2]. By [F4], it is null under the centered Gaussian as well. Therefore F5 gives $\lim_m E g_{N,m}(H-b)=E[\delta\sum_{k=1}^{N-1}\mathbf1_{\{L(H-b)>k\delta\}}]$. The expression inside the expectation differs from $L(H-b)$ by at most $\delta$: count the grid thresholds strictly below each value in $[0,M]$. Let $N\to\infty$ to obtain the second identity. [A1, F2, F4, F5, F9, F10, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

source_guards.exact_current_claim:
Assume AC, as inherited through [[thm-fano-packing]]. For every $n\ge1$,
$p\ge2$, $\tau>0$, $0\le q<1$ and $c\ge0$, the minimax squared operator
risk of [[def-minimax-squared-operator-risk]] over
$\mathcal P_q(\tau,c)$ of [[def-weak-lq-sparse-covariance-class]] satisfies
$$\mathfrak R_n(\mathcal P_q(\tau,c))\ge b\tau^2\min\{1,\log(p)/n\},$$
for an absolute constant $b>0$. In particular, the lower bound applies when
$c=0$ and when an effective sparse-row count rounds to zero.

current_steps.exact_text: Put $s=\tau/4$ and $\delta=\tfrac12\min\{1,\sqrt{\log(p+1)/n}\}$. Use $p+1$ Gaussian laws $P_0=N(0,sI_p)$ and $P_j=N(0,s(I_p+\delta e_je_j^{\mathsf T}))$, $1\le j\le p$. Each covariance has operator norm at most $3\tau/8<\tau$. If $Z$ is standard normal, $P(|Z|>t)=e^{-t^2/2}\sqrt{2/\pi}\int_0^\infty e^{-w^2/2-tw}dw\le e^{-t^2/2}$. Hence every unit-direction projection of these laws obeys the required tail with parameter $\tau$. Their covariance matrices are diagonal, so [F2] puts every law in every class in the statement. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

For $j\ge1$, the Gaussian covariance KL formula with $\Sigma_j=s(I_p+\delta e_je_j^{\mathsf T})$ and $\Sigma_0=sI_p$ gives $$D(P_j\|P_0)=\tfrac12(\delta-\log(1+\delta))\le\delta^2/4,$$ where $\delta-\log(1+\delta)=\int_0^\delta t/(1+t)\,dt\le\delta^2/2$. By finite-product KL additivity, $$D(P_j^{\otimes n}\|P_0^{\otimes n})=nD(P_j\|P_0)\le n\delta^2/4\le\log(p+1)/16.$$ The $j=0$ divergence is zero, so the reference-law average KL has the same bound. [given, F1, F7, step 1.1, algebra]

Use the full matrix action space $\mathcal T=\mathbb R^{p\times p}$ and set $\rho(A,B)=\|A-B\|_{\mathrm{op}}$. For a unit vector $v$, rowwise Cauchy–Schwarz [F5] gives $\|Av\|_2^2\le\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}^2=\|A\|_F^2$, so [F4] gives $\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le\|A\|_F$. Conversely each coordinate unit vector $e_j$ has norm one, so $\|A\|_F^2=\sum_j\|Ae_j\|_2^2\le p\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2$. Thus $\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le\|A\|_F\le\sqrt p\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}}$. The maximum definition also gives homogeneity, symmetry under $A\mapsto-A$, and $\|A+B\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}}+\|B\|_{\mathrm{op}}$ by the Euclidean triangle inequality on each unit vector. If $\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}}=0$, all columns $Ae_j$ vanish, so $A=0$. Hence $\rho$ is a finite metric by [F5]. The two norm inequalities imply each ball for either metric contains a ball for the other about the same center, so their open sets and therefore their Borel sigma-algebras coincide. Under the entry-list identification $\mathbb R^{p\times p}=\mathbb R^{p^2}$ this is exactly the Euclidean Borel action space in the minimax-risk definition. In particular the diagonal embedding $a\mapsto\operatorname{diag}(a)$ is continuous: its Frobenius difference norm is $\|a-b\|_2$, and its operator difference norm is at most that. All targets in step 1.1 are thus legitimate Borel metric-space points, and every estimator in the minimax definition is measurable into this metric Borel space and induces an admissible deterministic kernel by [F6]. No new choice axiom is used. [given, F4, F5, F6, algebra, step 1.1]

For a diagonal matrix $D=\operatorname{diag}(a)$ and a unit vector $v$, $\|Dv\|_2^2=\sum_j a_j^2v_j^2\le\max_j|a_j|^2$; equality holds at a coordinate unit vector attaining the finite maximum. Hence $\|D\|_{\mathrm{op}}=\max_j|a_j|$. A target difference from the base has one diagonal entry $s\delta$; a difference between two nonbase targets has two entries $s\delta,-s\delta$. Every distinct pair therefore has metric separation exactly $s\delta$. [F4, step 1.1, step 2.2, algebra]

Apply [F3] to these $p+1$ targets, with the base sample law as reference. Its bracket is at least $1-1/16-\log2/\log3>1/4$. Thus the risk is at least $s^2\delta^2/16\ge(\tau^2/1024)\min\{1,\log p/n\}$. These finite experiments are subsets of the full class, so the full minimax risk is no smaller. [given, F2, F3, F6, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 2.2, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

source_guards.exact_current_claim:
Let $X$ be a centered real random variable and let $\tau>0$. If
$$\mathbb P(|X|>t)\le2e^{-t^2/(2\tau)}\qquad(t>0),$$
then $X$ is sub-Gaussian with proxy $64\tau$ in the MGF convention of [[def-subgaussian-variable-and-vector]]:
$$\mathbb E e^{\lambda X}\le e^{32\tau\lambda^2}\qquad(\lambda\in\mathbb R).$$

current_steps.exact_text: The tail bound and [F1] imply $\mathbb E e^{a|X|}=1+a\int_0^\infty e^{at}\mathbb P(|X|>t)\,dt\le1+2a\int_0^\infty e^{at-t^2/(2\tau)}\,dt<\infty$ for every $a>0$, since completing the square gives $at-t^2/(2\tau)=-(t-a\tau)^2/(2\tau)+a^2\tau/2$. Thus all MGFs below are finite. [F1, F2, given, algebra]

Let $X_1,X_2$ be the coordinate variables on the product of two copies of the law of $X$; [F2] gives this probability space, and its rectangle formula makes them independent with law equal to that of $X$. Set $D=X_1-X_2$. Independence [F3] gives $\mathbb E e^{\lambda D}=(\mathbb E e^{\lambda X})(\mathbb E e^{-\lambda X})$. By [F4], the second factor is at least $1$, so $\mathbb E e^{\lambda X}\le\mathbb E e^{\lambda D}$. The product is unchanged when $\lambda$ is replaced by $-\lambda$, hence $\mathbb E e^{\lambda D}=\mathbb E\cosh(\lambda D)$. [F2, F3, F4, given, algebra]

A union bound gives $\mathbb P(|D|>t)\le4e^{-t^2/(8\tau)}$ because $|D|>t$ implies $|X_1|>t/2$ or $|X_2|>t/2$. For $m\ge1$, [F1] and the substitution $u=t^2/(8\tau)$ yield $\mathbb E|D|^{2m}=2m\int_0^\infty t^{2m-1}\mathbb P(|D|>t)\,dt\le4(8\tau)^m m!.$ The integral is evaluated using $\int_0^\infty t^{2m-1}e^{-t^2/(8\tau)}dt=\tfrac12(8\tau)^m(m-1)!$. [F1, step 1.2, algebra]

By [F5], the nonnegative power series for $\cosh$ may be integrated term by term. With $x=8\tau\lambda^2$, step 2.1 and $(2m)!\ge(m!)^2$ give $\mathbb E\cosh(\lambda D)\le1+4\sum_{m\ge1}\frac{x^m}{m!}=4e^x-3\le e^{4x}.$ For the last inequality, $f(x)=e^{4x}-4e^x+3$ satisfies $f(0)=0$ and $f'(x)=4(e^{4x}-e^x)\ge0$ for $x\ge0$. Therefore $\mathbb E e^{\lambda X}\le e^{32\tau\lambda^2}$ for every $\lambda$, which is the proxy-$64\tau$ assertion by [F6]. [F5, F6, step 2.1, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

source_guards.exact_current_claim:
Assume AC. Fix $\tau,M>0$, $\beta>1$, and $0\le q<1$. There are
$v,b>0$ and $P_0<\infty$, depending only on these fixed parameters, such
that the following holds. Let $p\ge P_0$, $n\ge1$, $p\ge n^\beta$ and
$$0\le c\le M n^{(1-q)/2}(\log p)^{-(3-q)/2}.$$
Put $a=\log(p)/n$, $s=\tau/4$, $\epsilon=v\sqrt a$ and
$$k=\left\lfloor\frac{c}{2(s\epsilon)^q}\right\rfloor.$$
If $c/[2(s\epsilon)^q]\ge2$, then
$$\mathfrak R_n(\mathcal P_q(\tau,c))\ge b c^2a^{1-q}.$$
For $q=0$, $(s\epsilon)^q=1$. The proof gives all Gaussian mixture and
conditional remainder estimates locally; no external mixture-affinity lemma
is assumed.

current_steps.exact_text: Choose $v^2<(\beta-1)/(4\beta)$ and put $r=\lfloor p/2\rfloor$. Write $x=c/[2(s\epsilon)^q]$, so $x\ge2$ and $k=\lfloor x\rfloor\ge x/2\ge2$. The radius condition gives $x\le C\sqrt n/(\log p)^{3/2}$, hence $k^2\le Cn/(\log p)^3$, $k\epsilon\le C/\log p$, and $n\epsilon^4k^2\le C/\log p$. Also $k^2p^{2v^2}/r\le Cp^{1/\beta+2v^2-1}/(\log p)^3\to0$, uniformly over admitted $n,c$. All constants depend only on fixed parameters. Increase $P_0$ so $r\ge16k$, $2k\epsilon\le1/3$, and the small bounds below hold. Let $\Lambda$ be all $r\times r$ zero-one matrices with every row sum $k$ and every column sum at most $2k$; cyclic shifts of a $k$-set show it is nonempty. For $\gamma\in\{0,1\}^r$, embed $D_\gamma\lambda$ as the upper-right block of a symmetric off-diagonal matrix $A(\gamma,\lambda)$, using two disjoint $r$-coordinate blocks and an extra zero coordinate if $p$ is odd, and put $\Sigma_{\gamma,\lambda}=s(I_p+\epsilon A(\gamma,\lambda))$. Every absolute row sum of $A$ is at most $2k$. For any $z$, $|z^{\mathsf T}Az|\le\frac12\sum_{j,l}|A_{jl}|(z_j^2+z_l^2)\le2k\|z\|_2^2$; applying this to unit eigenvectors and using [F4] bounds the eigenvalues of $A$ in $[-2k,2k]$. Thus $\Sigma_{\gamma,\lambda}$ is positive definite with eigenvalues in $[2s/3,4s/3]\subset(0,\tau]$. Each column has at most $2k$ off-diagonal entries of magnitude $s\epsilon$. If $0<q<1$, its weak-$\ell_q$ quantity is at most $2k(s\epsilon)^q\le c$; if $q=0$, its nonzero count is at most $2k\le c$. Hence [F2] puts every covariance in the radius-$c$ class. The standard-normal density gives $P(|Z|>t)=e^{-t^2/2}\sqrt{2/\pi}\int_0^\infty e^{-w^2/2-tw}\,dw\le e^{-t^2/2}$, so [F1] verifies the directional-tail condition. For any rectangular matrix $M$ and vector $z$, [F5] gives $|(Mz)_i|^2\le(\sum_j|M_{ij}|)(\sum_j|M_{ij}|z_j^2)$. Summing over rows yields $\|Mz\|_2^2\le(\max_i\sum_j|M_{ij}|)(\max_j\sum_i|M_{ij}|)\|z\|_2^2$, hence $\|M\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2\le(\max_i\sum_j|M_{ij}|)(\max_j\sum_i|M_{ij}|)$. Therefore each cross-block matrix $C=\epsilon D_{\gamma_{-1}}L$ below has $\|C\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le\sqrt2k\epsilon\le2k\epsilon$. [given, F1, F2, F4, F5, algebra, construct]

Give $(\gamma,\lambda)$ the uniform prior on $\{0,1\}^r\times\Lambda$. Fix bit $i$, say $i=1$ by row symmetry, and condition on the remaining bit vector $\gamma_{-1}$ and nuisance rows $L=(\lambda_2,\ldots,\lambda_r)$. The number of possible first-row supports is $N(L)=\binom{d(L)}k$, where $d(L)$ counts columns whose nuisance sum is less than $2k$. Since there are $(r-1)k$ nuisance ones, $d(L)\ge r/2$. The marginal prior of $L$ is $\pi(L)=N(L)/|\Lambda|$, independent of $\gamma_{-1}$; conditional on $L$, a support $A$ is uniform among its $N(L)$ available $k$-sets. For each fixed $\gamma_{-1}$, when $\gamma_1=0$ let $Q_{\gamma_{-1},L}$ be the Gaussian n-sample law, which does not depend on $A$; when $\gamma_1=1$, let $P_{\gamma_{-1},A,L}$ be the n-sample law and $\overline P_{\gamma_{-1},L}$ its uniform support mixture. In the chi-square expansion draw two independent available supports $A,B$ given $L$. Their joint mass with $L$ is proportional to $1/N(L)$, so given $A,B,\gamma_{-1}$ the nuisance rows are not asserted uniform. [given, step 1.1, algebra]

Fix $\gamma_{-1}$ and let $C\in\mathbb R^{r\times r}$ be the cross-block matrix with first row zero and remaining rows $\epsilon\gamma_l\lambda_l$. Under $Q_{\gamma_{-1},L}$, after canceling $s$, the covariance is $B_0=\begin{pmatrix}I_r&C\\C^{\mathsf T}&I_r\end{pmatrix}$, with an extra identity coordinate if $p$ is odd. Put $R=(I_r-C^{\mathsf T}C)^{1/2}$; it is positive definite because $\|C\|_{\mathrm{op}}<1$. The block matrix $T=\begin{pmatrix}I_r&0\\C^{\mathsf T}&R\end{pmatrix}$ satisfies $TT^{\mathsf T}=B_0$. Whiten by $T^{-1}$, extended by the identity on any extra coordinate. If $e=e_1$ is the first coordinate in the left block and $v_A=\mathbf1_A$ is the right-block support vector, then $T^{-1}e=e$ and $T^{-1}v_A=R^{-1}v_A$. Thus the alternative covariances become $I+\Delta_A$ and $I+\Delta_B$, where $\Delta_A=eu^{\mathsf T}+ue^{\mathsf T}$, $\Delta_B=ew^{\mathsf T}+we^{\mathsf T}$, $u=\epsilon R^{-1}v_A$, $w=\epsilon R^{-1}v_B$, and $u,w\perp e$. With $H=(I_r-C^{\mathsf T}C)^{-1}$, $u^{\mathsf T}w=t=\epsilon^2\mathbf1_A^{\mathsf T}H\mathbf1_B$. The operator norms of $\Delta_A,\Delta_B$ equal $\|u\|_2,\|w\|_2$, respectively. Since $\|R^{-1}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le(1-\|C\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2)^{-1/2}$, these norms are at most $\epsilon\sqrt{k}/\sqrt{1-\|C\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2}<1/4$ for large $P_0$; here $\epsilon\sqrt{k}=(k\epsilon)/\sqrt{k}\le C/(\sqrt2\log p)$. For positive-definite $S$, [F1], [F6] and [F7] give the Lebesgue density $f_S(x)=(2\pi)^{-p/2}(\det S)^{-1/2}\exp(-x^{\mathsf T}S^{-1}x/2)$: the independent standard-normal coordinates have product density, and the invertible linear map $S^{1/2}$ changes variables with determinant $(\det S)^{1/2}$. For the one-observation laws, write $f_A,f_B,f_0$ for the positive densities of the two alternatives and the whitened baseline. Put $M=(I+\Delta_A)^{-1}+(I+\Delta_B)^{-1}-I$. Each inverse has smallest eigenvalue at least $(1+1/4)^{-1}=4/5$, hence $M\succeq(3/5)I$. The product density $f_Af_B/f_0$ has exponent matrix $M$ and normalizing factor $(2\pi)^{-p/2}[\det(I+\Delta_A)\det(I+\Delta_B)]^{-1/2}$. Diagonalizing $M$ by [F4], applying an orthogonal change of variables and scaling each one-dimensional standard-normal density [F6, F7] gives $$\int \frac{f_A(x)f_B(x)}{f_0(x)}\,dx=[\det(I+\Delta_A)\det(I+\Delta_B)\det M]^{-1/2}.$$ The identity $(I+\Delta_A)M(I+\Delta_B)=I-\Delta_A\Delta_B$ and determinant multiplicativity [[thm-determinant-multiplicative]] reduce it to $\det(I-\Delta_A\Delta_B)^{-1/2}$. Since $u,w\perp e$, $\Delta_A\Delta_B=tee^{\mathsf T}+uw^{\mathsf T}$. On $\operatorname{span}\{e\}$, $I-\Delta_A\Delta_B$ contributes determinant $1-t$. On $e^\perp$, if $u=0$ the rank-one determinant is $1$; otherwise choose an orthonormal basis whose first vector is $u/\|u\|_2$, so $I-uw^{\mathsf T}$ has only its first row changed and determinant $1-w^{\mathsf T}u=1-t$. The full determinant is $(1-t)^2$, and the one-observation cross integral is $(1-t)^{-1}$. The n-sample laws have product densities by the product joint-law supplier in [F6]; repeated Tonelli [F8] therefore makes their cross integral the nth power, $(1-t)^{-n}$. [given, F1, F4, F6, F7, F8, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

Write $J=|A\cap B|$, $X_l=|A\cap\operatorname{supp}\lambda_l|$ and $Y_l=|B\cap\operatorname{supp}\lambda_l|$. The identity $H-I=C^{\mathsf T}(I-CC^{\mathsf T})^{-1}C$ follows from $H-I=(I-C^{\mathsf T}C)^{-1}C^{\mathsf T}C$ and $(I-C^{\mathsf T}C)C^{\mathsf T}=C^{\mathsf T}(I-CC^{\mathsf T})$. The Neumann series $(I-CC^{\mathsf T})^{-1}=\sum_{m\ge0}(CC^{\mathsf T})^m$ converges because $\|C\|_{\mathrm{op}}<1$; since $C$ has nonnegative entries, $H-I$ is entrywise nonnegative and $t-J\epsilon^2\ge0$. The eigenvalues of $CC^{\mathsf T}$ lie in $[0,\|C\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2]$, so [F4] gives $\|(I-CC^{\mathsf T})^{-1}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le(1-\|C\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2)^{-1}$. Also $(C\mathbf1_A)_l=\epsilon\gamma_lX_l$ and $(C\mathbf1_B)_l=\epsilon\gamma_lY_l$. Cauchy--Schwarz [F5] and $2ab\le a^2+b^2$ yield $$0\le t-J\epsilon^2\le\frac{\epsilon^4}{2(1-\|C\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2)}\sum_{l=2}^r(X_l^2+Y_l^2).$$ Since $\|H\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le(1-\|C\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2)^{-1}$ and $\|\mathbf1_A\|_2=\|\mathbf1_B\|_2=\sqrt{k}$, [F5] also gives $t\le\epsilon^2k/(1-\|C\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2)$. Since $k\ge2$ and $k\epsilon\le C/\log p$, $\epsilon^2k=(k\epsilon)^2/k=o(1)$, so $t=o(1)$. The derivative of $-\log(1-x)$ is at most $2$ for $0\le x\le t\le1/2$; since $1-\|C\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2\ge8/9$, the preceding bound gives $$(1-t)^{-n}\le(1-J\epsilon^2)^{-n}\exp\left\{\theta\sum_{l=2}^r(X_l^2+Y_l^2)\right\},\qquad\theta=2n\epsilon^4.$$ [given, F4, F5, step 1.1, step 3.1, algebra]

Fix $A,B,\gamma_{-1}$ and all nuisance rows except row $l$, and let $a_j$ be the sum in column $j$ over those fixed rows. A support $S$ for row $l$ is feasible exactly when $|S|=k$, $a_j+\mathbf1_{\{j\in S\}}\le2k$ for every column, and $a_j+\mathbf1_{\{j\in S\}}<2k$ for every $j\in A\cup B$ (so both first-row supports remain available). Thus before prior weighting row $l$ is uniform over the $k$-subsets of the fixed set $$V=\{j\in A\cup B:a_j\le2k-2\}\cup\{j\notin A\cup B:a_j\le2k-1\}.$$ At most $(r-2)k/(2k)\le r/2$ columns outside $A\cup B$ have $a_j=2k$, so deleting these and $A\cup B$ leaves at least $r/2-2k\ge r/4$ available columns; hence $d_0=|V|\ge r/4$. The first-row availability count is $d(L)=\#\{j:a_j+\mathbf1_{\{j\in S\}}<2k\}$; as $S$ varies, only columns outside $A\cup B$ with $a_j=2k-1$ can change this count, so its range has width at most $k\le2k$. Since $d(L)\ge r/2$ and $\binom{d+1}k/\binom dk=(d+1)/(d+1-k)$, the ratio of any two weights $1/N(L)$ is at most $\exp(Ck^2/r)\le2$ after increasing $P_0$. Thus the actual conditional density of the row support is at most twice the uniform-subset density on $V$. If $m=|A\cap V|$, singleton and ordered-pair inclusion probabilities give $E X_l=mk/d_0\le Ck^2/r$ and $E[X_l(X_l-1)]=m(m-1)k(k-1)/(d_0(d_0-1))\le Ck^4/r^2$. Hence $E X_l^2\le C(k^2/r+k^4/r^2)$; the same bound holds for $Y_l$ and under the weighted law with twice the constant. Since $\theta k^2=o(1)$, $e^z-1\le2z$ for $0\le z\le1$ yields $$E[\exp\{\theta(X_l^2+Y_l^2)\}\mid\text{all other rows},A,B,\gamma_{-1}]\le1+C\theta(k^2/r+k^4/r^2).$$ [given, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 4.1, algebra]

Put $f_l=\exp\{\theta(X_l^2+Y_l^2)\}$ and $B_0=1+C\theta(k^2/r+k^4/r^2)$. Every factor except $f_l$ is measurable when all rows except $l$ are fixed. Thus for any subset $S$ containing $l$, conditional expectation gives $$E[\prod_{j\in S}f_j\mid A,B,\gamma_{-1}]\le B_0 E[\prod_{j\in S\setminus\{l\}}f_j\mid A,B,\gamma_{-1}].$$ Iterating over the finitely many nuisance rows yields $$E[\exp\{\theta\sum_{l=2}^r(X_l^2+Y_l^2)\}\mid A,B,\gamma_{-1}]\le B_0^{r-1}\le\exp\{Cn\epsilon^4(k^2+k^4/r)\}=1+o(1)$$ uniformly in $A,B,\gamma_{-1}$. No row independence is used. [given, step 1.1, step 5.1, algebra]

Given $L$, $A,B$ are independent uniform $k$-subsets of a set of size $d\ge r/2$. Expanding $z^J=(1+(z-1))^J$ and using $$E\binom Jj=\binom kj\frac{(k)_j}{(d)_j}\le\frac{[k^2/(d-k+1)]^j}{j!}$$ gives $E[z^J\mid L]\le\exp\{k^2(z-1)/(d-k+1)\}$. Since $J\le k$ and $\epsilon^2k=o(1)$, $(1-J\epsilon^2)^{-n}\le\exp(2n\epsilon^2J)=p^{2v^2J}$. Define $\chi^2(\overline P_{\gamma_{-1},L},Q_{\gamma_{-1},L})=\int(d\overline P_{\gamma_{-1},L}/dQ_{\gamma_{-1},L}-1)^2\,dQ_{\gamma_{-1},L}$. Finite expansion of the mixture density gives $$1+\chi^2(\overline P_{\gamma_{-1},L},Q_{\gamma_{-1},L})=E_{A,B\mid L,\gamma_{-1}}(1-t)^{-n}.$$ The posterior of $L$ given $A,B,\gamma_{-1}$ has weights proportional to $1/N(L)$; step 6.1 bounds the conditional remainder factor by $1+o(1)$ uniformly in $A,B,\gamma_{-1}$. Since $d-k+1\ge r/3$, the overlap generating-function bound is uniform in $L,\gamma_{-1}$ and yields $$E_{\gamma_{-1},L}[1+\chi^2(\overline P_{\gamma_{-1},L},Q_{\gamma_{-1},L})]\le(1+o(1))\exp(Ck^2p^{2v^2}/r)=1+o(1),$$ using step 1.1. For each fixed $(\gamma_{-1},L)$, if $R=d\overline P/dQ$, then $E_Q(R-1)=0$, so the positive and negative parts of $R-1$ have equal integrals, and the event $\{R\ge1\}$ attains the supremum in [F9]; hence $\operatorname{TV}(\overline P,Q)=\tfrac12E_Q|R-1|$; [F10] bounds this by $\tfrac12\sqrt{\chi^2(\overline P,Q)}$. Finite Cauchy--Schwarz [F5] over the common prior weights on $(\gamma_{-1},L)$ bounds the average conditional total variation by $\tfrac12\sqrt{E_{\gamma_{-1},L}\chi^2}$, at most $1/2$ after increasing $P_0$. The same mixing weights are used under bit $i=0$ and bit $i=1$, so the full sample-law mixtures have total variation at most $1/2$ by the triangle inequality for the density integral. Their density affinity satisfies $$\int\min(dP_{i,0},dP_{i,1})=1-\operatorname{TV}(P_{i,0},P_{i,1})\ge1/2.$$ [given, F5, F9, F10, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, step 6.1, algebra]

For parameters with $h$ different bits, apply their covariance difference to the vector that is one on the right block and zero elsewhere. Each changed bit contributes a distinct left-block coordinate of magnitude $s\epsilon k$, independently of support choices, so the squared output norm is at least $h(s\epsilon k)^2$ while the input squared norm is $r$. Hence $\|\Sigma_\theta-\Sigma_{\theta'}\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2\ge h(s\epsilon k)^2/r$. Given any measurable matrix estimator, choose a nearest finite covariance target with a fixed tie order. The finite distance comparisons are measurable: [F5] bounds the operator norm by the Frobenius norm, and its triangle inequality follows by applying the Euclidean triangle inequality to every unit vector, so distance to each fixed target is continuous. A wrong target decision forces squared estimation loss at least one quarter of the squared target separation. For each bit, the sum of its two conditional testing errors is at least the density affinity, since pointwise the test contributes at least the minimum of the two densities. By step 7.1, under the uniform prior each bit error probability is at least $1/4$, so the average number of bit errors is at least $r/4$. The maximal risk is at least the average risk and therefore at least $(s\epsilon k)^2/16$. Finally, $k\ge c/[4(s\epsilon)^q]$ implies this is at least $b c^2a^{1-q}$ for a positive constant depending only on the fixed parameters. [given, F3, F4, F5, step 1.1, step 7.1, algebra] ∎

source_guards.exact_current_claim:
Let $X_i$ be iid real random variables with density $f$ continuous and
positive at a fixed point $x$. Let $K$ be finite-valued Borel, nonnegative,
symmetric, with $\int K=1$ and $0<\mu_2=\int u^2K(u)\,du<\infty$.
Assume compact kernel support, a globally bounded density $f$, or a bounded
rapid-tail kernel satisfying $\sup_{|u|\ge A}|u|^3K(u)\to0$.
For $h=h_n\to0$ with $nh_n\to\infty$, set $U_i=(x-X_i)/h_n$ and
$$M_n=\frac1{nh_n}\sum_{i=1}^nK(U_i)\begin{pmatrix}1\\U_i\end{pmatrix}(1,U_i).$$
Then
$$M_n\longrightarrow f(x)\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&\mu_2\end{pmatrix}\quad\text{in probability},$$
and $\mathbb P(M_n\text{ is nonsingular})\to1$.
More generally, the proof establishes $(nh_n)^{-1}\sum_i L(U_i)\to f(x)\int L$
for any integrable Borel function $L$, if $f$ is bounded globally or $L$
has compact support. Boundedness or square integrability of $L$ is unnecessary.

current_steps.exact_text: For the general assertion truncate $L$ to $L_A=L\mathbf1_{\{|u|\le A,\ |L(u)|\le A\}}$. The expectation of $(nh)^{-1}\sum_iL_A(U_i)$ is $\int L_A(u)f(x-hu)\,du\to f(x)\int L_A$ by uniform density convergence on its fixed compact support. Its variance is at most $(nh)^{-1}\int L_A(u)^2f(x-hu)\,du=O_A((nh)^{-1})\to0$. The elementary bound $\mathbb P(|V-\mathbb EV|>\epsilon)\le\operatorname{Var}(V)/\epsilon^2$ follows by integrating $\epsilon^2\mathbf1_{\{|V-\mathbb EV|>\epsilon\}}\le(V-\mathbb EV)^2$. Thus the truncated average converges in probability. [given, F1, F2, F3, F4, algebra]

The expectation of the absolute difference between the full and truncated averages is at most $C\int|L-L_A|$, using the global density bound or its bound on the shrinking image of the compact support of $L$. This tends to zero as $A\to\infty$. Markov's bound, obtained from $\epsilon\mathbf1_{\{Z>\epsilon\}}\le Z$ for $Z\ge0$, makes this difference uniformly small in probability. Also $\int L_A\to\int L$. First choosing $A$ large and then $n$ large proves the general assertion. [given, F2, F4, step 1.1, algebra]

For the rapid-tail case and $L(u)=u^jK(u)$, $j=0,1,2$, restrict first to $|x-X_i|\le\delta$, where the density is bounded. The same truncation proof works there. The expected absolute contribution of the remaining observations is at most $\epsilon_h h^{2-j}\int_{|z-x|>\delta}|z-x|^{j-3}f(z)\,dz\to0$, where $\epsilon_h=\sup_{|u|\ge\delta/h}|u|^3K(u)\to0$. Thus the same scalar limits hold for these three moments without a global density bound. [given, F2, F4, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

Apply steps 1.1–3.1 to $L(u)=K(u)u^j$ for $j=0,1,2$, all integrable by the finite second moment. Symmetry gives $\int uK=0$. The entries of $M_n$ therefore have the displayed limits. Its determinant tends in probability to $f(x)^2\mu_2>0$, since it is a polynomial in the entries. A zero determinant lies outside a fixed neighborhood of this positive limit, so its probability tends to zero. [given, F4, step 2.1, algebra, step 3.1] ∎

source_guards.exact_current_claim:
Let a dominated finite-dimensional parametric model be quadratic-mean
differentiable, with the supplied density family of [[def-qmd-path]], at an interior point $\theta_0\in\mathbb R^d$, with score
$s_{\theta_0}\in L^2(P_{\theta_0};\mathbb R^d)$. Then
$\mathbb E_{\theta_0}s_{\theta_0}=0$.

current_steps.exact_text: Write $q=\sqrt{p_{\theta_0}}$ and $r_h=\sqrt{p_{\theta_0+h}}-q-\tfrac12h^Ts_{\theta_0}q$. By [F1], $\|r_h\|_2=o(\|h\|)$. By [F3], each $q_h=\sqrt{p_{\theta_0+h}}$ is a probability square-root density, so $\|q_h\|_2^2=\|q\|_2^2=1$. Since $P_{\theta_0}$ is a probability and the score is square-integrable, [F2] with the constant function $1$ shows its coordinates are integrable. All products in the following norm expansion are integrable by [F2], since $q$, $r_h$, and $h^Ts_{\theta_0}q$ belong to $L^2(\mu)$. Thus [F4] permits integrating the finite expansion term by term, and [F3] transfers the score term to expectation under $P_{\theta_0}$. Expanding $q_h=q+\tfrac12h^Ts_{\theta_0}q+r_h$ gives $0=h^T\mathbb E_{\theta_0}s_{\theta_0}+2\langle q,r_h\rangle+ \|\tfrac12h^Ts_{\theta_0}q+r_h\|_2^2$. Cauchy–Schwarz [F2] bounds the inner product by $o(\|h\|)$; square-integrability of the score and $\|r_h\|_2=o(\|h\|)$ make the last term $O(\|h\|^2)$. Thus $h^T\mathbb E_{\theta_0}s_{\theta_0}=o(\|h\|)$. [F1, F2, F3, F4, algebra]

For each coordinate vector $e_j$, set $h=te_j$ with $t>0$ small enough that $\theta_0+te_j\in\Theta$. Divide the relation from step 1.1 by $t$ and let $t\downarrow0$ to obtain $\mathbb E_{\theta_0}s_{\theta_0,j}=0$. This holds for all $j=1,\ldots,d$, hence the score vector has mean zero. [F1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

source_guards.exact_current_claim:
Assume AC and [[def-qmd-path]] at $\theta_0$ with score $s$ and information $I$.
Let $h_n\to h$ in $\mathbb R^d$, put $u_n=h_n/\sqrt n$, and write
$P_0=P_{\theta_0}$ and $P_{u_n}=P_{\theta_0+u_n}$. On
$S=\{p_{\theta_0}>0\}$ define, for all sufficiently large $n$,
$$q_n(x)=\frac{\mathbf1_S(x)p_{\theta_0+u_n}(x)} {(1-\alpha_n)p_{\theta_0}(x)},\qquad \alpha_n=P_{u_n}(S^c).$$
Then $q_n$ is a probability density relative to $P_0$. For IID
$X_1,\ldots,X_n\sim P_0$, let $L_n=\prod_{i=1}^nq_n(X_i)$ and
$\Delta_n=n^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^ns(X_i)$. Under $P_0^{\otimes n}$,
$$\log L_n=h_n^T\Delta_n-\tfrac12h^TIh+o_P(1),\qquad P_0^{\otimes n}(L_n=0)\to0.$$
Moreover, if $\bar P_n=q_nP_0$ is the normalized absolutely continuous
component of $P_{u_n}$ relative to $P_0$, then
$$\|P_{u_n}^{\otimes n}-\bar P_n^{\otimes n}\|_{\rm TV}\to0.$$
No full likelihood ratio for $P_{u_n}^{\otimes n}$ is asserted.

current_steps.exact_text: Write $p_u=p_{\theta_0+u}$, $S=\{p_0>0\}$, and $\alpha(u)=\int_{S^c}p_u\,d\mu$. For small $u$, [F3] gives $\alpha(u)<1/2$. Define $q_u=\mathbf1_Sp_u/((1-\alpha(u))p_0)$ on $S$ and $q_u=0$ on $S^c$. It is nonnegative and measurable, and $\int q_u\,dP_0=(1-\alpha(u))^{-1}\int_Sp_u\,d\mu=1,$ so it is a probability density. At $u=0$, $\alpha(0)=0$ and $q_0=1$ $P_0$-almost surely, since $P_0(S^c)=\int_{S^c}p_0\,d\mu=0$. On $S$, $\sqrt{q_u}=(1-\alpha(u))^{-1/2} \left(1+\tfrac12u^Ts+\frac{r_u}{\sqrt{p_0}}\right).$ The residual term has $L^2(P_0)$ norm $\|r_u\mathbf1_S\|_{L^2(\mu)}=o(\|u\|_2)$. Also $|(1-\alpha)^{-1/2}-1| =\frac{\alpha}{\sqrt{1-\alpha}(1+\sqrt{1-\alpha})}=O(\alpha),$ and [F2], [F8] give $\|u^Ts\|_{L^2(P_0)}=O(\|u\|_2)$. Therefore $Y_u:=2(\sqrt{q_u}-1)=u^Ts+R_u, \qquad\|R_u\|_{L^2(P_0)}=o(\|u\|_2).$ This is the required square-root expansion. [A1, F1, F2, F3, F8, L1, given, algebra]

The product function $L_n=\prod_iq_{u_n}(X_i)$ is a density of $\bar P_n^{\otimes n}$ relative to $P_0^{\otimes n}$. For a measurable rectangle $A_1\times\cdots\times A_n$, Tonelli gives $\int_{A_1\times\cdots\times A_n}\prod_iq_{u_n}(x_i)\,dP_0^{\otimes n} =\prod_i\int_{A_i}q_{u_n}\,dP_0 =\prod_i\bar P_n(A_i).$ By [F6], agreement on rectangles identifies the product measures. Taking the whole space gives $E_{P_0^{\otimes n}}L_n=1$. [F5, F6, given, algebra]

Since $E_0q_u=1$, $E_0Y_u=-\tfrac14E_0Y_u^2.$ By step 1.1, [F2], and [F8], $E_0Y_u^2=u^TIu+o(\|u\|_2^2),\qquad E_0Y_u=-\tfrac14u^TIu+o(\|u\|_2^2).$ Indeed, the difference between $Y_u$ and $u^Ts$ has $L^2(P_0)$ norm $o(\|u\|_2)$, so Cauchy–Schwarz makes the difference of their squared norms $o(\|u\|_2^2)$. [F2, F8, step 1.1, given, algebra]

Apply [F4] to $Z_i=\|s(X_i)\|_2^2$, whose mean is finite by [F2]. Then $\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n(h_n^Ts(X_i))^2\to h^TIh$ in probability: for fixed $h$ this is [F4] applied to $(h^Ts)^2$, and the difference for $h_n$ is bounded by $\|h_n-h\|_2\|h_n+h\|_2\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\|s(X_i)\|_2^2\to0.$ Step 1.1 and [F8] also give $\sum_{i=1}^nY_{u_n}(X_i)^2 -\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n(h_n^Ts(X_i))^2\to0$ in probability, because its expected absolute value is at most $n\|R_{u_n}\|_2(\|Y_{u_n}\|_2+\|u_n^Ts\|_2) =o(n\|u_n\|_2^2)=o(1)$. Consequently $\sum_iY_{u_n}(X_i)^2\to h^TIh$. [F2, F4, F8, step 1.1, given, algebra]

Put $V_n=\sqrt nY_{u_n}(X_1)$. Step 1.1 implies $V_n-h_n^Ts(X_1)\to0$ in $L^2(P_0)$, so $V_n\to h^Ts(X_1)$ in $L^2$. By [F8], $V_n^2\to(h^Ts(X_1))^2$ in $L^1$; [F9] makes $(V_n^2)$ uniformly integrable. For every $\varepsilon>0$, [F10] and the union bound give $P_0^{\otimes n}\!\left(\max_{i\le n}|Y_{u_n}(X_i)|>\varepsilon\right) \le\varepsilon^{-2}E_0[V_n^2\mathbf1_{\{|V_n|>\varepsilon\sqrt n\}}] \to0.$ Also $P_0^{\otimes n}(L_n=0)\le n\beta(u_n)\to0$ by [F3] and the union bound. [F3, F8, F9, F10, step 1.1, given, algebra]

Let $R_{u_n}=Y_{u_n}-u_n^Ts$. Its centered IID sum has variance at most $nE_0R_{u_n}^2=o(n\|u_n\|_2^2)=o(1)$. By step 2.1, $nE_0R_{u_n}=nE_0Y_{u_n} =-\tfrac14h_n^TIh_n+o(1)\to-\tfrac14h^TIh.$ Markov's inequality [F10], applied to the square of the centered sum, gives $\sum_iY_{u_n}(X_i)=h_n^T\Delta_n-\tfrac14h^TIh+o_P(1).$ This is the required expansion of the sum. [F2, F5, F10, step 2.1, given, algebra]

On the event that every $q_{u_n}(X_i)>0$ and $\max_i|Y_{u_n}(X_i)|\le1$, Taylor's formula gives $\log q_{u_n}(X_i)=Y_{u_n}(X_i)-\tfrac14Y_{u_n}(X_i)^2 +O(|Y_{u_n}(X_i)|^3),$ with one constant valid for all $i,n$ by [F11], since the third derivative of $y\mapsto2\log(1+y/2)$ is bounded on $[-1,1]$. The total cubic remainder is bounded by a constant times $\max_i|Y_{u_n}(X_i)|\sum_iY_{u_n}(X_i)^2$, which tends to zero by the square-sum limit in step 2.2 and the maximum bound in step 2.3. Combining the sum expansion in step 3.1 with the square-sum limit gives $\log L_n=\sum_i\log q_{u_n}(X_i) =h_n^T\Delta_n-\tfrac12h^TIh+o_P(1).$ This is the normalized log-likelihood expansion. [F11, step 2.2, step 3.1, step 2.3, given]

The full one-observation law decomposes as $P_{u_n}=(1-\alpha_n)\bar P_n+\alpha_n S_n$, where $S_n$ is the normalized restriction of $P_{u_n}$ to $S^c$ when $\alpha_n>0$. In the product mixture, the probability that at least one coordinate is drawn from $S_n$ is at most $n\alpha_n$. Conditioning on the all-absolutely-continuous component shows, for every event, its probability under the full product differs from that under $\bar P_n^{\otimes n}$ by at most $n\alpha_n$. Since $n\alpha_n=o(n\|u_n\|_2^2)=o(1)$, [F7] proves the total-variation claim. If $\alpha_n=0$, the singular component is absent and the same bound is zero. [F3, F7, given, algebra] ∎

source_guards.exact_current_claim:
Fix $\tau>0$, $0\le q<1$ and $\beta>1$. Let $n\ge1$, $p\ge2$,
$p\ge n^\beta$ and $a=\log(p)/n\le1$. For iid observations from
$\mathcal P_q(\tau,c)$ of [[def-weak-lq-sparse-covariance-class]], use
[[alg-entrywise-thresholded-sample-covariance]] with
$\lambda=8192\tau\sqrt a$. There is $C=C(q,\tau)<\infty$ such that
$$\sup_{P\in\mathcal P_q(\tau,c)}\mathbb E_{P^{\otimes n}}\|\widehat\Sigma-\Sigma(P)\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2\le C\{c^2a^{1-q}+a\}.$$
The estimator uses sample centering and divisor $n$, including unknown means;
no independence between coordinates is assumed. This is the unmodified
threshold estimator, not a clipped version.

current_steps.exact_text: Put $u=\log(8p^{10})\le13\log p$. Since $a\le1$, $192\tau(\sqrt{u/n}+u/n)\le192\tau(\sqrt{13}+13)\sqrt a<4096\tau\sqrt a=\lambda/2$. The failure bound in [F2] is $1/(4p^9)+1/(32p^{18})\le p^{-8}$. Thus an event $G$ has $P^{\otimes n}$-probability at least $1-p^{-8}$, and on it [F3] bounds squared loss by $C(q,\tau)(c^2a^{1-q}+a)$. [given, F2, F3, algebra]

Write $U_{ij}=X_{ij}-EX_{ij}$. By [F1] and [F4], $E_{P^{\otimes n}}|U_{ij}|^8\le(2\tau)^4\,4!=384\tau^4$. Also, for unit $v$, $v^{\mathsf T}\Sigma v\le\int_0^\infty e^{-t/(2\tau)}dt=2\tau$; applying [F6] to centered coordinates gives $|\sigma_{jk}|\le2\tau$. The sample-centered diagonal obeys $0\le\widehat\sigma^*_{jj}\le n^{-1}\sum_iU_{ij}^2$. Applying [F7] to the two centered coordinate sample vectors gives $|\widehat\sigma^*_{jk}|^2\le\widehat\sigma^*_{jj}\widehat\sigma^*_{kk}$. Therefore $$E_{P^{\otimes n}}|\widehat\sigma^*_{jk}|^4\le\tfrac12 E_{P^{\otimes n}}[(\widehat\sigma^*_{jj})^4+(\widehat\sigma^*_{kk})^4]\le384\tau^4,$$ where the final inequality uses [F8] with $y_i=U_{ij}^2$ (and likewise for $k$). These bounds are independent of the unknown means. [given, F1, F4, F6, F7, F8, algebra]

By [F5], $E_{P^{\otimes n}}|\widehat\sigma_{jk}-\sigma_{jk}|^4\le8E_{P^{\otimes n}}(|\widehat\sigma^*_{jk}|^4+|\sigma_{jk}|^4)\le C\tau^4$. For any matrix $A$, [F7] gives $\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2\le\sum_{jk}|A_{jk}|^2$ by applying finite Cauchy–Schwarz to each row against a unit vector; [F7] also gives $(\sum_{jk}|A_{jk}|^2)^2\le p^2\sum_{jk}|A_{jk}|^4$. Thus $E_{P^{\otimes n}}\|\widehat\Sigma-\Sigma\|_{\mathrm{op}}^4\le C\tau^4p^4$. Applying [F6] to $\|\widehat\Sigma-\Sigma\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2$ and $\mathbf1_{G^c}$ and using step 1.1 gives $$E_{P^{\otimes n}}[\|\widehat\Sigma-\Sigma\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2;G^c]\le C\tau^2p^2p^{-4}=C\tau^2p^{-2}.$$ Since $p\ge n^\beta$ implies $n\le p^{1/\beta}\le p$ and $1/p\le\log p$, we have $p^{-2}\le\log p/n=a$. Adding the good-event bound proves the claim uniformly over the class. [given, F5, F6, F7, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

source_guards.exact_current_claim:
Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]).

Let $d\ge1$, let $\Theta_0\subseteq\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, and let $\theta_0\in\Theta_0$. Assume the full-model parameter set $\Theta$ is open in $\mathbb R^d$, so $\theta_0$ is interior for the QMD model. Under $P_{\theta_0}$, let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be IID and let $\ell_n(\theta)=\sum_{i=1}^n\log p_\theta(X_i)$ be their sample log-likelihood. Define local parameter sets $C_n:=\sqrt n(\Theta-\theta_0)$ and $C_{0n}:=\sqrt n(\Theta_0-\theta_0)$. Assume the model is QMD at $\theta_0$ as in [[def-qmd-path]], and write $I:=\mathbb E_{\theta_0}[s_{\theta_0}s_{\theta_0}^T]$ for its Fisher information; assume $I$ is positive definite, meaning $v^TIv>0$ for every nonzero $v$. Suppose $C_n$ and $C_{0n}$ are closed in the Euclidean metric (their complements are open), contain $0$, and converge locally to nonempty closed convex cones $C$ and $C_0$ with $C_0\subseteq C$. A cone contains $0$ and is closed under multiplication by every nonnegative scalar; convex means that the set contains the line segment between each pair of its points. Local convergence means that, for every $R>0$, there are $\delta_{n,R}\to0$ such that every point of $C_n\cap\overline B_2(0,R)$ or $C\cap\overline B_2(0,R)$ is within $\delta_{n,R}$ in Euclidean distance of the other set, and likewise for $C_{0n}$ and $C_0$. Here a point $x$ is within $\delta$ of a set $A$ when $\inf_{a\in A}\|x-a\|_2\le\delta$.

Assume a uniform local quadratic likelihood expansion: for $h\in C_n$,

$$\ell_n(\theta_0+h/\sqrt n)-\ell_n(\theta_0)=h^TZ_n-\tfrac12h^TIh+r_n(h),$$

where $Z_n\Rightarrow Z\sim N_d(0,I)$ under $P_{\theta_0}$ and, for every $R>0$, $\sup\{|r_n(h)|:h\in C_n,\ \|h\|_2\le R\}\to_P0$. Assume the full and null local log-likelihoods attain maxima at $\hat h_n\in C_n$ and $\hat h_{0n}\in C_{0n}$ and that both maximizer sequences are tight, meaning that for every $\eta>0$ some $R<\infty$ makes the limiting upper probability of either norm exceeding $R$ at most $\eta$. For

$$T_n:=2\left[\sup_{h\in C_n}\{\ell_n(\theta_0+h/\sqrt n)-\ell_n(\theta_0)\}-\sup_{h\in C_{0n}}\{\ell_n(\theta_0+h/\sqrt n)-\ell_n(\theta_0)\}\right],$$

the likelihood-ratio statistic satisfies

$$T_n\Rightarrow d_I^2(I^{-1}Z,C_0)-d_I^2(I^{-1}Z,C),$$

where $d_I$ is the Fisher-information distance of [[def-fisher-information-metric-distance]]. QMD alone is not asserted to imply the uniform expansion or tightness hypotheses.

current_steps.exact_text: Write $q_z(h)=h^Tz-\tfrac12h^TIh$ and $m_A(z)=\sup_{h\in A}q_z(h)$ for $A=C,C_0$. By [F3], $m_A(z)=\tfrac12z^TI^{-1}z-\tfrac12d_I^2(I^{-1}z,A)$. If $h_A(z)$ is a maximizer, then $q_z(h_A(z))\ge q_z(0)=0$. The lower bound in [F3] and [F10] imply $\|h_A(z)\|_2\le2\|z\|_2/\lambda$ (with the bound immediate when $h_A(z)=0$). [F3, F1, F10, given, algebra]

Let $\lambda$ be from [F3], fix $M>0$, and choose $R>2M/\lambda+1$. For $A_n=C_n$, $A=C$ (and likewise for $A_n=C_{0n}$, $A=C_0$), write $m_{A_n,R}(z)=\sup_{h\in A_n\cap\overline B_2(0,R)}q_z(h)$. For every $\|z\|_2\le M$, [F3] gives a maximizer $h(z)$ of $q_z$ on $A$ with $\|h(z)\|_2\le2M/\lambda<R-1$. Local set convergence supplies points of $A_n$ within $\delta_{n,R-1}+1/n$ of $h(z)$, hence inside the radius-$R$ ball for all large $n$. Conversely, every point of $A_n\cap\overline B_2(0,R)$ is within $\delta_{n,R}+1/n$ of a point of $A$. With $B_I=\sum_{j,k=1}^d|I_{jk}|$, [F1] and [F10] give $|q_z(h)-q_z(h')|\le(M+B_I(R+1))\|h-h'\|_2$ for $\|h\|_2,\|h'\|_2\le R+1$ and $\|z\|_2\le M$. These two directions show $\sup_{\|z\|_2\le M}|m_{A_n,R}(z)-m_A(z)|\to0$. The same bounds apply to both full and null sets. [F3, F1, F9, F10, given, algebra, choose]

The sequence $Z_n$ is tight. Indeed, for any $\eta>0$ choose $R$ with $P(\|Z\|_2\ge R)<\eta$, possible because [F4] supplies a Borel probability law on finite-dimensional $\mathbb R^d$. The set $\{z:\|z\|_2\ge R\}$ is closed, so [F5] bounds $\limsup_nP(\|Z_n\|_2\ge R)$ by $\eta$. step 1.1 then makes the maximizers of $q_{Z_n}$ over $C$ and $C_0$ tight as well. [A1, F4, F5, step 1.1, given, choose]

On the radius-$R$ ball, the difference between the supremum of the local log-likelihood and $m_{C_n,R}(Z_n)$ is at most $\sup_{h\in C_n,\ \|h\|_2\le R}|r_n(h)|$, which tends to zero in probability. step 1.2 and tightness of $Z_n$ then show that the full and null local likelihood suprema, when restricted to the radius-$R$ ball, differ in probability by a term tending to zero from $m_C(Z_n)$ and $m_{C_0}(Z_n)$, respectively. [F8, step 2.1, step 1.2, given]

Given $\eta>0$, tightness of $Z_n$ lets us choose $M$ so that $\|Z_n\|_2\le M$ with limiting probability at least $1-\eta/3$. Choose $R>2M/\lambda+1$ large enough that the joint event that both local likelihood maximizers lie in the radius-$R$ ball has limiting probability at least $1-\eta/3$. By step 1.1 both quadratic maximizers also lie in that ball whenever $\|Z_n\|_2\le M$. Thus all four full and truncated suprema agree except on events with total limiting upper probability at most $2\eta/3$. step 3.1 and arbitrariness of $\eta$ give $T_n-2(m_C(Z_n)-m_{C_0}(Z_n))\to_P0$. [F8, step 1.1, step 3.1, given, choose]

The form $\langle u,v\rangle_I=u^TIv$ is an inner product; its Cauchy–Schwarz inequality follows by requiring $(u-tv)^TI(u-tv)\ge0$ for every real $t$. Thus the induced norm satisfies the triangle inequality, and taking infima gives $|d_I(x,C)-d_I(y,C)|\le\|x-y\|_I$. Also $v^TIv\le B_I\|v\|_2^2$, where $B_I$ is the finite entry sum from step 1.2, so the distance map is Euclidean Lipschitz after composition with the fixed linear map $I^{-1}$. Therefore $g(z):=d_I^2(I^{-1}z,C_0)-d_I^2(I^{-1}z,C)$ is continuous. The formula in step 1.1 gives $2[m_C(z)-m_{C_0}(z)]=g(z)$. By [F6], $g(Z_n)\Rightarrow g(Z)$. step 4.1 and [F7] then give $T_n\Rightarrow g(Z)$, which is the stated distance-difference law. [F2, F3, F6, F7, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 4.1] ∎

source_guards.exact_current_claim:
Assume AC for the chosen regression version. Let $X_i$ be iid with density
$f$, with $f(x)>0$ at a fixed interior point $x$, and let $f,m$ be $C^2$
near $x$. Let $K$ be finite-valued Borel, nonnegative and symmetric, with
$\int K=1$, $0<\mu_2=\int u^2K<\infty$ and
$\int(1+u^2)K(u)^2\,du<\infty$. Assume either compact kernel support, or
that $f,m$ and their first two derivatives are bounded and continuous
globally. A further localization alternative, including the Gaussian kernel, is that
$\mathbb E[Y^2]<\infty$, $K$ is bounded, and
$$\lim_{A\to\infty}\sup_{|u|\ge A}|u|^3K(u)=0.$$
Under this rapid-tail alternative only the stated local smoothness of
$f,m$ is needed; no global boundedness of $m$ or of its derivatives is assumed.
Let $h_n\to0$ with $nh_n^3\to\infty$. For almost every realized design,
integrate the degree-one fit of [[def-local-polynomial-estimator]] against
the independent response laws $\prod_iQ(X_i,dy_i)$; call the resulting
finite response-law mean $b_n(x)$, with the same fixed fallback on singular
designs. Then
$$b_n(x)-m(x)=\frac{h_n^2\mu_2}{2}m''(x)+o_P(h_n^2).$$
Here $Z_n=o_P(h_n^2)$ means $Z_n/h_n^2\to0$ in probability. This is a
conditional response-law mean statement; it neither assumes nor asserts
that the estimator has an unconditional Lebesgue expectation.

current_steps.exact_text: Put $h=h_n$, $U_i=(x-X_i)/h$, $S_j=(nh)^{-1}\sum_iK(U_i)U_i^j$ and $r_h(u)=m(x-hu)-m(x)+hu m'(x)$. Then $S_0\to f(x)$, $S_2\to f(x)\mu_2$ by [F2]. Symmetry and the first-order density expansion give $\mathbb ES_1=-hf'(x)\mu_2+o(h)$; the tail is controlled by $u^2K$ under the global alternative. Also $\operatorname{Var}(S_1)\le C(nh)^{-1}\int u^2K^2$, using localization or the global density bound. In the rapid-tail alternative its local part has this bound, and the far contribution to $\operatorname{Var}(S_1)$ is at most $C h^2n^{-1}\int_{|z-x|>\delta}f(z)|z-x|^{-4}\,dz$, hence no larger than $O((nh)^{-1})$. Since $nh^3\to\infty$, $(S_1-\mathbb ES_1)/h\to0$ in probability by the variance bound, so $S_1=O_P(h)$. [given, F2, F4, algebra]

Set $R_j=(nh)^{-1}\sum_iK(U_i)U_i^jr_h(U_i)$. Taylor's integral formula gives $|r_h(u)|\le Ch^2u^2$ and $r_h(u)/h^2\to\tfrac12m''(x)u^2$. The truncation proof of [F2] applies to this varying integrand: on any fixed set where $|u|$ and $K(u)$ are bounded it converges uniformly, its average has variance $O_A((nh)^{-1})$, and the absolute tail expectation is at most $C\int_{\mathrm{tail}}u^2K$. Hence $R_0/h^2\to\tfrac12m''(x)f(x)\mu_2$ in probability. Furthermore $|r_h(u)|\le Ch|u|$ and $r_h(u)/(h|u|)\to0$ pointwise. Splitting the integral as before gives $\mathbb E|R_1|/h\le\int K(u)|u||r_h(u)|f(x-hu)/h\,du\to0$. Markov's bound yields $R_1=o_P(h)$. Under the rapid-tail alternative these arguments are first applied on $|X_i-x|\le\delta$. For the far part put $\epsilon_h=\sup_{|u|\ge\delta/h}|u|^3K(u)\to0$ and expand $r=m(z)-m(x)-m'(x)(z-x)$. Its expected absolute contributions to $R_0/h^2$ and $R_1/h$ are bounded by $C_\delta\epsilon_h\int(1+|m|)f\to0$. The same tail estimate gives the stated expectation expansion for $S_1$. Thus all limits hold without global smoothness. [given, F2, F4, step 1.1, algebra]

On a nonsingular design, [F1] and [F3] give $b_n-m(x)=(S_2R_0-S_1R_1)/(S_0S_2-S_1^2)$, since the constant and slope terms cancel exactly in the intercept. Steps 1.1–2.1 give $S_1R_1=o_P(h^2)$, and the denominator tends to $f(x)^2\mu_2>0$. Division gives the claimed coefficient. The singular-design event has probability tending to zero by [F2]; even after scaling by $h^{-2}$ the probability of any nonzero fallback contribution is at most that event probability, so it does not change convergence in probability. This argument integrates the response law separately for each design and never interchanges an undefined unconditional signed expectation. [given, F1, F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

source_guards.exact_current_claim:
Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]).

Let $X_1,X_2,\ldots$ be IID from a probability law $P$ that is misspecified relative to the density family $p_\theta$, and let $\ell_\theta=\log p_\theta$ be as in [[def-pseudo-true-parameter-under-misspecification]]. Write $P_nf=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^nf(X_i)$ and $M(\theta)=\mathbb E_P\ell_\theta(X)$. Assume that $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, $d\ge1$, and that $\theta^*$ is the unique separated interior maximizer of $M$, where interior means that some Euclidean open ball about $\theta^*$ lies in $\Theta$: for each $\varepsilon>0$ there is $\eta_\varepsilon>0$ such that $M(\theta^*)-M(\theta)\ge\eta_\varepsilon$ whenever $\theta\in\Theta$ and $\|\theta-\theta^*\|_2\ge\varepsilon$. Assume the uniform law $\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}|P_n\ell_\theta-M(\theta)|\to_P0$, and let $\hat\theta_n\in\Theta$ be a measurable approximate maximizer with $\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}P_n\ell_\theta-P_n\ell_{\hat\theta_n}\to_P0$.

Let $S_\theta(x)=\nabla_\theta\ell_\theta(x)$ be continuously differentiable in a neighborhood of $\theta^*$. Assume $\mathbb E_PS_{\theta^*}=0$, $\mathbb E_P\|S_{\theta^*}\|_2^2<\infty$, and set $J=\mathbb E_P[S_{\theta^*}S_{\theta^*}^{T}]$. Suppose $H=\mathbb E_P[\nabla_\theta S_{\theta^*}]$ is nonsingular, $D(\theta):=\mathbb E_P[\nabla_\theta S_\theta]$ exists and is continuous at $\theta^*$, and for every sufficiently small fixed $\delta>0$,

$$\sup_{\|\theta-\theta^*\|_2\le\delta}\|P_n\nabla_\theta S_\theta-D(\theta)\|_{op}\to_P0,$$

where $\|A\|_{op}:=\sup_{\|v\|_2\le1}\|Av\|_2$. Finally assume the approximate score equation $\sqrt n\,P_nS_{\hat\theta_n}=o_P(1)$. Then

$$\sqrt n(\hat\theta_n-\theta^*)\Rightarrow N_d\!\left(0,H^{-1}JH^{-T}\right).$$

The covariance is the sandwich matrix formed from the Hessian $H$ under $P$ and the score second moment $J$ under $P$. The theorem does not assert that it equals the inverse Fisher information of the fitted model.

current_steps.exact_text: Put $\Delta_n=\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}|P_n\ell_\theta-M(\theta)|$ and $r_n=\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}P_n\ell_\theta-P_n\ell_{\hat\theta_n}$. By assumption $\Delta_n\to_P0$ and $r_n\to_P0$. Since $\hat\theta_n$ is an approximate maximizer by [F8], $P_n\ell_{\hat\theta_n}\ge P_n\ell_{\theta^*}-r_n$, and therefore $0\le M(\theta^*)-M(\hat\theta_n)\le2\Delta_n+r_n$. [given, F1, F3, F7, F8, algebra]

For any fixed $\varepsilon>0$, separation gives a positive gap $\eta_\varepsilon$ whenever $\|\hat\theta_n-\theta^*\|_2\ge\varepsilon$. Step 1.1 then gives $P(\|\hat\theta_n-\theta^*\|_2\ge\varepsilon)\le P(2\Delta_n+r_n\ge\eta_\varepsilon)\to0$. Thus $\hat\theta_n-\theta^*=o_P(1)$ by [F6], so with probability tending to one the segment from $\theta^*$ to $\hat\theta_n$ lies in any fixed neighborhood on which the score is differentiable. [given, step 1.1, F6, F7]

On the event that the segment lies in the differentiability neighborhood define $A_n=\int_0^1 P_n\nabla_\theta S_{\theta^*+t(\hat\theta_n-\theta^*)}\,dt$; set $A_n=H$ off that event. Given $\varepsilon>0$, continuity of $D$ at $\theta^*$ supplies a sufficiently small fixed $\delta$ for which $\|D(\theta)-H\|_{op}<\varepsilon/2$ throughout the $\delta$-ball. Consistency from step 2.1 and the assumed uniform Hessian law imply $P(\|A_n-H\|_{op}>\varepsilon)\to0$. [given, step 2.1, F6, algebra]

On the same high-probability event, the componentwise fundamental theorem of calculus along the segment gives $P_nS_{\hat\theta_n}=P_nS_{\theta^*}+A_n(\hat\theta_n-\theta^*)$. By step 3.1, every entry of $A_n-H$ tends to zero in probability. The determinant and adjugate are polynomials in the entries, so $\det A_n\to_P\det H\ne0$ and $\operatorname{adj}(A_n)\to_P\operatorname{adj}(H)$; on the event $\det A_n\ne0$, $A_n^{-1}=\operatorname{adj}(A_n)/\det A_n$, hence every entry of $A_n^{-1}-H^{-1}$ tends to zero in probability. The finite-dimensional matrix bound $\|B\|_{op}\le d\max_{j,k}|B_{jk}|$ then gives $\|A_n^{-1}-H^{-1}\|_{op}\to_P0$. Rearranging gives $\sqrt n(\hat\theta_n-\theta^*)=-A_n^{-1}\sqrt nP_nS_{\theta^*}+A_n^{-1}\sqrt nP_nS_{\hat\theta_n}$ on an event whose probability tends to one. [given, step 3.1, F6, algebra]

By [F2], the score vectors $S_{\theta^*}(X_i)$ are IID; their mean is zero and their covariance is $J$. Their second moment is finite by the Statement, so [F4] and [A1] give $\sqrt nP_nS_{\theta^*}\Rightarrow G$ with $G\sim N_d(0,J)$. The matrix $A_n^{-1}$ converges in probability in operator norm to $H^{-1}$, and the residual vector $\sqrt nP_nS_{\hat\theta_n}=o_P(1)$ by the Statement. Flattening the matrix entries and concatenating the vectors gives a finite-dimensional vector converging in probability to $(H^{-1},0)$. Applying [F5] to the continuous map $(x,A,r)\mapsto-Ax+Ar$ gives the limit $-H^{-1}G$. Its covariance is $H^{-1}JH^{-T}$, proving the assertion. [A1, F2, F4, F5, F6, step 4.1] ∎

source_guards.exact_current_claim:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\{P_\theta:\theta\in\Theta\subseteq
\mathbb R^d\}$ be dominated by a common sigma-finite measure, with $\Theta$
open, and suppose the model is QMD at an interior $\theta_0$ with score $s$
and information $I=E_{\theta_0}[ss^T]$. Let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be IID
$P_{\theta_0}$, and for each fixed local sequence $h_n\to h$ set
$u_n=h_n/\sqrt n$. Then the local product laws
$P_{\theta_0+u_n}^{\otimes n}$ admit mean-one likelihood-ratio proxies
$L_n$ relative to $P_{\theta_0}^{\otimes n}$ such that
$$\left\|P_{\theta_0+u_n}^{\otimes n}-L_nP_{\theta_0}^{\otimes n}\right\|_{\rm TV} \to0,$$
and under $P_{\theta_0}^{\otimes n}$,
$$\log L_n=h_n^T\Delta_n-\tfrac12h^TIh+o_P(1),\qquad \Delta_n=n^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^ns(X_i)\Rightarrow N_d(0,I).$$
Thus the IID QMD experiment is LAN in the proxy sense of
[[def-lan-experiment]]. This assertion does not claim that the full local
product law has a Radon–Nikodym derivative relative to the base law.

current_steps.exact_text: By [A1, L1, F1] the path is QMD with the specified density versions. [F2] applies to the chosen sequence $u_n=h_n/\sqrt n$ and supplies the normalized proxy $L_n$, the total variation approximation, and the log expansion. Its normalizer is $1-\alpha_n>0$ for all sufficiently large $n$, since $\alpha_n=o(\|u_n\|_2^2)$ and $u_n\to0$. [A1, F1, F2, L1, given]

The score lemma gives $E_{\theta_0}s=0$ and covariance $E_{\theta_0}[ss^T]=I<\infty$. Thus [F3] applies to $s(X_i)$ and yields $\Delta_n\Rightarrow N_d(0,I)$, including singular information. [A1, F3, F5, given]

For each fixed $h$, steps 1.1 and 1.2 give the proxy approximation, the log expansion and the Gaussian central-sequence limit required in [F4]. Hence the local experiment is LAN. The proof used the full likelihood only for the normalized absolutely continuous component; singular mass is handled by the total-variation bound in [F2]. This proves the stated proxy-LAN conclusion. [F2, F4, step 1.1, step 1.2] ∎

source_guards.exact_current_claim:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $X_1,X_2,\ldots$ be iid with law
$P_{\theta_0}$ in a dominated parametric model
$\{P_\theta:\theta\in\Theta\}$, where $\Theta$ is open in $\mathbb R^d$,
$d\ge1$, and $\theta_0\in\Theta$. Let $p_\theta$ be densities with respect
to one supplied sigma-finite measure. Suppose the model is QMD at $\theta_0$
with score $s_{\theta_0}$ and positive-definite information
$I=\mathbb E_{\theta_0}[s_{\theta_0}s_{\theta_0}^T]$. Assume there are a
neighborhood $V$ of $\theta_0$ and a nonnegative measurable $L$ with
$\mathbb E_{\theta_0}L^2<\infty$ such that, on one $P_{\theta_0}$-full set,
$$
|\log p_{\theta_1}(x)-\log p_{\theta_2}(x)|\le L(x)\|\theta_1-\theta_2\| \qquad(\theta_1,\theta_2\in V).
$$
Suppose a measurable exact MLE $\hat\theta_n$ exists and is consistent, in
the sense that $P_{\theta_0}(\|\hat\theta_n-\theta_0\|>\varepsilon)\to0$
for every $\varepsilon>0$. Then
$$\sqrt n(\hat\theta_n-\theta_0)=I^{-1}\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_{i=1}^n s_{\theta_0}(X_i)+o_{P_{\theta_0}}(1)\ \Rightarrow\ N_d(0,I^{-1}).$$
Under the same local hypotheses, every consistent measurable exact likelihood
maximizer over a possibly $n$-dependent subset that contains $\theta_0$ is
also root-$n$ bounded in probability.
The conclusion is asymptotic; it gives no exact finite-sample normal law.

current_steps.exact_text: Write $P_0=P_{\theta_0}$, $S_0=\{p_{\theta_0}>0\}$, and $r_t=\sqrt{p_{\theta_0+t}}-\sqrt{p_{\theta_0}}- \tfrac12t^Ts_{\theta_0}\sqrt{p_{\theta_0}}$. By [F3], $\|r_t\|_{L^2(\mu)}=o(\|t\|)$, and [F12] gives $\mathbb E_0s_{\theta_0}=0$. On $S_0^c$ both $\sqrt{p_{\theta_0}}$ and $s_{\theta_0}\sqrt{p_{\theta_0}}$ vanish, so the probability mass $\alpha_t=\int_{S_0^c}p_{\theta_0+t}\,d\mu$ is $o(\|t\|^2)$. Expanding the QMD approximation in [F3] and applying [F9] to its cross term gives $\|\sqrt{p_{\theta_0+t}}-\sqrt{p_{\theta_0}}\|_2^2= \tfrac14t^TIt+o(\|t\|^2)$. [A2, F1, F2, F3, F9, F12, algebra]

Normalize the absolutely continuous part on $S_0$ by $q_t=p_{\theta_0+t}\mathbf1_{S_0}/(1-\alpha_t)$, and put $a_t=\sqrt{q_t/p_{\theta_0}}-1$ on $S_0$. Since $\alpha_t=o(\|t\|^2)$, [F3] gives $a_t=\tfrac12t^Ts_{\theta_0}+o_{L^2(P_0)}(\|t\|)$, so $\mathbb E_0a_t^2=\tfrac14t^TIt+o(\|t\|^2)$ and $2\mathbb E_0a_t+\mathbb E_0a_t^2=0$ from $\mathbb E_0(1+a_t)^2=1$. The local envelope makes $f_t=\log(p_{\theta_0+t}/p_{\theta_0})$ square-integrable on $S_0$ and $\|f_t\|_2=O(\|t\|)$. Along every sequence $t\to0$ with $t/\|t\|\to u$, the $L^2$ convergence of $a_t/\|t\|$ has an almost-everywhere convergent subsequence. On it, $2\log(1+a_t)/\|t\|\to u^Ts_{\theta_0}$ pointwise. Since $|f_t|/\|t\|\le L$ and $s_{\theta_0}\in L^2(P_0)$, $|f_t/\|t\|-u^Ts_{\theta_0}|^2\le2L^2+2\|s_{\theta_0}\|^2$; dominated convergence [F10] gives convergence in $L^2$ along that subsequence. Every subsequence has such a subsubsequence, so convergence holds for the full sequence. Sequential compactness of the unit sphere therefore yields $f_t=t^Ts_{\theta_0}+o_{L^2(P_0)}(\|t\|)$. Moreover, the squares $a_t^2/\|t\|^2$ are uniformly integrable because $a_t/\|t\|$ converges in $L^2$ along every convergent direction. Taking the logarithm expansion in expectation requires a tail check. Fix $\varepsilon>0$. On $|a_t|\le\varepsilon$, the Taylor remainder $2\log(1+a_t)-2a_t+a_t^2$ is bounded by $\omega(\varepsilon)a_t^2$, where $\omega(\varepsilon)\to0$. Uniform integrability gives $\mathbb E_0[a_t^2\mathbf1_{|a_t|>\varepsilon}] =o(\|t\|^2)$ and therefore $P_0(|a_t|>\varepsilon)=o(\|t\|^2)$. On this tail, $|2\log(1+a_t)|\le |f_t|+|\log(1-\alpha_t)|$; its expectation is $o(\|t\|^2)$ by the envelope, Cauchy–Schwarz [F9], and the tail probability. The tail expectations of $|a_t|$ and $a_t^2$ are also $o(\|t\|^2)$ by [F9] and uniform integrability. Letting $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ proves that the expected Taylor remainder is $o(\|t\|^2)$. Taking expectations then gives $\mathbb E_0 f_t=2\mathbb E_0a_t-\mathbb E_0a_t^2+o(\|t\|^2) =-\tfrac12t^TIt+o(\|t\|^2);$ the normalization term $\log(1-\alpha_t)$ is $o(\|t\|^2)$. [A2, A3, F2, F3, F9, F10, step 1.1, algebra]

The squared Hellinger distance $H^2(P_{\theta_0+t},P_0)=\int(\sqrt{p_{\theta_0+t}}-\sqrt{p_{\theta_0}})^2d\mu$ equals $\tfrac14t^TIt+o(\|t\|^2)$ by step 1.1. The affinity $\rho_t=\int\sqrt{p_{\theta_0+t}p_{\theta_0}}d\mu=1-H^2/2$. On $S_0$ let $Y=\sqrt{p_{\theta_0+t}/p_{\theta_0}}$, so $\mathbb E_0Y=\rho_t$. For $y>0$, $\log y\le\log\rho_t+(y-\rho_t)/\rho_t$ follows from $z-1-\log z\ge0$ for $z=y/\rho_t$, since this function has derivative $1-1/z$ and its minimum is $0$ at $z=1$; integrating gives $P_0f_t=2\mathbb E_0\log Y\le2\log\rho_t$. Since $\log(1-x)\le-x$ for $0\le x<1$ because $-x-\log(1-x)$ has derivative $x/(1-x)\ge0$ and value $0$ at $x=0$. Thus $2\log\rho_t\le-H^2$, so for some $c,\delta>0$, $P_0f_t\le-c\|t\|^2$ whenever $\|t\|\le\delta_0$. [step 1.1, algebra]

Let $\mathbb G_n f=\sqrt n(P_nf-P_0f)$ for the empirical measure $P_n$. The pointwise Lipschitz envelope gives $\|f_t-f_v\|_{L^2(P_0)}\le\|L\|_2\|t-v\|$. The sample and mean processes are continuous in $t$ on compact local balls, so their suprema equal suprema over countable dense subsets and are measurable. To bound the local supremum, take an independent ghost sample $X'_1,\ldots,X'_n$. For each fixed original sample, the supremum of absolute values is convex in the ghost sample vector, so Jensen's inequality replaces $P_0f$ by $n^{-1}\sum_i f(X'_i)$ in the expected supremum. Swapping each pair $(X_i,X'_i)$ with an independent sign and then using the triangle inequality bounds that supremum by twice the expected conditional Rademacher supremum. Condition on the observations for the latter. For the conditional Rademacher process $R_n(f)=n^{-1/2}\sum_i\epsilon_i f(X_i)$, Hoeffding's exponential bound $\mathbb E_\epsilon e^{\lambda(R_n(f)-R_n(g))}= \prod_i\cosh(\lambda(f-g)(X_i)/\sqrt n)\le \exp\{\lambda^2P_n(f-g)^2/2\}$, since $\log\cosh u\le u^2/2$ (integrate $\tanh u\le u$ for $u\ge0$ and use evenness), makes each increment sub-Gaussian with variance proxy $P_n(f-g)^2\le P_nL^2\|t-v\|^2$. Choose successively finer dyadic Euclidean nets of the radius-$r$ parameter ball. At level $k$ the net has at most $(C2^k)^d$ points, each increment from its level-$(k-1)$ parent has scale at most $Cr2^{-k}(P_nL^2)^{1/2}$, and the expected maximum of $N$ centered sub-Gaussian variables of scale $\sigma$ is at most $\sigma\sqrt{2\log(2N)}$, by the exponential-moment bound and optimizing $\lambda$. Summing the resulting bounds uses the convergent series $\sum_{k\ge1}2^{-k}\sqrt{k}$ and gives $\mathbb E_\epsilon\sup_{\|t\|\le r}|R_n(f_t-f_0)|\le C_dr(P_nL^2)^{1/2}$. Symmetrization and $\mathbb E(P_nL^2)^{1/2}\le(P_0L^2)^{1/2}$ therefore give $\mathbb E\sup_{\|t\|\le r}|\mathbb G_n(f_t-f_0)|\le C_d r\|L\|_2.$ For $r_t=f_t-t^Ts_{\theta_0}$, step 2.1 gives $\sup_{\|t\|\le M/\sqrt n}P_0r_t^2=o(n^{-1})$, and increments have the square-integrable pointwise envelope $L+\|s_{\theta_0}\|$. Fix a mesh $\varepsilon>0$ and cover the bounded $h$-ball by finitely many mesh-$\varepsilon$ points. At each center $h_j$, the variance of $\sqrt n\mathbb G_nr_{h_j/\sqrt n}$ is $n\operatorname{Var}_0(r_{h_j/\sqrt n})\le nP_0r_{h_j/\sqrt n}^2=o(1)$, so Chebyshev and finiteness of the net make the maximum over centers $o_P(1)$. For increments within cells, form $g_h=r_{h/\sqrt n}-r_{h_j/\sqrt n}$, where $h_j$ is the center of the cell containing $h$. Each $g_h$ is pointwise bounded by $\varepsilon(L+\|s_{\theta_0}\|)/\sqrt n$. Apply conditional Rademacher chaining to the union of cell classes: at dyadic level $k$ there are at most $C_M\varepsilon^{-d}2^{kd}$ links, each with conditional scale at most $C\varepsilon2^{-k}(P_n(L+\|s_{\theta_0}\|)^2)^{1/2}$ after the $\sqrt n$ normalization. Markov's inequality then shows that these cell increments vanish in probability as $\varepsilon\downarrow0$. Letting $n\to\infty$ and then $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ proves $\sup_{\|h\|\le M}|\sqrt n\mathbb G_nr_{h/\sqrt n}|=o_P(1)$. Thus, for each fixed $M$, uniformly over $\|h\|\le M$, $$\ell_n(\theta_0+h/\sqrt n)-\ell_n(\theta_0)=h^T\Delta_n-\tfrac12h^TIh+o_{P_0}(1),\qquad\Delta_n=n^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^ns_{\theta_0}(X_i).$$ The expectation term is step 2.1; the centered term follows by writing $f_t=t^Ts_{\theta_0}+(f_t-t^Ts_{\theta_0})$ and using the two net bounds. Reduce $\delta_0$ if needed so the log envelope holds on the radius $2\delta_0$ ball, and put $\delta=\delta_0/2$. Consistency makes $\hat\theta_n$ lie within $\delta$ of $\theta_0$ with probability tending to one. On the dyadic shells $r_j\le\|t\|\le2r_j$ with $r_j=2^jM/\sqrt n$, exact maximization and $\ell_n(\hat\theta_n)\ge\ell_n(\theta_0)$ require $\sqrt n\sup_{\|t\|\le2r_j}|\mathbb G_nf_t|\ge c n r_j^2$. The expectation bound in step 3.1 and Markov's inequality [F11] bound the probability of this event by $C/(\sqrt n r_j)=C/(2^jM)$. Summing the geometric series and then letting $M\to\infty$ proves $\sqrt n(\hat\theta_n-\theta_0)=O_{P_0}(1)$ using [F4]. The argument used only consistency, feasibility of $\theta_0$, and the maximizing inequality; it therefore proves the same bound for any exact maximizer over a subset containing $\theta_0$. [A3, F4, F11, step 3.1, step 2.2, algebra]

Put $\hat h_n=\sqrt n(\hat\theta_n-\theta_0)$ and $h_n^*=I^{-1}\Delta_n$. The multivariate CLT [F7] and [F5] make $h_n^*=O_{P_0}(1)$; step 4.1 makes $\hat h_n=O_{P_0}(1)$. For $Q_n(h)=h^T\Delta_n-\tfrac12h^TIh$, $Q_n(h_n^*)-Q_n(h)=\tfrac12(h-h_n^*)^TI(h-h_n^*) \ge\tfrac12\lambda_{\min}(I)\|h-h_n^*\|^2.$ Uniform convergence on bounded balls in step 3.1, feasibility of bounded local $h$ because $\theta_0$ is interior, and exact MLE maximization therefore force $\hat h_n-h_n^*=o_{P_0}(1)$. [A3, F4, F5, F7, step 3.1, step 4.1, algebra]

The CLT [F7] gives $\Delta_n\Rightarrow N_d(0,I)$; the limiting law exists by [F8]. Since $I$ is invertible, $h_n^*=I^{-1}\Delta_n\Rightarrow N_d(0,I^{-1})$ by the continuous linear map. Combining this with step 5.1 by [F6] proves both the asymptotic linear representation and the stated normal limit. AC is used only through [F7]–[F8]. [A1, A2, F4, F6, F7, F8, step 5.1] ∎

source_guards.exact_current_claim: Let $p\in\mathbb N_0$ and let $\xi$ be a clamped knot vector as in [[def-b-spline-space-and-basis]]. The recursively defined degree-$p$ B-splines are nonnegative, are supported on $[\xi_j,\xi_{j+p+1}]$, and are piecewise polynomials of degree at most $p$. At a knot of multiplicity $\mu\le p$, each B-spline is $C^{p-\mu}$; multiplicity $p+1$ imposes no continuity requirement. On every nonempty knot interval $[\xi_m,\xi_{m+1})$, the active functions $B_{m-p,p,\xi},\ldots,B_{m,p,\xi}$ form a basis of $\mathcal P_p$ and sum to one. Globally, the $n$ B-splines form a basis of $S_{p,\xi}$. In particular, every $q\in\mathcal P_p$ has a unique expansion $q=\sum_{j=1}^n c_jB_{j,p,\xi}$ on $[a,b]$.

current_steps.exact_text: For $p=0$, support, piecewise degree, and nonnegativity follow from the indicator definition in [F1]. Inductively, each degree-$p$ term is a lower-degree spline multiplied by an affine factor; on the lower-degree spline's support that factor is nonnegative, and the two supports lie inside $[\xi_j, \xi_{j+p+1}]$. Thus support, degree at most $p$, and nonnegativity hold for every $p$. [A1, F1, algebra]

Define $\psi_{j,0}(y)=1$ and $\psi_{j,p}(y)=\prod_{r=1}^{p}(y-\xi_{j+r})$. Factoring $\psi_{j,p-1}$ gives $(y-x)\psi_{j,p-1}(y)=\frac{x-\xi_j}{\xi_{j+p}-\xi_j}\psi_{j,p}(y)+\frac{\xi_{j+p}-x}{\xi_{j+p}-\xi_j}\psi_{j-1,p}(y),$ with zero-denominator terms omitted. For $p=0$, $(y-x)^p=1$ is the local identity on any nonempty knot interval. If the identity holds for degree $p-1$, multiply it by $y-x$, apply the displayed dual-polynomial identity to each summand, and regroup the two contributions to each coefficient using the recurrence in [F1]. The endpoint terms vanish by local support. Hence, for $x\in[\xi_m,\xi_{m+1})$, $(y-x)^p=\sum_{i=m-p}^{m}\psi_{i,p}(y)B_{i,p,\xi}(x).$ [F1, given, algebra]

Let the distinct interior knots be $\eta_1<\cdots<\eta_s$ with multiplicities $\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_s$. For $k\ge1$ set $u_{r,k}(x)=(x-\eta_r)^k\mathbf1_{[\eta_r,\infty)}(x)$ and set $u_{r,0}(x)=\mathbf1_{[\eta_r,\infty)}(x)$; the value at $\eta_r$ follows the right-cell convention of [F1]. The functions $1,x,\ldots,x^p$ together with $u_{r,k}$ for $p-\mu_r+1\le k\le p$ span $S_{p,\xi}$: start with the polynomial on the first interval, then at each knot the difference of adjacent pieces has its derivatives through $p-\mu_r$ equal to zero, so it is a linear combination of the listed powers, including the right-continuous step when $\mu_r=p+1$. They are independent because restriction to successive knot intervals first forces the initial polynomial coefficients, then each new knot's coefficients, to vanish. Thus $\dim S_{p,\xi}=p+1+\sum_r\mu_r=n$. [A1, F1, algebra]

Differentiate the identity in step 1.2 exactly $p-k$ times in $y$ and set $y=0$, for each $0\le k\le p$. Since $\frac{d^{p-k}}{dy^{p-k}}(y-x)^p|_{y=0}=\frac{p!}{k!}(-x)^k$, this yields $x^k=\sum_{i=m-p}^{m}\left[(-1)^k\frac{k!}{p!}\psi_{i, p}^{(p-k)}(0)\right]B_{i,p,\xi}(x).$ The coefficients do not depend on $m$, so this is a single expansion valid on every knot interval. Linear combination proves reproduction of every member of $\mathcal P_p$. [A1, step 1.2, algebra]

For $p=1$, differentiating the two affine pieces gives the derivative formula below. For $p\ge2$, differentiate the recurrence in [F1] and substitute the degree-$(p-1)$ formula inductively. The coefficients of $B_{j,p-2,\xi}$ and $B_{j+2,p-2,\xi}$ become respectively $p(x-\xi_j)/((\xi_{j+p}-\xi_j)(\xi_{j+p-1}-\xi_j))$ and $-p(\xi_{j+p+1}-x)/((\xi_{j+p+1}-\xi_{j+1})(\xi_{j+p+1}-\xi_{j+2}))$; the middle coefficient is the sum $\frac{\xi_{j+p}-x-(p-1)(x-\xi_j)}{(\xi_{j+p}-\xi_j)(\xi_{j+p}-\xi_{j+1})}+\frac{-(x-\xi_{j+1})+(p-1)(\xi_{j+p+1}-x)}{(\xi_{j+p+1}-\xi_{j+1})(\xi_{j+p}-\xi_{j+1})},$ The target middle coefficient from expanding the right side of the claimed formula with [F1] is $\frac{p(\xi_{j+p}-x)}{(\xi_{j+p}-\xi_j)(\xi_{j+p}-\xi_{j+1})}-\frac{p(x-\xi_{j+1})}{(\xi_{j+p+1}-\xi_{j+1})(\xi_{j+p}-\xi_{j+1})}.$ The first summand in the previous display differs from the first target summand by $-(p-1)/(\xi_{j+p}-\xi_{j+1})$, while the second differs from the second target summand by $+(p-1)/(\xi_{j+p}-\xi_{j+1})$; these excess terms cancel. Zero-denominator terms vanish by [F1]. Thus, on each open knot interval, $B'_{j,p,\xi}=p\left(\frac{B_{j,p-1,\xi}}{\xi_{j+p}-\xi_j}-\frac{B_{j+1,p-1,\xi}}{\xi_{j+p+1}-\xi_{j+1}}\right).$ [A1, F1, step 1.2, algebra]

Taking $k=0$ in step 2.1 gives $\sum_{i=m-p}^{m}B_{i,p,\xi}(x)=1$. Step 2.1 also shows that these $p+1$ active functions span $\mathcal P_p$ on the interval. Because $\dim\mathcal P_p=p+1$, they are linearly independent there and are a local basis. [A1, step 2.1, algebra]

Induct on $p$. If the knot multiplicity $\mu\le p-1$, the lower-degree splines in the recurrence are continuous there by induction, so the recurrence makes $B_{j,p,\xi}$ continuous; the derivative formula then makes its derivative $C^{p-1-\mu}$, hence $B_{j,p,\xi}\in C^{p-\mu}$. If $\mu=p$, a B-spline whose support crosses the repeated knot has one nonzero piece on either side, namely $(x-\xi_j)^p/(\xi_{j+p}-\xi_j)^p$ and $(\xi_{j+p+1}-x)^p/(\xi_{j+p+1}-\xi_{j+1})^p$; both one-sided limits equal $1$, while any B-spline not crossing it has zero endpoint value there. If $\mu=p+1$, the required order is $C^{-1}$ and no matching is asserted. [A1, step 2.2, F1, algebra]

The smoothness and piecewise-degree properties from steps 1.1 and 3.2 put every B-spline in $S_{p,\xi}$. If a linear combination of all $n$ B-splines is zero, then on every nonempty knot interval its active coefficients vanish by the local basis property in step 3.1. Each B-spline has a nonempty support interval by the clamped-knot hypothesis, so every coefficient occurs on at least one such interval and is zero. The B-splines are therefore $n$ independent members of the $n$-dimensional space in step 1.3, hence form its basis. The unique global expansion includes every polynomial from step 2.1. [A1, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 1.3, step 1.1, step 3.2, algebra] ∎
