Assume AC. Fix $\beta>1$, $M,\tau>0$, and $0\le q<1$. For all integers
$n\ge1$, $p\ge2$ with $p\ge n^\beta$, and every radius
$$0\le c=c_{n,p}\le M n^{(1-q)/2}(\log p)^{-(3-q)/2},$$
put $a=\log(p)/n$ and $r_{n,p}=c^2a^{1-q}+a$. Over the law class
$\mathcal P_q(\tau,c)$ of [[def-weak-lq-sparse-covariance-class]], the
minimax squared operator risk of [[def-minimax-squared-operator-risk]] satisfies
$$C_1\min\{1,r_{n,p}\}\le\mathfrak R_n(\mathcal P_q(\tau,c))\le C_2\min\{1,r_{n,p}\},$$
where $0<C_1\le C_2<\infty$ depend only on $\beta,M,\tau,q$.
For $a\le1$, the unmodified estimator of
[[alg-entrywise-thresholded-sample-covariance]], with
$\lambda=8192\tau\sqrt a$, has expected squared operator risk at most
$C(q,\tau)r_{n,p}$. A rule attaining the capped upper bound in every
dimension is explicit: use that estimator when $r_{n,p}<1$, and output
the zero matrix when $r_{n,p}\ge1$. All original dimension regimes,
including super-exponential $p$, are retained; the risk saturates instead
of diverging. The raw threshold estimator alone is not claimed to attain
the cap outside its stated regime.

current_steps.exact_text: For any unit vector $v$, put $Y=v^{\mathsf T}(X-EX)$. By [F4] and layer cake [F6], $v^{\mathsf T}\Sigma v=E[Y^2]=\int_0^\infty P(Y^2>u)\,du\le\int_0^\infty e^{-u/(2\tau)}\,du=2\tau$. By [F5], $\Sigma$ is symmetric positive semidefinite, so [F7] gives $\|\Sigma\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le2\tau$. The constant zero estimator therefore has squared loss at most $4\tau^2$. If $r_{n,p}\ge1$, this proves the capped upper bound for the specified switch. If $r_{n,p}<1$, then $a<1$, and [F1] proves it for the threshold branch. The switch is measurable, since its branch depends only on the known dimensions and class radius; the threshold operations are measurable entrywise. [given, F1, F4, F5, F6, F7, algebra]

Let $P_0$ and $v$ be the fixed constants in [F3]. For $p<P_0$, $n\le p^{1/\beta}<P_0^{1/\beta}$, so $a\ge\log2/P_0^{1/\beta}$. Thus [F2] is bounded below by a positive fixed-parameter constant, which dominates a constant multiple of $\min\{1,r_{n,p}\}\le1$. For $a\ge1$, [F2] likewise gives this constant lower bound, regardless of $p$. These arguments cover all finite-size and saturated-dimension cases without a hidden asymptotic restriction. [given, F2, F3, algebra]

It remains to consider $p\ge P_0$ and $a<1$. If $c/[2(sv\sqrt a)^q]<2$, then $c^2a^{1-q}<16(sv)^{2q}a$, and [F2] alone bounds the risk below by a positive fixed-parameter multiple of $r_{n,p}$; this includes all effective sparse counts rounding to zero and $q=0$. Otherwise [F3] supplies the sparse term, while [F2] supplies the $a$ term. The maximum of two nonnegative lower bounds is at least half their sum, giving a fixed-parameter multiple of $r_{n,p}$ and hence of its cap. Combining with step 1.2 and the upper bound proves the result. [given, F2, F3, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

source_guards.exact_current_claim:
Let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be iid from $\mathcal P_q(\tau,c_{n,p})$ of [[def-weak-lq-sparse-covariance-class]], with $n\ge1$, $p\ge2$, and $\tau>0$. Let $u>0$ and let $\widehat\Sigma^\ast$ be the sample-centered covariance. Then
$$\mathbb P\!\left(\max_{1\le j,k\le p}|\widehat\sigma^\ast_{jk}-\sigma_{jk}| \le192\tau\left(\sqrt{\frac un}+\frac un\right)\right)\ge1-2pe^{-u}-2p^2e^{-2u}.$$
In particular $u=\log(8p^4)$ gives the original probability $1-p^{-2}$.
No independence between coordinates of a single observation is assumed.

current_steps.exact_text: Put $U_i=X_i-\mu$. For coordinate unit vectors $e_j,e_k$, [F1] gives the required tail bounds for $U_{ij}$ and $U_{ik}$. Hence [F2] makes $W_i^{jk}=U_{ij}U_{ik}-\sigma_{jk}$ centered sub-exponential with parameters $(1024\tau^2,16\tau)$. For fixed $(j,k)$ these variables are independent across $i$ by [F6]. [F1, F2, F6, F8, given]

By [F4], each $U_{ij}$ is sub-Gaussian with proxy $64\tau$. Independence across $i$ and [F7] give $\mathbb E e^{\lambda n^{-1}\sum_iU_{ij}}\le\prod_i e^{32\tau\lambda^2/n^2}=e^{32\tau\lambda^2/n},$ so each $\bar U_j=n^{-1}\sum_iU_{ij}$ has proxy $64\tau/n$. Apply [F5] at $s=\sqrt{128\tau u/n}$ to obtain $\mathbb P\!\left(\max_j|\bar U_j|>s\right)\le2p e^{-u}.$ [F4, F5, F6, F7, algebra]

Set $r=u/n$ and $t=64\tau(\sqrt r+r)$. Applying [F3] to $n^{-1}\sum_iW_i^{jk}$ gives $\mathbb P\!\left(\left|n^{-1}\sum_iW_i^{jk}\right|>t\right)\le2\exp\!\left[-\frac12\min\!\left\{\frac{nt^2}{1024\tau^2},\frac{nt}{16\tau}\right\}\right]\le2e^{-2u},$ because each expression inside the minimum is at least $4u$. A union bound over $p^2$ ordered pairs gives failure probability at most $2p^2e^{-2u}$. [F3, F9, step 1.1, algebra]

Expanding [F8] gives $\widehat\sigma^\ast_{jk}=n^{-1}\sum_iU_{ij}U_{ik}-\bar U_j\bar U_k$. On the intersection of the mean event in step 1.2 and the entrywise event in step 2.1, $|\bar U_j\bar U_k|\le(\bar U_j^2+\bar U_k^2)/2\le s^2$, so every entry error is at most $64\tau(\sqrt r+r)+128\tau r\le192\tau(\sqrt r+r).$ The two failure probabilities sum to at most $2pe^{-u}+2p^2e^{-2u}$ by [F9]. At $u=\log(8p^4)$ this is at most $p^{-2}$, proving the original specialization as well. [F8, F9, step 2.1, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

source_guards.exact_current_claim:
Assume the Axiom of Choice (AC), as required by the library's multivariate iid central limit theorem. Let $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ be a measurable space, let $\Theta\subset\mathbb R^d$ be open with its Borel sigma-algebra, and let $\theta_0\in\Theta$. Let $X_1,X_2,\ldots$ be iid $\mathcal X$-valued observations with law $P$. Let $\psi:\Theta\times\mathcal X\to\mathbb R^d$ be jointly measurable and satisfy $P\|\psi_\theta\|<\infty$ for every $\theta\in\Theta$; write $\psi_\theta(x)=\psi(\theta,x)$. Let $\hat\theta_n:(\mathcal X^n,\mathcal A^{\otimes n})\to(\Theta,\mathcal B(\Theta))$ be a measurable estimator sequence as in [[def-estimator-sequence-in-iid-experiments]] and a Z-estimator as in [[def-z-estimator]], with the stronger root-rate condition below. Write
$$P\psi_\theta=\mathbb E[\psi_\theta(X_1)],\qquad P_n\psi_\theta=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\psi_\theta(X_i),\qquad \mathbb G_n\psi_\theta=\sqrt n(P_n-P)\psi_\theta.$$
Assume the displayed random vectors and suprema below are measurable, and suppose:

1. $\|\hat\theta_n-\theta_0\|=o_P(1)$ and $\sqrt n\,\|P_n\psi_{\hat\theta_n}\|=o_P(1)$.
2. $P\psi_{\theta_0}=0$, $P\|\psi_{\theta_0}\|^2<\infty$, and $\Sigma=P[\psi_{\theta_0}\psi_{\theta_0}^{T}]$.
3. The mean map $\Psi(\theta)=P\psi_\theta$ has expansion $\Psi(\theta_0+h)=Vh+\rho(h)$ with $V$ nonsingular and $\|\rho(h)\|/\|h\|\to0$ as $h\to0$, $h\ne0$.
4. The local stochastic-equicontinuity condition holds: for every $\varepsilon>0$,
$$\lim_{\delta\downarrow0}\limsup_{n\to\infty}P^n\!\left(\sup_{\theta\in\Theta:\,\|\theta-\theta_0\|<\delta}\|\mathbb G_n(\psi_\theta-\psi_{\theta_0})\|>\varepsilon\right)=0.$$

Here $P^n$ denotes the product sampling law of $(X_1,\ldots,X_n)$.

Then
$$\sqrt n(\hat\theta_n-\theta_0)=-V^{-1}\mathbb G_n\psi_{\theta_0}+o_P(1)\Rightarrow N_d(0,V^{-1}\Sigma V^{-T}).$$
This theorem assumes consistency and the local empirical-process condition; it asserts neither. The local equicontinuity condition is the direct process hypothesis used in the proof, and consistency alone does not replace it.

current_steps.exact_text: Fix $\varepsilon,\eta>0$. By [A2] choose $\delta>0$ such that the limiting upper probability of the displayed supremum exceeding $\varepsilon$ is at most $\eta$. By [A1], $P^n(\|\hat\theta_n-\theta_0\|\ge\delta)\to0$. On the complementary event, $\|\mathbb G_n(\psi_{\hat\theta_n}-\psi_{\theta_0})\|$ is bounded by that supremum. Hence its limiting upper tail probability is at most $\eta$; letting $\eta\downarrow0$ proves $\mathbb G_n(\psi_{\hat\theta_n}-\psi_{\theta_0})=o_P(1)$. [A1, A2, choose]

By [F12], applying the same measurable map $\psi_{\theta_0}$ to the iid observations preserves independence; identical distribution follows because every $X_i$ has the same law. By [A4] and [F5], $\mathbb G_n\psi_{\theta_0}=n^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^n\psi_{\theta_0}(X_i)$ is a centered iid sum with finite covariance $\Sigma$. AC is available by [F9], so [F7] gives $\mathbb G_n\psi_{\theta_0}\Rightarrow N_d(0,\Sigma)$, where convergence in distribution is weak convergence of laws by [F4]. In particular $\mathbb G_n\psi_{\theta_0}=O_P(1)$ by [F2]. [A4, F2, F4, F5, F7, F9, F12]

Put $h_n=\hat\theta_n-\theta_0$ and $W_n=\sqrt n\,h_n$. By [F10]–[F11], the estimator and root have the stated Z-estimator and data-measurability conventions; [A1] imposes the stronger root-rate residual, which is also $o_P(1)$ since $n^{-1/2}\le1$. The identity $\sqrt nP_n\psi_{\hat\theta_n}=\mathbb G_n\psi_{\hat\theta_n}+\sqrt n\Psi(\hat\theta_n)$, [A1], step 1.1 and the derivative expansion in [A3], as specified by [F6], give $VW_n+\sqrt n\,\rho(h_n)=-\mathbb G_n\psi_{\theta_0}+o_P(1)$. Moreover $\|\rho(h_n)\|/\|h_n\|=o_P(1)$ by [A1] and [A3], with the ratio set to zero when $h_n=0$. [A1, A3, F6, F10, F11, step 1.1, algebra]

Since $V$ is nonsingular, [A3] and step 2.1 imply $\|W_n\|\le\|V^{-1}\|(\|\mathbb G_n\psi_{\theta_0}\|+e_n+a_n\|W_n\|)$, where $e_n=o_P(1)$ and $a_n=\|\rho(h_n)\|/\|h_n\|=o_P(1)$ (set $a_n=0$ if $h_n=0$). With probability tending to one, $\|V^{-1}\|a_n\le1/2$. Absorbing that term and using $\mathbb G_n\psi_{\theta_0}=O_P(1)$ from step 1.2 proves $W_n=O_P(1)$. [A3, F2, step 1.2, step 2.1, algebra]

Now $\sqrt n\,\rho(h_n)=o_P(1)$ because it is the product of $\|W_n\|=O_P(1)$ and $\|\rho(h_n)\|/\|h_n\|=o_P(1)$. Substituting into step 2.1 gives $W_n=-V^{-1}\mathbb G_n\psi_{\theta_0}+o_P(1)$. [A3, F1, F2, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra]

By [F4], [F7], and [F8], the continuous linear image $-V^{-1}\mathbb G_n\psi_{\theta_0}$ converges to a centered Gaussian with covariance $V^{-1}\Sigma V^{-T}$: for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$, the projection of $N_d(0,\Sigma)$ along $-V^{-T}u$ is centered normal with variance $u^TV^{-1}\Sigma V^{-T}u$. Applying [F3] to the $o_P(1)$ remainder in step 4.1 proves the asserted normal limit. AC is used in the multivariate iid CLT and the normal-law supplier, not in the stochastic-order or Taylor steps. [F3, F4, F7, F8, F9, step 1.2, step 4.1] ∎

source_guards.exact_current_claim:
Let $H$ be a separable real Hilbert space, let $n\ge1$, and let $1\le k\le n$ be an integer. Given $(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\in H^n$, put $q=\lfloor n/k\rfloor$ and $r=n-kq$. Form consecutive blocks $B_1,\ldots,B_k$ in index order, with $|B_j|=q+1$ for $j\le r$ and $|B_j|=q$ for $j>r$. Compute the block means $m_j=|B_j|^{-1}\sum_{i\in B_j}x_i$. Return the unique minimum-norm point of
$$
\operatorname*{argmin}_{z\in H}\sum_{j=1}^k\|z-m_j\|.
$$

The objective minimizers are called geometric medians of the block means. The minimum-norm rule makes the output single-valued. Existence, uniqueness of that selected point, and Borel measurability as a function of the input tuple are proved in [[lem-measurable-minimum-norm-geometric-median-selection]].

$$

$$
For $v\in S^{d-1}$, sort $\langle\widetilde Y_i,v\rangle$ nondecreasingly and let $\alpha_v$ and $\beta_v$ be its order statistics of ranks $\lceil\varepsilon N/2\rceil$ and $\lceil(1-\varepsilon/2)N\rceil$. Write $\phi_{a,b}(t)=\min\{b,\max\{a,t\}\}$. For $Q>0$ define
$$U_Q(v)=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\phi_{\alpha_v-Q,\,\beta_v+Q}(\langle\widetilde X_i,v\rangle),\qquad \Gamma(v,Q)=\{z\in\mathbb R^d:|\langle z,v\rangle-U_Q(v)|\le2\varepsilon Q\}.$$
and $\Gamma(Q)=\bigcap_{v\in S^{d-1}}\Gamma(v,Q)$. For each $j\in\mathbb Z$, put
$$
K_j=\bigcap_{i\ge j}\Gamma(2^i),\qquad S=\{j\in\mathbb Z:K_j\ne\varnothing\}.
$$
Return the unique minimum-norm point of $K_j$ if $S$ has least element $j$; if $S=\mathbb Z$, return the unique minimum-norm point of $\bigcap_{i\in\mathbb Z}\Gamma(2^i)$; if $S=\varnothing$, return the first-half sample mean $N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^N\widetilde X_i$. This three-branch selector is total on the displayed input domain; its existence and Borel measurability are proved in [[lem-multivariate-trimmed-mean-selector-total-and-measurable]].

Let $N\ge1$ be an integer, let $\eta\ge0$, $0<\delta<1$, and set
$$
\varepsilon=8\eta+\frac{12\log(4/\delta)}{N}.

The procedure is admissible when $0<\varepsilon\le1/4$. Its input is two observed real samples $\widetilde X_1,\ldots,\widetilde X_N$ and $\widetilde Y_1,\ldots,\widetilde Y_N$. Sort the second sample nondecreasingly as $\widetilde Y^*_{(1)}\le\cdots\le\widetilde Y^*_{(N)}$ and define $r(u)=\lceil uN\rceil$ for $0<u\le1$. Set
$$
\alpha=\widetilde Y^*_{(r(\varepsilon))},\qquad \beta=\widetilde Y^*_{(r(1-\varepsilon))},
$$
and, for $\alpha\le\beta$, let $\phi_{\alpha,\beta}(x)=\min\{\beta,\max\{\alpha,x\}\}$. Return
$$
\widehat\mu=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\phi_{\alpha,\beta}(\widetilde X_i).
$$
The operation is defined for every admissible input, including tied observations.

This definition alone does not assert regularity under local alternatives, pathwise differentiability of $\psi$, or asymptotic normality.

$$p(y)=\frac1{m+1}\sum_{i=1}^{m+1}\mathbf1\{R_i(y)\ge R_{m+1}(y)\}.$$

$$p_U(y)=\frac{\#\{i\le m:R_i(y)>r\}+U\bigl(1+\#\{i\le m:R_i(y)=r\}\bigr)}{m+1}.$$

A **causal Bernoulli shift** with innovation law $\nu$ is a process
$$X_t=f(\delta_t,\delta_{t-1},\delta_{t-2},\ldots),\qquad t\in\mathbb Z,$$
where $f:S^{\mathbb N_0}\to H$ is measurable from the product sigma-algebra $\mathcal S^{\otimes\mathbb N_0}$ to the Borel sigma-algebra of $H$. This product-measurability formulation is meaningful for a merely measurable innovation space $S$.

On an independent product extension, take replacement innovations $\delta'_{t,m,k}$, indexed by $t\in\mathbb Z$, $m\in\mathbb N_0$, and integers $k\le t-m$, all with law $\nu$, mutually independent, and independent of the original innovations. and define the full replacement $X_{t,0}=f(\delta'_{t,0,t},\delta'_{t,0,t-1},\ldots)$. Each $X_{t,m}$ has the same marginal law as $X_t$; for fixed $m\ge1$ the sequence $(X_{t,m})_{t\in\mathbb Z}$ is strictly stationary and $m$-dependent because its original-innovation windows have length $m$ and its replacement arrays are independent across $t$.

Consequently $D_{t,m}:=X_t-X_{t,m}$ is stationary and $\|D_{t,m}\|_{L^2(H)}=\delta_m$ for every $t$.

$$\delta_m=\|X_0-X_{0,m}\|_{L^2(H)},\qquad m\ge0.$$

$$\mathbb E\|X_0\|_H^2<\infty\qquad\hbox{and}\qquad\sum_{m\ge1}\delta_m<\infty.$$

Subtracting its partial sums from those for $X_0$ cancels the terms $k<m$ and leaves $$X_0-X_{0,m}=e\sum_{k=m}^{\infty}\frac{\epsilon_{-k}-\epsilon'_{0,m,-k}}{k+1} \quad\text{in }L^2.$$ The summands are independent, centered, and have variance $2/(k+1)^2$ by [F4]; finite-tail variance computation followed by $L^2$ convergence therefore gives $\delta_m^2=2\sum_{k=m}^{\infty}(k+1)^{-2}$. [F1, F2, F4, step 2.1, algebra]

Since $x\mapsto x^{-2}$ is decreasing on $(0,\infty)$, $$\sum_{k=m}^{\infty}(k+1)^{-2} \ge\int_{m+1}^{\infty}x^{-2}\,dx=\frac1{m+1}.$$ Thus $\delta_m\ge\sqrt{2/(m+1)}$, and the decreasing-function integral comparison gives $$\sum_{m\ge1}\delta_m\ge\sqrt2\sum_{j\ge2}j^{-1/2}\ge\sqrt2\int_2^{\infty}x^{-1/2}\,dx=+\infty$$ by [F6]. The moment condition holds by step 2.1, but the required dependence-coefficient summability fails. [F6, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

source_guards.exact_current_claim:
Let $(S_i,\Sigma_i)$, $1\le i\le n$, be finitely many measurable spaces, with
$n\ge1$, and equip $\prod_{i=1}^nS_i$ with its finite product sigma-algebra.
If $f_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ are measurable, then the tuple
$f=(f_1,\ldots,f_n)$ is measurable. If all factors equal one measurable space
$(S,\Sigma)$, every coordinate permutation $\tau_\pi:S^n\to S^n$ is
measurable, where $(\tau_\pi z)_i=z_{\pi(i)}$.

current_steps.exact_text: By induction on $n$, the finite product sigma-algebra is generated by the $n$-coordinate rectangles. The base case is $n=1$. At the induction step, let $\mathcal S$ be the sigma-algebra generated by $(n+1)$-coordinate rectangles. For each measurable last-coordinate set $B$, the class of first-coordinate sets $A$ with $A\times B\in\mathcal S$ is a sigma-algebra: it contains the whole first product since the whole-first-product times $B$ is a coordinate rectangle, and complements and countable unions follow by relative difference inside that set and by countable unions. It contains the $n$-coordinate rectangles by construction, so it contains the recursively defined $n$-fold product sigma-algebra. Thus $\mathcal S$ contains every rectangle used in the recursive binary product. Conversely, each $(n+1)$-coordinate rectangle belongs to that recursive product sigma-algebra by its defining binary rectangle clause, so the two generated sigma-algebras agree. [F1, F2, F4]

For a generating rectangle $E_1\times\cdots\times E_n$, its preimage under $f$ is $\bigcap_{i=1}^n f_i^{-1}(E_i)$. Each set in this finite intersection belongs to $\mathcal F$ by [A1], so the preimage belongs to $\mathcal F$ by [F4]. The class of target sets whose preimages under $f$ lie in $\mathcal F$ is a sigma-algebra because preimages preserve complements and countable unions; by step 1.1 it contains the generators, so it contains the product sigma-algebra and [F3] makes $f$ measurable. [A1, F1, F2, F3, F4, step 1.1]

For $\pi$ a permutation, $\tau_\pi^{-1}(E_1\times\cdots\times E_n)=E_{\pi^{-1}(1)}\times\cdots\times E_{\pi^{-1}(n)}$, which is a generating rectangle by [F2]. The same generated-sigma-algebra argument of step 2.1 proves that $\tau_\pi$ is measurable. [F1, F2, step 1.1, step 2.1] ∎

source_guards.exact_current_claim:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $d\ge1$ and $m\ge0$ be finite integers, and let $(Y_t)_{t\in\mathbb Z}$ be a centered strictly stationary sequence of $\mathbb R^d$-valued random vectors with $\mathbb E\|Y_0\|^2<\infty$. Strict stationarity means that every finite-dimensional law is invariant under integer shifts. Assume $m$-dependence: for each $a\in\mathbb Z$, the sigma-algebras generated by $(Y_t)_{t\le a}$ and $(Y_t)_{t\ge a+m+1}$ are independent, in the sense of [[def-independent-sigma-algebras-and-events]]. Set
$$\Sigma_m=\sum_{|j|\le m}\operatorname{Cov}(Y_0,Y_j),$$
where $\operatorname{Cov}(U,V)=\mathbb E[(U-\mathbb EU)(V-\mathbb EV)^T]$ ([[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]]). Then $\Sigma_m$ is symmetric positive semidefinite and
$$\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_{t=1}^nY_t\ \Rightarrow\ N_d(0,\Sigma_m).$$
The conclusion allows singular $\Sigma_m$, including $\Sigma_m=0$.

current_steps.exact_text: For $h\in\mathbb Z$ put $C_h=\operatorname{Cov}(Y_0,Y_h)$. These covariance terms are finite by [F8]. Strict stationarity gives $C_{-h}=C_h^T$, and $m$-dependence gives $C_h=0$ when $|h|>m$. Expanding the finite variance of the sum yields $$\frac1n\operatorname{Cov}\!\left(\sum_{t=1}^nY_t\right)=\sum_{|h|\le m}\left(1-\frac{|h|}{n}\right)_+C_h\longrightarrow\Sigma_m.$$ Thus $\Sigma_m$ is symmetric, and for every $a\in\mathbb R^d$, $a^T\Sigma_ma$ is the limit of nonnegative variances divided by $n$, so it is nonnegative. Hence $N_d(0,\Sigma_m)$ exists by [F5]. [A1, given, F5, F8, algebra]

Fix $a\in\mathbb R^d$ and let $Z_t=a^TY_t$ and $\sigma^2=a^T\Sigma_ma$. If $\sigma^2=0$, step 1.1 gives $\mathbb E|n^{-1/2}\sum_{t=1}^nZ_t|^2\to0$; [F6] and then [F3] give convergence in distribution to zero. Suppose $\sigma^2>0$. For $K\ge1$ define $Z_t^{(K)}=\max(-K,\min(K,Z_t))-\mathbb E[\max(-K,\min(K,Z_0))]$. This is centered, stationary, $m$-dependent and bounded by $2K$; [F7] gives $\|Z_0-Z_0^{(K)}\|_2\to0$. Write $\sigma_K^2=\lim_n n^{-1}\operatorname{Var}(\sum_{t=1}^n Z_t^{(K)})=\sum_{|h|\le m}\operatorname{Cov}(Z_0^{(K)},Z_h^{(K)})$. Finite summation and [F8] give $\sigma_K^2\to\sigma^2$, so $\sigma_K^2>0$ for all sufficiently large $K$. [given, F3, F6, F7, F8, step 1.1, algebra]

Fix such a $K$, put $\ell_n=\lfloor n^{1/4}\rfloor$, and retain $q_n=\lfloor n/(\ell_n+m)\rfloor$ blocks of length $\ell_n$, with $m$ omitted indices between successive blocks. Write $b$ for the last index in a retained block. The next block starts at $b+m+1$, so $m$-dependence makes its sigma-algebra independent of the sigma-algebra generated by all earlier blocks; induction gives row-wise independence of the block sums $B_{n,r}$. If $\gamma_h^{(K)}=\operatorname{Cov}(Z_0^{(K)},Z_h^{(K)})$, stationarity gives $$\operatorname{Var}(B_{n,r})=\ell_n\gamma_0^{(K)}+2\sum_{h=1}^m(\ell_n-h)\gamma_h^{(K)},\qquad \frac{s_n^2}{n}:=\frac{q_n\operatorname{Var}(B_{n,1})}{n}\longrightarrow\sigma_K^2.$$ Here $q_n\ell_n/n\to1$ and $q_n/n\to0$. Also $|B_{n,r}|\le2K\ell_n$ and $s_n/\sqrt n\to\sigma_K>0$. Thus $q_n\ge1$ and $s_n>0$ for all sufficiently large $n$; on this tail, for each $\varepsilon>0$ every block is eventually bounded by $\varepsilon s_n$, so the Lindeberg sum is zero. Applying [F1] to this tail of rows, $s_n^{-1}\sum_rB_{n,r}\Rightarrow N(0,1)$, and [F2] gives $n^{-1/2}\sum_rB_{n,r}\Rightarrow N(0,\sigma_K^2)$. [A1, F1, F2, given, step 2.1, choose, algebra]

The omitted gaps and terminal remainder contain $r_n\le m q_n+\ell_n+m=O(n/\ell_n+\ell_n)=o(n)$ indices. For a centered $m$-dependent sequence bounded by $2K$, at most $(2m+1)r_n$ ordered pairs of omitted terms can have nonzero covariance, each covariance having absolute value at most $4K^2$. Therefore the omitted sum divided by $\sqrt n$ tends to zero in $L^2$, hence in probability by [F6]. By [F3], $n^{-1/2}\sum_{t=1}^n Z_t^{(K)}\Rightarrow N(0,\sigma_K^2)$. [F3, F6, given, step 3.1, algebra]

The centered $m$-dependent truncation errors $W_t^{(K)}=Z_t-Z_t^{(K)}$ satisfy $$\mathbb E\left|n^{-1/2}\sum_{t=1}^nW_t^{(K)}\right|^2\le(2m+1)\mathbb E|W_0^{(K)}|^2\longrightarrow0\quad(K\to\infty),$$ by expanding the variance and bounding each of its at most $2m+1$ nonzero lag terms with [F8]. For fixed real $u$, $|e^{iu x}-e^{iu y}|\le|u||x-y|$; thus the characteristic function of $n^{-1/2}\sum Z_t$ differs from that of its $K$-truncation by at most $|u|\sqrt{(2m+1)\mathbb E|W_0^{(K)}|^2}$. First taking $n\to\infty$ using step 4.1 and then $K\to\infty$ using $\sigma_K^2\to\sigma^2$ proves convergence to $e^{-u^2\sigma^2/2}$. By [F4], $n^{-1/2}\sum Z_t\Rightarrow N(0,\sigma^2)$. This also covers every projection with positive variance; the zero-variance case was handled in step 2.1. [A1, F4, F8, step 2.1, step 4.1, algebra]

Steps 2.1 and 5.1 show for every $a\in\mathbb R^d$ that $a^Tn^{-1/2}\sum_{t=1}^nY_t\Rightarrow N(0,a^T\Sigma_ma)$. These are precisely the projections of the law $N_d(0,\Sigma_m)$ established in step 1.1, so [F5] gives the asserted vector convergence, including singular and zero covariance. [A1, F5, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 5.1] ∎

source_guards.exact_current_claim:
Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ be a measurable space, let $n\ge1$, and let $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in X$. Define

$$P_n(A):=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\delta_{x_i}(A),\qquad A\in\mathcal A.$$

Then $P_n$ is a probability measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$.

current_steps.exact_text: Each summand in $P_n(A)$ is nonnegative, $P_n(\varnothing)=0$, and $P_n(X)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n1=1$ by [F1]. [given, F1, algebra]

Let $(A_j)_{j\ge1}$ be pairwise disjoint. For each $j$, let $I_j:=\{i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}:x_i\in A_j\}$. The sets $I_j$ are pairwise disjoint, and at most $n$ of them are nonempty, because each index $i$ belongs to at most one $I_j$. Their union is $\{i:x_i\in\bigcup_jA_j\}$. Hence the number of sample indices in $\bigcup_jA_j$ is $\sum_j\#I_j$, and dividing by $n$ gives $P_n(\bigcup_jA_j)=\sum_jP_n(A_j)$. [given, F1, algebra]
Steps 1.1–1.2 show that $P_n$ is a nonnegative countably additive set function with total mass one; by [F2] it is a probability measure. [step 1.1, step 1.2, F2] ∎

source_guards.exact_current_claim:
Let $H$ be a real Hilbert space, let $k\ge1$ be an integer, let $m_1,\ldots,m_k\in H$, and let $m$ minimize $F(z)=\sum_{j=1}^k\|z-m_j\|$. For $0<a<1/2$ and $r>0$, put
$$
C_a=\frac{1-a}{\sqrt{1-2a}}.
$$
If $z\in H$ satisfies $\|m-z\|>C_a r$, then more than $ak$ of the points $m_j$ satisfy $\|m_j-z\|>r$.

current_steps.exact_text: Suppose at most $ak$ points satisfy $\|m_j-z\|>r$. Write $D=\|z-m\|>C_a r>r$ and $d=(z-m)/D$. For each of the at least $(1-a)k$ remaining points, the vector $m_j-m$ is nonzero and has positive inner product with $d$, because $\langle m_j-m,d\rangle\ge D-\|m_j-z\|\ge D-r>0$. The distance from $z$ to the line through $m$ and $m_j$ is $D\sin\theta_j$, where $\theta_j$ is the angle between $m_j-m$ and $d$; it is at most $\|z-m_j\|\le r$. Hence $\cos\theta_j\ge\sqrt{1-(r/D)^2}>\sqrt{1-C_a^{-2}}=a/(1-a)$. [F2, algebra]

The right directional derivative of $F(m+td)$ at $t=0$ is $-\sum_{m_j\ne m}\cos\theta_j+\#\{j:m_j=m\}$. Each good point from step 1.1 contributes less than $-a/(1-a)$, and every other point contributes at most $1$. Since at least $(1-a)k$ points are good, this derivative is at most $k-(1-a)k(1+a/(1-a))=0$, with strict inequality from step 1.1. A negative right derivative contradicts minimality of $m$. Thus more than $ak$ points lie outside the radius-$r$ ball about $z$. [F1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

source_guards.exact_current_claim:
Let $H$ be a real Hilbert space and let $(e_k)$ be a finite or countable
orthonormal family whose finite linear span is dense in $H$. Here
orthonormal means $\langle e_j,e_k\rangle_H=1$ when $j=k$ and $0$ otherwise;
density means every $x\in H$ is arbitrarily close in norm to a finite linear
combination of the $e_k$. For $x\in H$, define
$$P_Nx=\sum_{k\le N}\langle x,e_k\rangle_H e_k,$$
using all basis vectors once $N$ reaches the size of a finite family. Then
$P_Nx\to x$ in norm and
$$\|x\|_H^2=\lim_{N\to\infty}\sum_{k\le N}|\langle x,e_k\rangle_H|^2.$$

current_steps.exact_text: Fix $x\in H$ and $N$. Orthonormality gives $\langle x-P_Nx,e_j\rangle_H=0$ for each $j\le N$, so $x-P_Nx$ is orthogonal to both $P_Nx$ and every vector in the first-$N$ span. By [F1], $$\|x\|_H^2=\|P_Nx\|_H^2+\|x-P_Nx\|_H^2, \qquad \|P_Nx\|_H^2=\sum_{k\le N}|\langle x,e_k\rangle_H|^2.$$ For any $y$ in that span, $P_Nx-y$ also lies in the span and is orthogonal to $x-P_Nx$, hence $$\|x-y\|_H^2=\|x-P_Nx\|_H^2+\|P_Nx-y\|_H^2 \ge\|x-P_Nx\|_H^2.$$ Thus $P_Nx$ is a closest vector to $x$ in the first-$N$ span. [given, F1, algebra]

Let $\varepsilon>0$. By density choose a finite linear combination $y$ of the $e_k$ with $\|x-y\|_H<\varepsilon$, and choose $N$ at least as large as every index used in $y$. Then $y$ lies in the first-$N$ span, so step 1.1 gives $\|x-P_Nx\|_H\le\|x-y\|_H<\varepsilon$. Hence $P_Nx\to x$; the first identity in step 1.1 then gives the asserted Parseval limit. For a finite family, $P_Nx=x$ once all its vectors are included. [given, step 1.1, choose, algebra] ∎

source_guards.exact_current_claim:
Assume Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. Let $H=L^2([0,1],dt;\mathbb R)$,
let $(X_t)_{t\in\mathbb Z}$ be a centered causal Bernoulli shift as in
[[def-l2-m-approximable-causal-bernoulli-shift]], and suppose it is
$L^2$-$m$-approximable. Write $\sigma=(\mathbb E\|X_0\|_H^2)^{1/2}$,
let $S_1(H)$ be the trace-class Banach space with trace norm $\|\cdot\|_1$
([[def-trace-class-operator]], [[thm-trace-class-is-a-two-sided-banach-operator-ideal]]),
write $\mathbb E_B$ for a Bochner integral, and define $x\otimes y:H\to H$ by
$(x\otimes y)h=\langle h,y\rangle_Hx$. The Bochner series
$$ \Gamma=\mathbb E_B[X_0\otimes X_0]+ \sum_{j=1}^{\infty}\bigl(\mathbb E_B[X_0\otimes X_j] +\mathbb E_B[X_j\otimes X_0]\bigr) $$
converges absolutely in trace norm to a positive self-adjoint trace-class
operator. For $S_n=\sum_{t=1}^nX_t$, the Bochner covariance operators
$\Gamma_n=n^{-1}\mathbb E_B[S_n\otimes S_n]$ satisfy
$\|\Gamma_n-\Gamma\|_1\to0$. If $\boxtimes$ is the product-kernel class from
[[lem-real-l-two-kernel-operator-is-bounded-and-rank-one-compatible]], then
$$ \kappa_j=\mathbb E_B[X_0\boxtimes X_j],\qquad \widetilde\kappa_j=\mathbb E_B[X_j\boxtimes X_0] $$
are well-defined elements of $K=L^2([0,1]^2,dt\times dt;\mathbb R)$, and
$$ c=\kappa_0+\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}(\kappa_j+\widetilde\kappa_j) $$
converges absolutely in $K$ and satisfies $T_c=\Gamma$. Equivalently, $c$ is
the design's long-run covariance-kernel series interpreted as an
$L^2([0,1]^2)$ equivalence class; no pointwise representatives are fixed.

current_steps.exact_text: Put $\sigma=(\mathbb E\|X_0\|_H^2)^{1/2}$. For each $j\ge0$, the map $(x,y)\mapsto x\otimes y$ is continuous into $S_1(H)$, since [F2] and the triangle inequality give $$ \|x\otimes y-x'\otimes y'\|_1 \le \|x-x'\|_H\|y\|_H+\|x'\|_H\|y-y'\|_H. $$ Likewise $(x,y)\mapsto x\boxtimes y$ is continuous into $K$ by [F5]. Strong simple approximants to $X_0$ and $X_j$ therefore make both tensor-valued maps strongly measurable. Their norms have expectations at most $(\mathbb E\|X_0\|^2)^{1/2}(\mathbb E\|X_j\|^2)^{1/2}=\sigma^2$ by Cauchy–Schwarz and stationarity. [F1, F2, F3, F5, algebra]

Fix $j\ge1$ and put $Z_j=X_{j,j-1}$. For any $h,g\in H$, the scalar maps $x\mapsto\langle x,g\rangle_H$ and $y\mapsto\langle h,y\rangle_H$ are continuous. By [F1] and [F4] their values at $X_0$ and $Z_j$ are independent, and the first has mean zero. The bounded linear functional $L_{h,g}(T)=\langle Th,g\rangle_H$ on $S_1(H)$ commutes with Bochner integration by [F2]–[F3], so $$ L_{h,g}(\mathbb E_B[X_0\otimes Z_j]) =\mathbb E[\langle h,Z_j\rangle_H\langle X_0,g\rangle_H]=0. $$ For each $h$, taking $g=\mathbb E_B[X_0\otimes Z_j]h$ shows that this vector has zero squared norm, so $\mathbb E_B[X_0\otimes Z_j]=0$; reversing the tensor factors gives $\mathbb E_B[Z_j\otimes X_0]=0$ as well. For the kernel expectation, pair $\mathbb E_B[X_0\boxtimes Z_j]$ with any product kernel $g\boxtimes h$. By [F3] and [F5], the scalar pairing is $\mathbb E[\langle X_0,g\rangle_H\langle Z_j,h\rangle_H]$, which is zero by independence and centering. Such product kernels span a dense subspace of $K$ by [F5], so $\mathbb E_B[X_0\boxtimes Z_j]=0$; similarly $\mathbb E_B[Z_j\boxtimes X_0]=0$. [F1, F2, F3, F4, F5]

By step 1.2, stationarity, and [F1], for every $j\ge1$, $$ \begin{aligned} \|\mathbb E_B[X_0\otimes X_j]\|_1 &=\|\mathbb E_B[X_0\otimes(X_j-Z_j)]\|_1\\ &\le \mathbb E[\|X_0\|_H\|X_j-Z_j\|_H]\le\sigma\delta_{j-1}. \end{aligned} $$ The same bound holds for $\mathbb E_B[X_j\otimes X_0]$. It also holds for $\|\kappa_j\|_K$ and $\|\widetilde\kappa_j\|_K$ by [F3] and [F5]. Since $\delta_0\le2\sigma$ and $\sum_{m\ge1}\delta_m<\infty$, both series of trace-class terms and product-kernel terms are absolutely summable. The Banach property of $S_1(H)$ in [F2] and the Hilbert completeness of $K$ in [A1], [F5] give their norm limits. [A1, F1, F2, F3, F5, step 1.2]

For $n\ge1$, set $S_n=\sum_{t=1}^nX_t$ and $\Gamma_n=n^{-1}\mathbb E_B[S_n\otimes S_n]$. Step 1.1 makes this Bochner expectation well-defined. It is positive and self-adjoint because for every $h\in H$, $$ \langle\Gamma_n h,h\rangle_H=n^{-1}\mathbb E\langle S_n,h\rangle_H^2\ge0. $$ Expanding the finite sum and using stationarity gives $$ \Gamma_n=\mathbb E_B[X_0\otimes X_0] +\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}\left(1-\frac jn\right) \left(\mathbb E_B[X_0\otimes X_j]+\mathbb E_B[X_j\otimes X_0]\right). $$ Absolute summability from step 2.1 implies $\Gamma_n\to\Gamma$ in trace norm: for any fixed finite lag cutoff the coefficients tend to $1$, and the remaining trace-norm tail is uniformly bounded by the tail of the absolutely convergent series. Since $\|T\|\le\|T\|_1$, positivity and self-adjointness pass to the limit. Thus $\Gamma$ is positive self-adjoint and trace class. [F1, F2, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

For $f,g\in H$, define the bounded linear functional $\Lambda_{f,g}(k)=\langle T_k f,g\rangle_H$ on $K$; [F5] gives $|\Lambda_{f,g}(k)|\le\|k\|_K\|f\|_H\|g\|_H$. For each $j\ge0$, [F5] and [F3] therefore give $$ \Lambda_{f,g}(\kappa_j) =\mathbb E\langle (X_0\otimes X_j)f,g\rangle_H =\langle (\mathbb E_B[X_0\otimes X_j])f,g\rangle_H, $$ and the same identity holds for the reversed terms. Passing to the absolutely convergent kernel and trace-norm series in step 2.1 yields $\langle T_c f,g\rangle_H=\langle\Gamma f,g\rangle_H$ for every $f,g$. Hence $T_c=\Gamma$, and $c$ is exactly the design's $L^2$ covariance-kernel equivalence class. [F2, F3, F5, step 2.1] ∎

source_guards.exact_current_claim: Fix a separable real Hilbert space $H$ and an integer $k\ge1$. The rule in [[alg-geometric-median-of-block-means]] defines a single-valued Borel map $H^k\to H$: for every tuple $(m_1,\ldots,m_k)$ the function $F_m(z)=\sum_{j=1}^k\|z-m_j\|$ has a nonempty closed convex minimizer set, and that set has a unique point of minimum norm. The choice-free Borel construction below does not use weak compactness or reflexivity. Countable Choice is used only for the published Hilbert projection supplier that identifies the minimum-norm point.

current_steps.exact_text: Let $V=\operatorname{span}\{m_1,\ldots,m_k\}$. In the given center order, Gram–Schmidt replaces $m_j$ by $r_j=m_j-\sum_{\ell<j}\langle m_j,e_\ell\rangle e_\ell$ using the previously retained orthonormal vectors; if $r_j=0$ it is skipped, and otherwise $e=r_j/\|r_j\|$ is appended. Induction on the finite list shows the retained vectors are orthonormal and span $V$. For $d=\dim V>0$, if $v_n=\sum_{\ell=1}^d a_{n\ell}e_\ell\in V$ converges in $H$ to $v$, then [F4] gives $a_{n\ell}=\langle v_n,e_\ell\rangle\to\langle v,e_\ell\rangle$ for each $\ell$; the finite sums converge to $\sum_\ell\langle v,e_\ell\rangle e_\ell=v$, so $V$ is closed. If $d=0$, all centers are zero and $F_m(z)=k\|z\|$ has the unique minimizer $0$. For $d>0$, set $P_Vz=\sum_\ell\langle z,e_\ell\rangle e_\ell$; its residual is orthogonal to $V$. Pythagoras gives $\|z-m_j\|^2=\|P_Vz-m_j\|^2+\|z-P_Vz\|^2$, so $F_m(P_Vz)<F_m(z)$ whenever $z\notin V$. Thus every minimizer lies in $V$. The function $F_m$ is continuous and coercive because $F_m(z)\ge k\|z\|-\sum_j\|m_j\|$; its sublevel set $\{z\in V:F_m(z)\le F_m(0)\}$ is nonempty, closed and bounded in the finite-dimensional coordinate space $\mathbb R^d$, hence compact by [F3]. By [F5], $F_m$ attains a minimum there; the full minimizer set $C_m$ is nonempty, closed, bounded and compact, and it is convex because $F_m$ is convex. [F1, F3, F4, F5, algebra]

By [F2], $C_m$ has a unique point $z_*(m)$ nearest to $0$, its unique minimum-norm point. Fix a countable dense sequence $(d_a)_{a\ge1}$ in $H$. For $\lambda>0$, $G_{\lambda,m}(z)=F_m(z)+\lambda\|z\|^2$ is continuous, coercive and strictly convex. Projection to $V$ cannot increase $F_m$ and strictly decreases the squared norm off $V$, so every minimizer lies in $V$; if $d=0$ the single candidate is $0$. For $d>0$, a closed bounded sublevel set in $V$ is compact by [F3], so [F5] gives a unique minimizer $z_\lambda(m)$. By continuity and density, $h_\lambda(m)=\inf_aG_{\lambda,m}(d_a)=G_{\lambda,m}(z_\lambda(m))$. Each map $m\mapsto G_{\lambda,m}(d_a)$ is continuous, so [F7] makes their countable infimum $h_\lambda$ Borel. For $s\ge1$, the sets $A_{a,s}=\{m:G_{\lambda,m}(d_a)<h_\lambda(m)+1/s\}$ are Borel; at least one contains each $m$ by density, and the least such $a$ is a Borel, countably-valued map because its level set at $a$ is $A_{a,s}\setminus\bigcup_{b<a}A_{b,s}$. The selected point is within $(\lambda s)^{-1/2}$ of $z_\lambda(m)$: convexity of $F_m$ and $\|(1-t)z+ty\|^2=(1-t)\|z\|^2+t\|y\|^2-t(1-t)\|y-z\|^2$, applied at the minimizer and followed by $t\downarrow0$, give $G_{\lambda,m}(y)-G_{\lambda,m}(z_\lambda)\ge\lambda\|y-z_\lambda\|^2$. Hence the selected maps converge pointwise to $z_\lambda$. To see the limit is Borel, for each dense center $d_a$ the scalar distances from the selected maps to $d_a$ are Borel and converge to $\|z_\lambda-d_a\|$; [F7] makes these limits Borel. Balls with centers $d_a$ and positive rational radii form a countable basis of the separable metric space $H$: every open neighborhood of a point contains such a ball around a sufficiently close dense center. Thus inverse images of open sets are countable unions of Borel inverse images of these balls, proving $m\mapsto z_\lambda(m)$ is Borel. [F1, F2, F3, F5, F7, construct]

$$q_t(x)=\frac{\mathbf1_S(x)p_t(x)}{(1-\alpha_t)p_0(x)}\quad\text{on }S,\qquad q_t(x)=0\quad\text{on }S^c.$$

Then $q_t$ is a probability density relative to $P$. With $L_n=\prod_{i=1}^nq_{t_n}(X_i)$ and $\Delta_n=n^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^ns(X_i)$,

$$\left\|P_{t_n}^{\otimes n}-L_nP^{\otimes n}\right\|_{\rm TV}\longrightarrow0,\qquad \log L_n=h\Delta_n-\tfrac12h^2I+o_P(1),\qquad \Delta_n\Rightarrow N(0,I).$$

Since $P(B_t)\to0$ and $s^2$ is integrable, truncating $s^2$ at a fixed bound and then increasing that bound shows $P[s^2\mathbf1_{B_t}]\to0$. Thus $\beta_t:=P(p_t=0)=P(B_t)=o(t^2)$. Since $Pq_t=1$ and $q_t=(1+Y_t/2)^2$ $P$-almost surely, linearity [F10] expands this normalization identity to $PY_t=-\frac14P[Y_t^2]$. By [F2], [F3], and step 2.1, $P[Y_t^2]=t^2I+o(t^2)$, so $PY_t=-\frac14t^2I+o(t^2)$. [F2, F3, F10, step 2.1, algebra]

current_steps.exact_text: For positive bounded $U$ bounded away from zero, define $\operatorname{Ent}(U)=E[U\log U]-EU\log EU$. The function $\Phi(u,a)=u\log(u/a)-u+a$ is jointly convex: its Hessian quadratic form is $(du-(u/a)da)^2/u\ge0$. Direct differentiation in $a$ gives $\operatorname{Ent}(U)=\inf_{a>0}E\Phi(U,a)$, attained at $a=EU$. If $E_i$ integrates coordinate $i$, the product identity $\operatorname{Ent}(U)=E_{-i}\operatorname{Ent}_i(U)+\operatorname{Ent}_{-i}(E_iU)$ is obtained by adding and subtracting $E[(E_iU)\log(E_iU)]$. Joint convexity gives $\operatorname{Ent}_j(E_iU)\le E_i\operatorname{Ent}_j(U)$ for $j\ne i$: apply Jensen to $\Phi(E_iU,E_iE_jU)$ and integrate coordinate $j$. Induction in the product identity proves tensorization $\operatorname{Ent}(U)\le E\sum_i\operatorname{Ent}_i(U)$. All integrations here are on finite product laws. [F1, F2, F3, algebra]

Let $Z_i'$ replace $X_i$ by an independent copy and put $V_+=\sum_i E_i'(Z-Z_i')_+^2$. Jensen for the logarithm gives $\operatorname{Ent}_i(e^{tZ})\le\operatorname{Cov}_i(e^{tZ},tZ)$ for $t>0$. A fresh-copy expansion expresses this covariance as $\frac t2E_{i,i'}[(e^{tZ}-e^{tZ_i'})(Z-Z_i')]$. Swap the two copies to restrict to $Z>Z_i'$ and use $1-e^{-ta}\le ta$ for $a\ge0$. Tensorization from step 1.1 then yields $\operatorname{Ent}(e^{tZ})\le t^2E[e^{tZ}V_+]$. Choose the first maximizing function $f_*$ for $Z$ in a fixed finite ordering. Since $Z-Z_i'\le f_*(X_i)-f_*(X_i')$, the bound $(a-b)^2\le2a^2+2b^2$ gives $V_+\le2W+2ns^2$. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

Use the conditional variational formula of step 1.1 with comparator $e^{aW_i}$, which is independent of coordinate $i$. With $\psi(u)=e^u-u-1$, it gives $\operatorname{Ent}_i(e^{aW})\le E_i[e^{aW}\psi(-a\Delta_i)]$. Convexity and $\psi(0)=0$ imply $\psi(-a\Delta_i)\le(\Delta_i/c)\psi(-ac)$. Otherwise differentiating $L(a)/(e^{ac}-1)$ shows it is nonincreasing; its limit at zero is $m/c$. Thus $L(a)\le(m/c)(e^{ac}-1)\le2am$ whenever $0\le ac\le1/2$, where the last scalar inequality follows by integrating $e^u\le2$ on $[0,1/2]$. [F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

Consequently $\Gamma(R)\subseteq\Gamma(2R)$, and $K_{i_0}=\Gamma(Q)$ is nonempty with the required radius. The three exceptional events in steps 2.1 and 2.2 have total probability at most $3e^{-x}\le3(\delta/2)^2\le\delta$, because $\varepsilon N\ge2560\log(2/\delta)$ and $0<\delta<1$. This proves the proposition simultaneously for every admissible replacement of the clean samples. [F4, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, algebra] ∎

Assume AC and Countable Choice. Let $\psi$ be pathwise differentiable at $P$ with tangent space $\mathcal T$ and canonical gradient $\phi_{\rm can}\in\mathcal T^k$, and write $V_{\rm can}=P[\phi_{\rm can}\phi_{\rm can}^T]$. If $\mathcal T\ne\{0\}$, suppose a directed family of finite-dimensional, dominated QMD models $\{P_{\gamma,\theta}:\theta\in\Theta_\gamma\subseteq\mathbb R^{d_\gamma}\}$, with each $\Theta_\gamma$ open and $P_{\gamma,\theta_{\gamma,0}}=P$, has score spans $\mathcal S_\gamma\subseteq\mathcal T$ whose union is dense in $\mathcal T$. In each model let $S_\gamma\in L^2_0(P)^{d_\gamma}$ be a score basis, let $I_\gamma=P[S_\gamma S_\gamma^T]$ be nonsingular, and let $D_\gamma=P[\phi_{\rm can}S_\gamma^T]$. Assume for each fixed $h\in\mathbb R^{d_\gamma}$ that $\sqrt n\{\psi(P_{\gamma,\theta_{\gamma,0}+h/\sqrt n})-\psi(P)\}\to D_\gamma h$, and that under each local law the centered estimator $\sqrt n\{\widehat\psi_n-\psi(P_{\gamma,\theta_{\gamma,0}+h/\sqrt n})\}$ converges to one common law $L$, independent of $\gamma$ and $h$. Suppose $L$ has finite covariance. By [[thm-qmd-implies-lan-for-iid]], each model has the required LAN proxy; [[lem-finite-dimensional-functional-convolution-bound]] then applies with derivative matrix $D_\gamma$. If $\mathcal T=\{0\}$, no submodel family is needed. Then

$$\operatorname{Cov}(L)\succeq V_{\rm can}.$$

This is a lower bound for general regular estimators; asymptotic linearity is not assumed.

current_steps.exact_text: For any $a\in\mathbb R^k$, the projection of $a^T\phi_{\rm can}$ onto $\mathcal S$ is $a^TDI^{-1}S$: its residual has inner product $a^TD-a^TDI^{-1}P[SS^T]=0$ with every linear combination of the score coordinates. Therefore the covariance matrix of the projected gradient is $DI^{-1}D^T$. [A2, F1, given, algebra]

By [F2] and [[thm-qmd-implies-lan-for-iid]], this finite-dimensional submodel has the required LAN proxy and total-variation control. The regularity premise in the statement and [F4] give $L\stackrel d=G_\gamma+W_\gamma$, where $G_\gamma\sim N_k(0,DI^{-1}D^T)$ is independent of $W_\gamma$. Since $L$ has finite covariance and $G_\gamma$ does, $W_\gamma$ has finite covariance as well; independence yields $\operatorname{Cov}(L)=DI^{-1}D^T+\operatorname{Cov}(W_\gamma)\succeq DI^{-1}D^T$. [A1, F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, given]

If $\mathcal T=\{0\}$, then $\phi_{\rm can}=0$ and $\operatorname{Cov}(L)\succeq0=V_{\rm can}$. Otherwise fix $a\in\mathbb R^k$ and $\varepsilon>0$. Density of the union of the $\mathcal S_\gamma$ in $\mathcal T$ provides an index $\gamma$ and $g\in\mathcal S_\gamma$ with $\|g-a^T\phi_{\rm can}\|_{L^2(P)}<\varepsilon$. The projection formula in step 1.1 is orthogonal, so for any $g\in\mathcal S_\gamma$, $\|a^T\phi_{\rm can}-g\|_2^2=\|a^T\phi_{\rm can}-\Pi_{\mathcal S_\gamma}(a^T\phi_{\rm can})\|_2^2+\|\Pi_{\mathcal S_\gamma}(a^T\phi_{\rm can})-g\|_2^2$. Thus the projection error is below $\varepsilon$, and the quadratic forms $a^TD_\gamma I_\gamma^{-1}D_\gamma^Ta$ approach $a^TV_{\rm can}a$ as $\varepsilon\downarrow0$. [F1, step 1.1, given, choose, algebra]

When $\mathcal T\ne\{0\}$, step 2.1 gives $a^T\operatorname{Cov}(L)a\ge a^TD_\gamma I_\gamma^{-1}D_\gamma^Ta$ for every $\gamma$. Take the approximation in step 2.2 with arbitrarily small $\varepsilon$ to obtain $a^T\operatorname{Cov}(L)a\ge a^TV_{\rm can}a$. Since this holds for every $a$, $\operatorname{Cov}(L)\succeq V_{\rm can}$. Together with the zero-tangent case in step 2.2, this proves the claim. [step 2.1, step 2.2, algebra] ∎

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H=L^2([0,1],dt;\mathbb R)$ and let
$(X_t)_{t\in\mathbb Z}$ be a centered, $L^2$-$m$-approximable causal
Bernoulli shift as defined in
[[def-l2-m-approximable-causal-bernoulli-shift]], with Bochner mean
$\mathbb E_BX_0=0$. Let $\Gamma$ be its long-run covariance operator from
[[lem-long-run-covariance-is-trace-class]], and let $G$ be a centered
$H$-valued Gaussian random element with covariance $\Gamma$, whose existence
is given by [[lem-positive-trace-class-covariance-defines-hilbert-gaussian]].
Then, for $S_n=\sum_{t=1}^nX_t$,
$$n^{-1/2}S_n\ \Rightarrow\ G$$
in the weak topology of Borel probability measures on $H$. The covariance
kernel is the $L^2([0,1]^2)$ equivalence class $c$ in the long-run covariance
lemma, and its integral operator is $T_c=\Gamma$. This is a CLT for the
$H$-valued sample sums; it is not a functional CLT for the time-indexed
partial-sum process.

current_steps.exact_text: Put $\sigma=\|X_0\|_{L^2(H)}$ and $D_{t,m}=X_t-X_{t,m}$ for $m\ge1$. Both terms have the same centered law, so $D_{t,m}$ is centered. For $h\ge1$, $X_{h,h}$ is independent of $D_{0,m}$: its original inputs have indices $1,\ldots,h$, while $D_{0,m}$ uses original indices at most $0$ and its own replacement array; $X_{h,h}$ uses a distinct independent replacement array. It has the centered law of $X_0$, so [F10] gives $\mathbb E\langle D_{0,m},X_{h,h}\rangle_H=0$. Also $\|X_h-X_{h,h}\|_{L^2(H)}=\delta_h$. Hence Cauchy--Schwarz gives $$|\mathbb E\langle D_{0,m},X_h\rangle_H| =|\mathbb E\langle D_{0,m},X_h-X_{h,h}\rangle_H| \le\delta_m\delta_h.$$ If $h\ge m$, the original inputs of $X_{h,m}$ have indices $h-m+1,\ldots,h$, all positive, and its replacement array is independent of the coordinates in $D_{0,m}$; hence it is independent of $D_{0,m}$ and centered. [F10] gives $\mathbb E\langle D_{0,m},X_{h,m}\rangle_H=0$. If $1\le h<m$, its marginal second moment is $\sigma^2$, giving $|\mathbb E\langle D_{0,m},X_{h,m}\rangle_H|\le\delta_m\sigma$. Therefore $$|\mathbb E\langle D_{0,m},D_{h,m}\rangle_H| \le\begin{cases}\delta_m(\delta_h+\sigma),&1\le h<m,\\ \delta_m\delta_h,&h\ge m.\end{cases}$$ Stationarity makes the negative-lag inner products equal to the corresponding positive-lag ones. Expanding the squared norm of the normalized sum and bounding each finite-lag weight by one yields, for $U_n=n^{-1/2}S_n$ and $U_n^{(m)}=n^{-1/2}\sum_{t=1}^nX_{t,m}$, $$\sup_n\mathbb E\|U_n-U_n^{(m)}\|_H^2 \le\delta_m^2+2\delta_m\sum_{h\ge1}\delta_h+2\sigma(m-1)\delta_m.$$ The $m=1$ empty middle-lag sum is zero. [F1, F9, F10, given, algebra]

Since $\sum_{m\ge1}\delta_m<\infty$, $\liminf_{m\to\infty}m\delta_m=0$: otherwise $\delta_m\ge c/m$ eventually for some $c>0$, contradicting summability. Recursively choose strictly increasing integers $m_r$ with $m_r\delta_{m_r}<1/r$; the least eligible integer at each stage exists by the liminf statement. Thus the right side of step 1.1 tends to zero along $m=m_r$. Write $\varepsilon_m$ for its square root. For each fixed $K$, the covariance matrices of $P_KU_n$ are bounded because $\operatorname{Cov}(U_n)=\Gamma_n$ and [F2] bounds $\operatorname{tr}(P_K\Gamma_nP_K)$. For any $v\in P_KH$, the scalar variance difference satisfies $$|\mathbb E\langle U_n^{(m)}-\mathbb EU_n^{(m)},v\rangle_H^2 -\mathbb E\langle U_n,v\rangle_H^2| \le\|v\|_H^2\varepsilon_m(2M_K+\varepsilon_m),$$ where $M_K=\sup_n(\mathbb E\|P_KU_n\|_H^2)^{1/2}<\infty$; this follows from $|a^2-b^2|\le|a-b|(|a|+|b|)$ and [F9]. [A1, F2, F9, step 1.1, choose, algebra]

For fixed $m$ and $K$, the coordinate vectors $(\langle X_{t,m},e_1\rangle_H,\ldots,\langle X_{t,m},e_K\rangle_H)_t$ are centered, stationary, $m$-dependent and square-integrable in $\mathbb R^K$; they identify $P_KX_{t,m}$ isometrically with $P_KH$. By [F4], their normalized sums converge to a centered Gaussian with covariance matrix $\Sigma_{m,K}=\sum_{|j|\le m}\operatorname{Cov}(P_KX_{0,m},P_KX_{j,m})$. The finite covariance expansion shows $\operatorname{Cov}(P_KU_n^{(m)})=\sum_{|j|\le m}(1-|j|/n)_+\, \operatorname{Cov}(P_KX_{0,m},P_KX_{j,m})\to\Sigma_{m,K}$; terms with $|j|>m$ vanish by $m$-dependence, and each of the finitely many coefficients tends to one. Letting $n\to\infty$ in step 2.1 and using [F2] gives $$\|\Sigma_{m,K}-P_K\Gamma P_K\|_{op} \le\varepsilon_m(2M_K+\varepsilon_m).$$ In particular $\Sigma_{m_r,K}\to P_K\Gamma P_K$. Because these operators are symmetric and finite-dimensional, their operator norm is the supremum of the absolute quadratic form over unit vectors. For each real $v\in P_KH$, [F11] therefore gives convergence of the characteristic functions of the scalar projections of $N(0,\Sigma_{m_r,K})$ to that of $N(0,P_K\Gamma P_K)$; [F5] and Cramér--Wold give convergence of these finite-dimensional Gaussian laws. [F2, F3, F4, F5, F11, step 2.1, algebra]

For $a\in P_KH$, compare the characteristic functions of $\langle U_n,a\rangle_H$ and $\langle U_n^{(m)},a\rangle_H$. The inequality $|e^{ix}-e^{iy}|\le|x-y|$ and step 1.1 bound their difference by $\|a\|_H\varepsilon_m$. For each fixed $m$, [F4] gives the limit law of the second projection; along $m=m_r$, step 3.1 and [F11] make those Gaussian limit laws converge to $N(0,\langle\Gamma a,a\rangle_H)$. Taking first $n\to\infty$ and then $r\to\infty$ proves convergence of the characteristic functions of $\langle U_n,a\rangle_H$ to that normal law. Explicitly, their limsup difference from the target characteristic function is at most $$\|a\|_H\varepsilon_m+ \left|e^{-\langle\Sigma_{m,K}a,a\rangle_H/2} -e^{-\langle\Gamma a,a\rangle_H/2}\right|,$$ which tends to zero along $m=m_r$ by steps 1.1 and 3.1. Since $a$ ranges over all vectors, for any fixed projection direction $b$ this also gives its characteristic-function convergence at every frequency $t$ by taking $a=tb$. Thus [F5] and Cramér--Wold give $$P_KU_n\Rightarrow P_KG$$ for every fixed $K$, since $G$ has covariance $\Gamma$. [F4, F5, F11, step 1.1, step 3.1, algebra]

Let $R_K=I-P_K$ and $\alpha_K=(\mathbb E\|R_KX_0\|_H^2)^{1/2}$. Completeness of the eigenbasis and Parseval give $R_KX_0\to0$ almost surely in $H$; the bound $\|R_KX_0\|_H^2\le\|X_0\|_H^2$ and [F6] imply $\alpha_K\to0$. For $h\ge1$, $X_0$ is independent of $X_{h,h-1}$ by [F1]; bounded linear projection preserves independence and centering, so [F10] gives $\mathbb E\langle R_KX_0,R_KX_{h,h-1}\rangle_H=0$. Hence $$|\mathbb E\langle R_KX_0,R_KX_h\rangle_H| =|\mathbb E\langle R_KX_0,R_K(X_h-X_{h,h-1})\rangle_H| \le\alpha_K\delta_{h-1}.$$ Expanding the variance of $R_KU_n$ and using [F9] now gives $$\sup_n\mathbb E\|R_KU_n\|_H^2 \le\alpha_K^2+2\alpha_K\left(\delta_0+\sum_{m\ge1}\delta_m\right)\longrightarrow0.$$ Also [F3], [F3a] and the covariance of $G$ give $\mathbb E\|R_KG\|_H^2=\sum_{k>K}\lambda_k\to0$; if the basis is finite, take $P_K=I$ once all basis vectors are included. [F1, F3, F6, F9, F10, step 4.1, algebra]

Let $\phi:H\to\mathbb R$ be bounded and uniformly continuous, with $M=\sup_x|\phi(x)|$. For $\eta>0$ put $\omega_\phi(\eta)=\sup_{\|x-y\|\le\eta}|\phi(x)-\phi(y)|$, which tends to zero as $\eta\downarrow0$. Markov's inequality [F7] and step 5.1 imply $$|\mathbb E\phi(U_n)-\mathbb E\phi(P_KU_n)| \le\omega_\phi(\eta)+2M\eta^{-2}\sup_n\mathbb E\|R_KU_n\|_H^2,$$ and the same bound for $G$ and $P_KG$ with $\mathbb E\|R_KG\|_H^2$. For fixed $K$, step 4.1 gives $\mathbb E\phi(P_KU_n)\to\mathbb E\phi(P_KG)$. First let $K\to\infty$ in these inequalities and then let $\eta\downarrow0$. It follows that $\mathbb E\phi(U_n)\to\mathbb E\phi(G)$ for every bounded uniformly continuous $\phi$. By [F8], $U_n\Rightarrow G$ in the Borel weak topology of $H$. The kernel assertion is the conclusion of the long-run covariance lemma; the theorem asserts no time-indexed process convergence. [F7, F8, step 4.1, step 5.1] ∎

source_guards.exact_current_claim: For any fixed sample $x\in\mathbb R^n$, the sample mean $\bar x=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n x_i$ has finite-sample replacement breakdown fraction $1/n$. If $n=2r+1$ is odd and the conventional sample median is the $(r+1)$-st order statistic, its finite-sample replacement breakdown fraction is $(r+1)/n=\lfloor(n+1)/2\rfloor/n$.

current_steps.exact_text: With no replacements the mean displacement is zero. Replacing coordinate $i$ by $M$ changes the sample mean to $\bar x+(M-x_i)/n$, whose displacement is unbounded as $M\to+\infty$. Thus the smallest breaking count for the mean is one, and [F1] gives $1/n$. [given, F1, algebra]

Let $n=2r+1$. If at most $r$ coordinates are replaced, at least $r+1$ original observations remain. Writing $x_{\min}=\min_i x_i$ and $x_{\max}=\max_i x_i$, at least $r+1$ resulting observations are at most $x_{\max}$ and at least $r+1$ are at least $x_{\min}$. Therefore the $(r+1)$-st order statistic lies in $[x_{\min},x_{\max}]$, so its displacement from the original median is bounded uniformly over all such replacements. [given, F1, algebra]

Replace $r+1$ coordinates by the same value $M>x_{\max}$. The $r$ unchanged observations are the first $r$ order statistics and the $r+1$ copies of $M$ occupy positions $r+1$ through $2r+1$. The median is therefore $M$, which is unbounded as $M\to+\infty$. [given, algebra]
Steps 1.2–1.3 show that the smallest breaking count for the odd-sample median is $r+1$. By [F1] its breakdown fraction is $(r+1)/(2r+1)=\lfloor(n+1)/2\rfloor/n$. [step 1.2, step 1.3, F1, algebra] ∎

Let $X$ be an absolutely continuous random vector in $\mathbb R^d$ with mean $\mu$ and finite covariance matrix $\Sigma$ as defined in [[lem-finite-covariance-matrix-basic-properties]]. Set $\varepsilon=\max\{10\eta,2560\log(2/\delta)/N\}$ and let $\widehat\mu$ be the repaired, total selector in [[alg-multivariate-trimmed-mean]]. Then there is a universal constant $c>0$ such that
$$
P\!\left(\|\widehat\mu-\mu\|\le c\left[\sqrt{\frac{\operatorname{tr}\Sigma}{N}}+\sqrt{\frac{\lambda_{\max}(\Sigma)\log(1/\delta)}{N}}+\sqrt{\lambda_{\max}(\Sigma)\eta}\right]\right)\ge1-\delta.
$$
The claim is restricted to the displayed domain, which ensures $\varepsilon\le1$. No guarantee is asserted for $1/10<\eta<1/2$, for $\eta\ge1/2$, or for atomic laws.

current_steps.exact_text: If $\operatorname{tr}\Sigma>0$, [F1] supplies, with probability at least $1-\delta$, the nonempty correct-scale tail intersection of radius $16\varepsilon Q_0$. On that event [F2] at $b=16$ bounds the output of [F4] by exactly the displayed three-term rate, with universal constant $c_{16}$. The selector's measurability in [F4] makes the error event measurable. [F1, F2, F4, given]

If $\operatorname{tr}\Sigma=0$, [F3] gives exact recovery almost surely, so the error bound holds with probability one. These are the only cases by [F3], and the same positive constant $c_{16}$ works in both. Thus the claimed probability is at least $1-\delta$ throughout the stated domain. [F3, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

Let $X_1,\ldots,X_N,Y_1,\ldots,Y_N$ be $2N$ iid clean copies of $X$, and let $(\widetilde X_1,\ldots,\widetilde X_N,\widetilde Y_1,\ldots,\widetilde Y_N)$ be a sample-replacement version with at most $\lfloor2\eta N\rfloor$ changed coordinates in total ([[def-adversarial-sample-replacement]]). Let $0<\delta<1$, $\delta\ge e^{-N/4}$, and
$$
\varepsilon=8\eta+\frac{12\log(4/\delta)}{N}\in(0,1/4].
$$
Apply [[alg-univariate-trimmed-mean]] with these parameters. For the centered variable $Z=X-\mu$, define, for $0<u\le1$,
$$
Q_u(Z)=\sup\{t\in\mathbb R:P(Z\ge t)\ge1-u\},
$$
and
$$
E(u,X)=\max\left\{E\bigl[|Z|\mathbf1_{\{Z\le Q_{u/2}(Z)\}}\bigr],\ E\bigl[|Z|\mathbf1_{\{Z\ge Q_{1-u/2}(Z)\}}\bigr]\right\}.
$$
Here $E$ is the raw centered-tail functional, distinct from the excess-tail lower-bound functional. The claims are
$$
P\!\left(|\widehat\mu-\mu|\le3E(4\varepsilon,X)+2\sigma\sqrt{\frac{\log(4/\delta)}{N}}\right)\ge1-\delta
$$
and
$$
P\!\left(|\widehat\mu-\mu|\le10\sqrt{\varepsilon}\,\sigma\right)\ge1-4e^{-\varepsilon N/12}.
$$

current_steps.exact_text: For every $p\in(0,1)$, $|q_p|\le\sigma/\sqrt{\min(p,1-p)}$: if $q_p\ge0$, use $\sigma^2\ge q_p^2P(Z\ge q_p)$; if $q_p<0$, use $\sigma^2\ge q_p^2P(Z\le q_p)$. Also $T$ is nondecreasing, since its tail sets expand with $u$, and $T(4\varepsilon)\le\sigma\sqrt{2\varepsilon}$ by Cauchy--Schwarz and the exact tail masses. For a lower clipping endpoint $a=q_p$ with $p\le1/2$, put $L=E[|Z|\mathbf1_{\{Z\le a\}}]$. If $a\le0$, $E[(a-Z)\mathbf1_{\{Z\le a\}}]\le L$. If $a>0$, centering implies $a(1-p)\le E[Z\mathbf1_{\{Z>a\}}]=-E[Z\mathbf1_{\{Z\le a\}}]\le L$; hence $ap\le L$ and the clipping excess is at most $2L$. The symmetric upper-endpoint argument is identical. A deterministic clip $W=\phi_{a,b}(Z)$ has $\operatorname{Var}W\le E[(W-\phi_{a,b}(0))^2]\le\sigma^2$, because clipping is 1-Lipschitz; its centered absolute bound is at most the interval width $b-a$. [F1, F4, given, algebra]

First use inner endpoints $q_{2\varepsilon},q_{1-2\varepsilon}$ and outer endpoints $q_{\varepsilon/2},q_{1-\varepsilon/2}$. Require each of the two inner clean $Y$ tail counts to exceed $N(\varepsilon+2\eta)$ and each outer count to be less than $N(\varepsilon-2\eta)$. Put $a=\eta/t\ge0$. Since $\varepsilon=(8a+12)t$, [F3] for the binomial counts bounds each inner failure by $\exp[-36(a+2)^2\ell/(36a+56)]\le e^{-18\ell/7}$, and each outer failure by $\exp[-(2a+6)^2\ell/((28/3)a+16)]\le e^{-9\ell/4}$. The two rational functions are increasing for $a\ge0$, as direct differentiation shows, so their minima are their values at zero. Thus all four count conditions hold outside probability $4e^{-9\ell/4}\le\delta/2$, since $\ell>\log4$. After $M\le2\eta N$ changes the inner counts are still strictly greater than $\varepsilon N$ and outer counts strictly less than $\varepsilon N$. Integer counts and the ranks $r_-=\lceil\varepsilon N\rceil$, $r_+=N-\lfloor\varepsilon N\rfloor$ therefore give $q_{\varepsilon/2}\le\alpha-\mu\le q_{2\varepsilon}$ and $q_{1-2\varepsilon}\le\beta-\mu\le q_{1-\varepsilon/2}$. For example fewer than $\varepsilon N$ values below an outer lower endpoint means at most $r_--1$ such values, while more than $\varepsilon N$ values above an inner upper endpoint means at least $\lfloor\varepsilon N\rfloor+1$ such values. These strict inequalities cover noninteger ranks and the integral boundary without a rounding loss. [F1, F2, F3, F4, algebra]

On the count event, monotonicity of clipping endpoints bounds the clean first-half clipped average above by the average of $W^+=\phi_{q_{2\varepsilon},q_{1-\varepsilon/2}}(Z)$ and below by the average of $W^-=\phi_{q_{\varepsilon/2},q_{1-2\varepsilon}}(Z)$. Step 1.1 bounds $EW^+\le2T(4\varepsilon)$ and $EW^-\ge-2T(4\varepsilon)$, their variances by $\sigma^2$, and their interval widths by $2\sqrt2\sigma/\sqrt\varepsilon$. These comparison variables have fixed endpoints, so their deviation events are functions of the clean $X$ half and do not rely on the corrupted cutoffs being independent of it. Their total exceptional probability is $2e^{-\ell}=\delta/2$. [F2, F3, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra]

Write $A=q_{\varepsilon/2}$, $B=q_{1-\varepsilon/2}$. Replacing at most $M$ first-half points changes the clipped average by at most $2\eta(B-A)\le(\varepsilon/4)(B-A)$. If $A\le0\le B$, $(\varepsilon/4)(B-A)\le\max\{(\varepsilon/2)|A|,(\varepsilon/2)|B|\}\le T(\varepsilon)$. If both endpoints are positive, use $B-A\le B$ and the same upper-tail bound; if both are negative, use $B-A\le|A|$ and its lower-tail bound. By monotonicity $T(\varepsilon)\le T(4\varepsilon)$. Combining this with step 2.1 and the two exceptional probabilities proves the first displayed bound with its exact constants $3$ and $2$, uniformly over every admissible sample-dependent replacement. [F1, F2, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1, algebra]

For the second bound put $s=\varepsilon N/12\ge\ell>\log4$ and keep the same inner quantiles but use wider outer endpoints $q_{\varepsilon/4},q_{1-\varepsilon/4}$. Use the same count thresholds $N(\varepsilon\pm2\eta)$. Since $2\eta\le\varepsilon/4$, the inner downward gap is at least $3\varepsilon/4$ from mean $2\varepsilon$, and the outer upward gap is at least $\varepsilon/2$ from mean $\varepsilon/4$. The function $u^2/(2(p+u/3))$ increases for $u>0$, so [F3] bounds each inner failure by $e^{-\varepsilon N/8}=e^{-3s/2}$ and each outer failure by $e^{-3\varepsilon N/10}=e^{-18s/5}$. The same strict rank argument of step 1.2 brackets the corrupted cutoffs. For the fixed comparison clips, step 1.1 gives directional bias at most $2T(4\varepsilon)\le2\sqrt2\sigma\sqrt\varepsilon$, variance at most $\sigma^2$ and width at most $4\sigma/\sqrt\varepsilon$. Bernstein at $a=s$ therefore bounds each directional clean-average noise by $(1/\sqrt6+2/9)\sigma\sqrt\varepsilon$. The replacement shift is at most $2\eta\cdot4\sigma/\sqrt\varepsilon\le\sigma\sqrt\varepsilon$. The total error is consequently at most $(2\sqrt2+1/\sqrt6+2/9+1)\sigma\sqrt\varepsilon<10\sigma\sqrt\varepsilon$. Its exceptional probability is at most $2e^{-3s/2}+2e^{-18s/5}+2e^{-s}\le4e^{-s}$, because the first two terms sum to at most $4e^{-3s/2}\le2e^{-s}$. This proves the second assertion. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

For $S\subseteq[p]$, let
$$G(S):=\{A=A^T\in\mathbb R^{p\times p}:A_{ij}=0 \text{ whenever }i\notin S\text{ or }j\notin S\},$$
and, for an integer $1\le s\le p$, let
$$G(s):=\bigcup_{\substack{S\subseteq[p]\\|S|\le s}}G(S),\qquad \mathcal F_{p,s}(M):=\{\Sigma\in\mathcal F_p(M): \Sigma-\operatorname{diag}(\Sigma)\in G(s)\}.$$
Here $\operatorname{diag}(\Sigma)$ is the diagonal matrix with the same
diagonal entries as $\Sigma$. Thus all nonzero off-diagonal entries lie in
one common coordinate block of size at most $s$; no row-sparsity condition
is implied.

For $S\subseteq[p]$, define
$$V_S:=\{u\in\mathbb R^p:\|u\|_2=1,\ u_i=0\text{ for }i\notin S\}.$$
When $1\le s\le p/2$, the restricted direction set is
$$U_s:=\bigcup_{\substack{S\subseteq[p]\\|S|=2s}}V_S.$$

For $M>0$ and $p\ge1$, define
$$\mathcal F_p(M):=\{\Sigma\in\mathbb R^{p\times p}: \Sigma=\Sigma^T,\ \Sigma\succeq0,\ \|\Sigma\|_{\rm op}\le M\}.$$
For positive semidefinite $\Sigma$, the operator norm is its largest
eigenvalue, so this is the bounded-spectrum covariance class.

Let $X=(X_1,\ldots,X_p)$ be a measurable random vector in $\mathbb R^p$,
where $p\ge1$ is finite, and assume $\mathbb E\|X\|_2^2<\infty$. Define
the mean coordinatewise by $\mu_j=\mathbb E X_j$ and define the covariance
matrix by
$$\Sigma:=\mathbb E[(X-\mu)(X-\mu)^T],$$
where each entry is the expectation of the corresponding real random
variable. Write $\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma)=\sum_{j=1}^p\Sigma_{jj}$.

The well-definedness lemma proves these expectations are finite,
$\Sigma$ is symmetric positive semidefinite, and
$\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma)=\mathbb E\|X-\mu\|_2^2$.

Let $p\ge1$, $0\le\epsilon\le1$, and let $\Sigma$ be a real positive
semidefinite $p\times p$ covariance matrix. For any Borel probability law
$Q$ on $\mathbb R^p$, define
$$P_{\epsilon,\Sigma,Q}:=(1-\epsilon)N_p(0,\Sigma)+\epsilon Q,$$
where $N_p(0,\Sigma)$ is the finite-dimensional Gaussian law from
[[def-multivariate-normal-law]]. A sample in this model consists of
independent observations with common law $P_{\epsilon,\Sigma,Q}$. The target
is the covariance $\Sigma$ of the uncontaminated Gaussian component, not the
covariance of the mixture.

This is the covariance specialization of the Huber model in
[[def-huber-contamination-model]]. It is distinct from a clean heavy-tail
moment model and from adversarial sample replacement.

For $p\ge1$, write $S^{p-1}:=\{u\in\mathbb R^p:\|u\|_2=1\}$. Let
$U$ be a nonempty subset of this sphere, let $P$ be a probability law on
$\mathbb R^p$, and let $\Gamma\succeq0$. Its **matrix depth relative to
$U$** is
$$D_U(\Gamma,P):=\inf_{u\in U}\min\left\{ P((u^TX)^2\le u^T\Gamma u),P((u^TX)^2\ge u^T\Gamma u)\right\},$$
where $X$ has law $P$. Both weak inequalities include ties.

For observations $x_1,\ldots,x_n$, let
$P_n=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n\delta_{x_i}$ be their empirical law. Let $\beta>0$
be the constant of [[lem-matrix-depth-gaussian-scale-constant-exists-uniquely]].
The **global dense** depth correspondence is $\operatorname{Argmax}_{\Gamma\succeq0}D_{S^{p-1}}(\Gamma,P_n)$, over symmetric positive semidefinite matrices. For $1\le s\le p/2$, define the global single-block class $\mathcal F_{p,s}:=\bigcup_{c>0}\mathcal F_{p,s}(c)$ and the **global single-block sparse** correspondence $\operatorname{Argmax}_{\Gamma\in\mathcal F_{p,s}}D_{U_s}(\Gamma,P_n)$. These are the unrestricted-spectrum versions; no known spectral bound is needed to define their selectors.

For known $M>0$, the dense bounded-class depth correspondence is
$$\operatorname{Argmax}_{\Gamma\in\mathcal F_p(\beta M)} D_{S^{p-1}}(\Gamma,P_n).$$
For known integer $1\le s\le p/2$, the single-block sparse version is
$$\operatorname{Argmax}_{\Gamma\in\mathcal F_{p,s}(\beta M)} D_{U_s}(\Gamma,P_n),$$
where the classes and $U_s$ are defined in
[[def-bounded-spectrum-covariance-class]] and
[[def-block-sparse-covariance-class]]. A **measurable matrix-depth estimator**
is a Borel measurable selector $\widehat\Gamma$ from the applicable argmax
correspondence, with covariance output $\widehat\Sigma=\widehat\Gamma/\beta$.
Either global correspondence or the applicable bounded-class correspondence may be used. The compact search restriction contains $\beta\Sigma$ whenever the target
belongs to the corresponding class; it makes no computational feasibility
claim.

For a random vector $X\in\mathbb R^p$ with mean $\mu$ and covariance
$\Sigma$ as in [[def-covariance-matrix-of-a-random-vector]], assume
$\mathbb E\|X-\mu\|_2^4<\infty$. Its **matrix variance** is
$$\sigma_0^2:=\left\|\mathbb E\!\left[\|X-\mu\|_2^2 (X-\mu)(X-\mu)^T\right]\right\|_{\rm op}.$$
When $\|\Sigma\|_{\rm op}>0$, define the intrinsic ratio
$$d:=\frac{\sigma_0^2}{\|\Sigma\|_{\rm op}^2}.$$

The expectation is entrywise. The finite fourth moment makes every entry
integrable. This definition imposes neither Huber contamination nor sample
replacement.
